en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.1 (SN 22.1, PTS SN iii 1) 1. Nakulapituvagga Nakulapitusutta Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, does identity arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do the six bases arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, does craving arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, does feeling arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, does contact arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do the six sense bases arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, does name-and-form arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, does consciousness arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do mental formations arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, does ignorance arise? “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and take recourse in the Blessed One. It would be good if the Blessed One would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from him, the bhikkhus will remember it. “Then listen, bhikkhus, and attend closely. I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when there is a self, by clinging to a self, with the arising of a self, identity arises. When there is a self, by clinging to a self, with the arising of a self, the six bases arise. When there is a self, by clinging to a self, with the arising of a self, craving arises. When there is a self, by clinging to a self, with the arising of a self, feeling arises. When there is a self, by clinging to a self, with the arising of a self, contact arises. When there is a self, by clinging to a self, with the arising of a self, the six sense bases arise. When there is a self, by clinging to a self, with the arising of a self, name-and-form arises. When there is a self, by clinging to a self, with the arising of a self, consciousness arises. When there is a self, by clinging to a self, with the arising of a self, mental formations arise. When there is a self, by clinging to a self, with the arising of a self, ignorance arises. “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘When there is a self, by clinging to a self, with the arising of a self, identity arises… with the arising of a self, ignorance arises. But, venerable sir, when what does not exist, by not clinging to what, with the cessation of what, does identity cease? When what does not exist, by not clinging to what, with the cessation of what, do the six bases cease? When what does not exist, by not clinging to what, with the cessation of what, does craving cease? When what does not exist, by not clinging to what, with the cessation of what, does feeling cease? When what does not exist, by not clinging to what, with the cessation of what, does contact cease? When what does not exist, by not clinging to what, with the cessation of what, do the six sense bases cease? When what does not exist, by not clinging to what, with the cessation of what, does name-and-form cease? When what does not exist, by not clinging to what, with the cessation of what, does consciousness cease? When what does not exist, by not clinging to what, with the cessation of what, do mental formations cease? When what does not exist, by not clinging to what, with the cessation of what, does ignorance cease? “Bhikkhus, when a self does not exist, by not clinging to a self, with the cessation of a self, identity ceases. When a self does not exist, by not clinging to a self, with the cessation of a self, the six bases cease. When a self does not exist, by not clinging to a self, with the cessation of a self, craving ceases. When a self does not exist, by not clinging to a self, with the cessation of a self, feeling ceases. When a self does not exist, by not clinging to a self, with the cessation of a self, contact ceases. When a self does not exist, by not clinging to a self, with the cessation of a self, the six sense bases cease. When a self does not exist, by not clinging to a self, with the cessation of a self, name-and-form ceases. When a self does not exist, by not clinging to a self, with the cessation of a self, consciousness ceases. When a self does not exist, by not clinging to a self, with the cessation of a self, mental formations cease. When a self does not exist, by not clinging to a self, with the cessation of a self, ignorance ceases. “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One:

‘When a self does not exist, by not clinging to a self, with the cessation of a self, identity ceases… with the cessation of a self, ignorance ceases. Venerable sir, suppose there were a house or a hall with a peaked roof, with windows on the eastern side, and the sun were to rise. Its eastern wall would cast a shadow over its interior, its northern wall would cast a shadow over its interior, and its southern wall would cast a shadow over its interior. But as the day goes by, the shadows of those walls would gradually recede and eventually disappear. So too, venerable sir, when a self does not exist, by not clinging to a self, with the cessation of a self, identity ceases… with the cessation of a self, ignorance ceases. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, does identity arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do the six bases arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, does craving arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, does feeling arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, does contact arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do the six sense bases arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, does name-and-form arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, does consciousness arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do mental formations arise? When what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, does ignorance arise? “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and take recourse in the Blessed One. It would be good if the Blessed One would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from him, the bhikkhus will remember it. “Then listen, bhikkhus, and attend closely. I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when there is form, by clinging to form, with the arising of form, identity arises. When there is form, by clinging to form, with the arising of form, the six bases arise. When there is form, by clinging to form, with the arising of form, craving arises. When there is form, by clinging to form, with the arising of form, feeling arises. When there is form, by clinging to form, with the arising of form, contact arises. When there is form, by clinging to form, with the arising of form, the six sense bases arise. When there is form, by clinging to form, with the arising of form, name-and-form arises. When there is form, by clinging to form, with the arising of form, consciousness arises. When there is form, by clinging to form, with the arising of form, mental formations arise. When there is form, by clinging to form, with the arising of form, ignorance arises. When there is feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness, by clinging to consciousness, with the arising of consciousness, identity arises. When there is consciousness, by clinging to consciousness, with the arising of consciousness, the six bases arise. When there is consciousness, by clinging to consciousness, with the arising of consciousness, craving arises. When there is consciousness, by clinging to consciousness, with the arising of consciousness, feeling arises. When there is consciousness, by clinging to consciousness, with the arising of consciousness, contact arises. Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas in the Deer Park at Bhesakalā Grove, near the village of Sumsumāragira.

Then the householder Nakulapitā approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the householder Nakulapitā said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I am old, aged, advanced in years, come to the last stage of life, afflicted in body, and constantly plagued by illness.
Yet, venerable sir, I am one who perceives impermanence regarding the Blessed One and the venerable monks who are dear to his heart.
May the Blessed One exhort me, venerable sir.”
“May the Blessed One instruct me, venerable sir,
so that it may be for my welfare and happiness for a long time.
“It is so, householder, it is so, householder.”
"Householder, this body is indeed afflicted, like an egg, enveloped in membranes.
For if, householder, one who maintains this body were to claim health even for a moment, what would that be other than folly?
Therefore, householder, you should train yourself thus:"
‘While my body is afflicted, may my mind remain unafflicted.
In this way, householder, you should train yourself.
Then Nakulapitā the householder, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat.
Having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, he approached the Venerable Sāriputta;
having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Sāriputta and sat down to one side.
As the householder Nakulapitā was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to him:
“Householder, your faculties are serene;
the color of your face is pure and bright.
Did you receive a discourse on the Dhamma from the Blessed One’s own presence today?”
“How could it not be so, Bhante?
Just now, Bhante, I have been anointed with the nectar of the Blessed One’s Dhamma talk.
“But in what way, householder, have you been anointed by the Blessed One with the nectar of the Dhamma talk?”
“Here, Bhante, I approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, I sat down to one side. Sitting there, Bhante, I said this to the Blessed One:
‘Bhante, I am old, aged, advanced in years, come to the last stage of life, with a body afflicted by illness, constantly subject to sickness.
Yet, Bhante, I am one who perceives impermanence in the Blessed One and in the venerable bhikkhus.’”
“May the Blessed One exhort me, venerable sir;
may the Blessed One instruct me, venerable sir,
so that it may be for my welfare and happiness for a long time.”
When this was said, venerable sir, the Blessed One said this to me:
“It is so, householder, it is so, householder.
This body, householder, is diseased, a mere heap of boils, wrapped in skin.”
For if, householder, one who maintains this body were to claim health even for a moment, what could that be other than folly?
Therefore, householder, you should train yourself in this way:
"Though my body is afflicted, my mind shall remain unafflicted."
“In this way, householder, you should train yourself.
“In this way, venerable sir, I have been anointed by the Blessed One with the nectar of a Dhamma talk.
“But, householder, did it not occur to you to ask the Blessed One further?”
“In what way, venerable sir, is one both sick in body and sick in mind, and in what way is one sick in body but not sick in mind?
“Venerable sir, we would have traveled even from afar to the presence of the Venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement.
It would be well if the Venerable Sāriputta himself were to clarify the meaning of this statement.”
“In that case, householder, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” the householder Nakulapitā replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“And how, householder, is one both sick in body and sick in mind?

Here, householder, an uninstructed worldling—who has no regard for the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has no regard for true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as being in self, or self as being in form.
One dwells obsessed with the thought, “I am form, form is mine.
For one who dwells obsessed with the thought, “I am form, form is mine,” that form undergoes change and becomes otherwise.
Due to the change and alteration of that form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in him.
One regards feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling, or feeling as in self, or self as in feeling.
One remains obsessed with the thought, “I am feeling, feeling is mine.
For one who remains obsessed with the thought, “I am feeling, feeling is mine,” that feeling undergoes change and becomes otherwise.
With the change and alteration of feeling, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in him.
He regards perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception as in self, or self as in perception.
He remains obsessed with the thought: "I am perception, perception is mine."
For one who dwells obsessed with the thought, “I am perception, perception is mine,” that perception changes and becomes otherwise.
Due to that change and alteration of perception, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in him.
He regards volitional formations as self, or self as possessing volitional formations, or volitional formations as in self, or self as in volitional formations.
‘I am volitional formations; volitional formations are mine’—thus one dwells obsessed.
For one who dwells obsessed with the thought, ‘I am volitional formations; volitional formations are mine,’ those volitional formations undergo change and become otherwise.
From the change and alteration of volitional formations, there arise in him sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
One regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.
One remains obsessed with the thought: "I am consciousness, consciousness is mine.
For one who remains obsessed with the thought "I am consciousness, consciousness is mine," that consciousness undergoes change and becomes otherwise.
From the change and alteration of that consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.
In this way, householder, one is both sick in body and sick in mind.
And how, householder, is one sick in body but not sick in mind?
Here, householder, the well-taught noble disciple—who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and is well-disciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones;

who has seen the true persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of the true persons, and is well-disciplined in the Dhamma of the true persons—does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as being in self, nor self as being in form.
He does not dwell obsessed with the thought, "I am form" or "form is mine."

For one who does not dwell obsessed with the thought, "I am form, form is mine," when that form undergoes change and becomes otherwise, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise on account of that change and alteration of form.
One does not regard feeling as self, nor self as possessing feeling; nor feeling as in self, nor self as in feeling.
He does not dwell obsessed by the thought, ‘I am feeling, feeling is mine.
For him who does not dwell obsessed by the thought, ‘I am feeling, feeling is mine,’ that feeling changes and becomes otherwise.
With the change and alteration of that feeling, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise in him.
He does not regard perception as self, nor self as possessing perception; nor perception as in self, nor self as in perception.
He does not dwell obsessed with the thought, “I am perception, perception is mine.
For him who does not dwell obsessed with the thought, “I am perception, perception is mine,” that perception undergoes change and becomes otherwise.
With the change and alteration of perception, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise in him.
He does not regard volitional formations as self, nor self as possessing volitional formations; he does not regard volitional formations as in self, nor self as in volitional formations.
He does not dwell obsessed by the thought, “I am volitional formations, volitional formations are mine.”
For one who does not dwell obsessed with the thought, “I am volitional formations, volitional formations are mine,” those volitional formations undergo change and become otherwise.
Due to that change and alteration of volitional formations, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise in him.
He does not regard consciousness as self, nor self as possessing consciousness, nor consciousness as in self, nor self as in consciousness.
He does not dwell obsessed by the thought, ‘I am consciousness, consciousness is mine.
For one who does not dwell obsessed by the thought, ‘I am consciousness, consciousness is mine,’ that consciousness undergoes change and becomes otherwise.
With the change and becoming otherwise of that consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise in him.
"In this way, householder, one has a sick body but not a sick mind.
This is what the Venerable Sāriputta said.
The householder Nakulapitā was satisfied and delighted in the Venerable Sāriputta's words.
First.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.2 (SN 22.2, PTS SN iii 5) 1.
Nakulapituvagga (The Chapter on Nakula’s Father)
The Devadaha Sutta.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans; there is a town of the Sakyans named Devadaha.
Then a number of bhikkhus who were traveling through the western country approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, we wish to go to the western country and to take up residence in the western country."
“Bhikkhus, have you taken leave of Sāriputta?
“No, venerable sir, we have not taken leave of the Venerable Sāriputta.
“Take leave of Sāriputta, bhikkhus.”
“Bhikkhus, Sāriputta is wise; he is one who assists his fellow monks, his companions in the holy life.
“Yes, Bhante,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
Now at that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Blessed One in a certain thicket of *eḷagalā* creepers.
Then those bhikkhus, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One,
and keeping him to their right, approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached,
they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhus said to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Friend Sāriputta, we wish to go to the western provinces and make our dwelling in the western provinces.
We have asked leave of the Teacher."
“Friends, there are those who come from various kingdoms to question a bhikkhu—
wise khattiyas, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise recluses. For friends,
such people are wise and inquisitive.”
"What does the venerable ones' teacher say? What does he proclaim?

"Have you venerable ones heard the Dhamma well, grasped it well, attended to it with a well-directed mind, retained it well, and penetrated it well with wisdom, such that in answering you would be speakers of what was said by the Blessed One, and would not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is false?"
“Would you explain it in accordance with the Dhamma, such that no legitimate criticism or objection could find ground for reproach?
“Friend, we would come from afar to the presence of the Venerable Sāriputta in order to understand the meaning of this statement.”
"It would be well if the Venerable Sāriputta himself would clarify the meaning of this statement.
"Then listen, friends, and attend closely; I shall speak," he said.
"Yes, friend," those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
"Friends, there are those who come from various kingdoms to question a bhikkhu—wise khattiyas...
[and so on] ...wise ascetics."
"Friends, people are wise and inquisitive:
'But what does the venerable ones' teacher say? What does he proclaim?
When you are asked this, friends, you should answer thus:"
"Friends, our Teacher is one who teaches the subduing of desire and lust.
Even when this has been declared, friends, there are still those who would ask further questions—the wise khattiyas...
and even the wise ascetics.
"Friends, people are wise and inquisitive:

'In what, friends, does the Teacher's teaching consist regarding the removal of desire and lust? When asked thus, friends, you should answer: 'Friends, our Teacher teaches the removal of desire and lust for form.'"
"Friends, the Teacher teaches the removal of desire and lust for form; [he teaches the removal of desire and lust] for feeling … for perception …"
‘The Teacher teaches the removal of desire and lust for volitional formations… for consciousness.
Even when this has been thus explained, friends, there would still be those who ask further questions.
There are wise khattiyas... [and so on] ...wise ascetics as well.
Wise people, friends, are inquisitive:
"What drawback have these venerable ones seen that the Teacher teaches the removal of desire and lust for form?"
In regard to feeling … perception … volitional formations …
‘The Teacher is one who teaches the removal of desire and lust for consciousness’?”—
being asked thus, friends, you should answer: “Friends,
for one who is not free from lust, not free from desire, not free from affection, and not free from thirst for form...”
For one who has not abandoned fever and has not abandoned craving, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise due to the change and alteration of that form.
[The same applies to] feeling...
For one who has not become free from lust for perceptions...
[and] for one who has not become free from craving for volitional formations, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise due to the change and alteration of those volitional formations.
For one who has not removed lust for consciousness, who has not removed desire for it, who has not removed affection for it, who has not removed thirst for it, who has not removed fever for it,
and who has not removed craving for it, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise due to the change and alteration of that consciousness.
It is, friends, having seen this danger, that the Teacher taught the removal of desire and lust for form.
In regard to feeling … perception … volitional formations …
‘The Teacher is one who teaches the removal of desire and lust for consciousness.
Even when this has been thus explained, friends, there are still those who would ask further questions—
the wise khattiyas, the wise brahmins, the wise householders, and the wise ascetics.”
"Friends, wise people are inquisitive:
'But what benefit have the venerable ones seen that the Teacher has declared the removal of desire and lust for form,
[and so on] for feeling...'"
‘The Teacher teaches the removal of desire and lust for perception… for volitional formations… for consciousness’?”
Being asked thus, friends, you should answer: “Friends,
for one who is free from lust, free from desire, free from affection, free from thirst, free from fever,
and free from craving for form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise due to the change and alteration of that form.”
For one who is free from lust for feeling... free from lust for perception... and free from lust for mental formations, free from desire, free from affection, free from thirst, and free from fever.
For one who is free from craving, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise due to the change and alteration of those formations.
For one who is free from lust, free from desire, free from affection, free from thirst, free from fever,
and free from craving for consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise due to the change and alteration of that consciousness.
"Indeed, friends, it is because we see this benefit that the Teacher has taught the removal of desire and lust for form, for feeling,
for perception,
and for volitional formations."
‘The Teacher teaches the removal of desire and lust for consciousness.
Friends, if one were to enter upon and abide in unwholesome states, there would be a dwelling in this very life that is pleasant, free from vexation, free from despair, and free from fever;
and after the breakup of the body, following death, a good destination might be expected—but this is not so.
The Blessed One would praise the abandoning of unwholesome states.
For, friend, when one dwells having entered upon unwholesome states, there is dwelling in suffering in this very life—
with vexation, despair, and fever— and after the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination is to be expected.
Therefore, the Blessed One praises the abandoning of unwholesome states.
And, friends, if for one who has entered upon and dwells in wholesome states there were dwelling in this very life that is painful,
vexing, distressing, and feverish, and if after the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination were to be expected, [then he would not praise them].
The Blessed One would not praise the attainment of wholesome states were it not so;
rather, friends, because for one who dwells having attained wholesome states, there is a dwelling that is happy in this very life—
free from affliction, free from distress, and free from fever— and because after the breakup of the body, following death, a good destination is to be expected.
"Therefore, the Blessed One praises the undertaking of wholesome states.
This is what the Venerable Sāriputta said.
The monks, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Second.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.3 (SN 22.3, PTS SN iii 9) 1.
Nakulapituvagga (The Chapter on Nakula’s Father)
The Hāliddikāni Sutta:
Thus have I heard—
on one occasion the Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling among the Avantīs at Kuraraghara on the Papāta mountain.
Then the householder Hāliddikāni approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna;
having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Mahākaccāna and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the householder Hāliddikāni said this to the Venerable Mahākaccāna:
“Bhante, this was said by the Blessed One in the *Māgaṇḍiya* questions of the *Aṭṭhakavagga*:
‘Having abandoned his home, wandering without a fixed abode,
the sage forms no intimacies in the village;’”
“Empty of sensual pleasures and not looking forward [to them],
how could one not engage in disputes with people?
“Venerable sir, how should the meaning of this statement, which was spoken in brief by the Blessed One, be understood in detail?”
“The form element, householder, is the abode of consciousness.
And when consciousness is bound by craving for the form element, it is called ‘one who courses in an abode.
The feeling element, householder, is the abode of consciousness.”
Furthermore, consciousness that is bound by craving for the element of feeling is said to "wander in its abode.
The element of perception, householder, is the abode of consciousness;
and consciousness that is bound by craving for the element of perception is said to "wander in its abode."
The element of volitional formations, householder, is the abode of consciousness.
And when consciousness is bound by craving for the element of volitional formations, it is called "one who wanders in an abode.
It is in this way, householder, that one is a wanderer in an abode.
And how, householder, is one a wanderer without a home?

Householder, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, whatever engagement and clinging, whatever mental fixation, adherence, and underlying tendencies there are regarding the element of form—
these have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered incapable of further growth.
They are subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is called "one who wanders homeless.
It is the same with the element of feeling, householder...

Householder, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, and whatever engagement and clinging there is regarding the element of perception … regarding the element of volitional formations … regarding the element of consciousness, [that is the source of suffering].
The mental fixations, adherences, and underlying tendencies of the Tathāgata have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump,
rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future. Therefore,
the Tathāgata is called "one who wanders homeless."
In this way, householder, one is a wanderer without a home.
And how, householder, is one a wanderer with a home?
One who is bound by the spreading out of the sign of form as a home, householder, is said to be “a wanderer with a home.”
The sign of sound … [and so on] … the sign of odor … the sign of taste …
The sign of tangible objects... the sign of mental phenomena:
householders, one who wanders with a tendency toward and attachment to these abodes is called "one who wanders in an abode.
It is in this way, householder, that one wanders in an abode.
And how, householder, is one a wanderer without a home?

For the Tathāgata, householder, the wandering and bondage within the home of the sign of form have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and rendered incapable of arising in the future.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is called "a wanderer without a home."
The sign of sound … the sign of odor … the sign of taste …

“Householder, the Tathāgata has abandoned the attachment and bondage of wandering toward the signs of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena; he has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, rendered them non-existent, so that they are subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is called ‘one who wanders without a home.’”
In this way, householder, one is a wanderer without a home.
And how, householder, is one born of intimacy in the village?

Here, householder, a certain person dwells in close association with householders, sharing their joys and sorrows; he is happy when they are happy and sorrowful when they are sorrowful; and when there are duties or tasks that have arisen, he personally engages himself in them.
"In this way, householder, one becomes intimate with the village.
And how, householder, does one not become intimate with the village?

Here, householder, a bhikkhu dwells unassociated with householders; he does not share their joys, nor share their sorrows; he is not happy when they are happy, nor distressed when they are distressed; and when duties or tasks arise, he does not personally involve himself in them."
In this way, householder, one is not born of intimacy in the village.
And how, householder, is one destitute of sensual pleasures?

Here, householder, a certain person has not departed from lust for sensual pleasures, has not departed from desire for them, has not departed from affection for them, has not departed from thirst for them, has not departed from fever for them, and has not departed from craving for them.
In this way, householder, one is not empty of sensual pleasures.
And how, householder, is one empty of sensual pleasures?

Here, householder, a certain person is free from lust for sensual pleasures, free from desire for them, free from affection for them, free from thirst for them, free from fever for them, and free from craving for them.
"In this way, householder, one is empty of sensual pleasures.
And how, householder, is one full of expectations?
Here, householder, it occurs to a certain person: [text continues]"

‘May I be of such form in the future, may I have such feeling in the future, may I have such perception in the future, may I have such volitional formations in the future, may I have such consciousness in the future. In this way, householder, one has expectations. And how, householder, does one not have expectations? [One thinks: ‘May I not be of such form in the future, may I not have such feeling in the future, may I not have such perception in the future, may I not have such volitional formations in the future, may I not have such consciousness in the future.
In this way, householder, one does not have expectations.
"Here, householder, it does not occur to someone:

‘May I be such in form in the future; may I be such in feeling in the future; may I be such in perception in the future; may I be such in volitional formations in the future; may I be such in consciousness in the future.
In this way, householder, one is without a forward projection."
And how, householder, is one a speaker who quarrels with people?
Here, householder, a certain person is a speaker of such talk as this:
“You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline; I understand this Dhamma and Discipline. What, you?”
“Will you understand the Dhamma and Vinaya? You have practiced wrongly; I have practiced rightly.
What should have been said first, you said last; what should have been said last, you said first. My argument is consistent, yours is inconsistent.
Your position has been overturned. Your thesis has been refuted; go forth to defend it! You are defeated; try to extricate yourself if you can.”
In this way, householder, one is a speaker who quarrels with people.
And how, householder, is one a speaker who does not quarrel with people?
Here, householder, a bhikkhu is not a speaker of such talk as this:
“You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline... [as before] ...or unravel it if you are able.
In this way, householder, one does not engage in dispute with people.
Thus, householder, as for what was said by the Blessed One in the *Aṭṭhakavagga*, in the *Māgaṇḍiya-pañha*:
“Having abandoned home, wandering without a fixed abode,
making no intimacies with sages in the village,
empty of sensual desires and seeking nothing further— ”
"How should one not engage in dispute with people?
"Householder, this is how the meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One is to be understood in detail.
The third [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.4 (SN 22.4, PTS SN iii 12) 1. Nakulapituvagga Second Discourse on Hāliddikāni At Sāvatthī. Then the householder Hāliddikāni approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the world, the world. In what way, venerable sir, is it said, ‘the world’? “It is broken, householder, therefore it is called ‘the world. By what is it broken? It is broken by aging and death; therefore it is called ‘the world. “But, venerable sir, who breaks this world? “The world is not a person, householder, nor is it a being, nor is it a soul, nor is it a self. It is simply that this body, together with consciousness and all its various phenomena, is called ‘the world. “Venerable sir, is it only this much that is the world? “That is so, householder. That is just how far the world extends, that is just how far the world reaches, that is just how far the world goes. “Venerable sir, is there anything else besides this world? “There is nothing else besides this world, householder. “But, venerable sir, is there both this world and something else besides it? “There is neither this world nor anything else besides it, householder. “Then, venerable sir, is there neither this world nor anything else besides it? “There is neither ‘there is’ nor ‘there is not,’ householder, nor ‘both is and is not,’ nor ‘neither is nor is not. When this was said, the householder Hāliddikāni sat silent, dejected, with shoulders drooping and head downcast, glum, and without response. Seeing the householder Hāliddikāni thus, the Blessed One said to him: “Householder, when one does not understand as they really are the origin and the passing away of the world, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it, this is called ‘confusion of the world. But when one understands as they really are the origin and the passing away of the world, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it, this is called ‘non-confusion of the world. Then the householder Hāliddikāni, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after the householder Hāliddikāni had left, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the householder Hāliddikāni has departed after being taught by the Blessed One. What now will he declare himself to be? “Ānanda, if the householder Hāliddikāni, being questioned about the past, should declare himself to be a follower of the eternalist view, that would be a mistake for him. If he should declare himself to be a follower of the annihilationist view, that would be a mistake for him. If he should declare himself to be a follower of the fortuitous-origination view, that would be a mistake for him. If he should declare himself to be a follower of the nihilist view, that would be a mistake for him. If he should declare himself to be a follower of the identity view, that would be a mistake for him. If he should declare himself to be a follower of the diversity view, that would be a mistake for him. If he should declare himself to be a follower of the view of existence, that would be a mistake for him. If he should declare himself to be a follower of the view of non-existence, that would be a mistake for him. If he should declare himself to be a follower of the view of both existence and non-existence, that would be a mistake for him. If he should declare himself to be a follower of the view of neither existence nor non-existence, that would be a mistake for him. But if, Ānanda, the householder Hāliddikāni, being questioned about the past, should remain silent, that would be fitting for him. For the householder Hāliddikāni, Ānanda, has been taught by me through a gradual training, a gradual practice, a gradual progress. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well the Blessed One has explained the gradual training, the gradual practice, the gradual progress! “This is the gradual training, Ānanda, this is the gradual practice, this is the gradual progress: first, a person of integrity is to be associated with; then, one hears the true Dhamma; then, one gains faith in the Tathāgata;

then, having gained faith, one reflects: ‘Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open. It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well the Blessed One has explained the gradual training, the gradual practice, the gradual progress! “This is the gradual training, Ānanda, this is the gradual practice, this is the gradual progress: first, a person of integrity is to be associated with; then, one hears the true Dhamma; then, one gains faith in the Tathāgata; then, having gained faith, one reflects: ‘Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open. This is called the training in the higher wisdom. Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.5 (SN 22.5, PTS SN iii 13) 1. Nakulapituvagga Samādhisutta (The Discourse on Concentration) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when concentration is developed and cultivated, it yields two fruits: either final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how is concentration developed and cultivated so that it yields these two fruits? “Ānanda, herein a bhikkhu develops concentration with applied thought and sustained thought; he develops concentration without applied thought but with sustained thought; he develops concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought; he develops concentration accompanied by rapture; he develops concentration accompanied by pleasure; he develops concentration accompanied by equanimity; he develops concentration that has the formless as its domain. It is in this way, Ānanda, that concentration is developed and cultivated so that it yields these two fruits. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does a bhikkhu develop concentration with applied thought and sustained thought? How does he develop concentration without applied thought but with sustained thought? How does he develop concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought? How does he develop concentration accompanied by rapture? How does he develop concentration accompanied by pleasure? How does he develop concentration accompanied by equanimity? How does he develop concentration that has the formless as its domain? “Ānanda, herein a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down. Having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This is how, Ānanda, a bhikkhu develops concentration with applied thought and sustained thought. Furthermore, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters upon and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This is how, Ānanda, a bhikkhu develops concentration without applied thought but with sustained thought. Furthermore, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body; he enters upon and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily. This is how, Ānanda, a bhikkhu develops concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought. Furthermore, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters upon and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This is how, Ānanda, a bhikkhu develops concentration accompanied by equanimity. Furthermore, by completely transcending forms, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impingement, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] ‘space is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters upon and dwells in the base of infinite space. This is how, Ānanda, a bhikkhu develops concentration that has the formless as its domain. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does a bhikkhu develop concentration with applied thought and sustained thought? How does he develop concentration without applied thought but with sustained thought? How does he develop concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought? How does he develop concentration accompanied by rapture? How does he develop concentration accompanied by pleasure? How does he develop concentration accompanied by equanimity? How does he develop concentration that has the formless as its domain? [The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, herein a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest... [as above] ...enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna... [and so on through the four jhānas and the four formless attainments]. “This is how, Ānanda, a bhikkhu develops concentration with applied thought and sustained thought... [and so on]. “It is in this way, Ānanda, that concentration is developed and cultivated so that it yields these two fruits. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”—“Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when concentration is developed and cultivated, it yields two fruits: either final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning.

Thus have I heard:
... at Sāvatthī ...
there [the Blessed One] said this:
“Monks, develop concentration;
for a monk who is concentrated, monks, understands things as they truly are.
And what does he understand as it truly is?

The arising and passing away of form, the arising and passing away of feeling, the arising and passing away of perception, the arising and passing away of volitional formations, and the arising and passing away of consciousness.
And what, monks, is the arising of form? What is the arising of feeling? What is the arising of perception? What is the arising of volitional formations? What is the arising of consciousness?
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu delights in, welcomes, and remains clinging to something.
And what is it that he delights in, welcomes, and remains clinging to?
He delights in, welcomes, and remains clinging to form.
For one who delights in form, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it, delight arises.
That delight in form is grasping.
With that grasping as condition, there is existence.
With existence as condition, birth arises;
with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
One delights in feeling … [as before] … one delights in perception … one delights in volitional formations …
One delights in consciousness, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it.
For one who delights in consciousness, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it, delight arises.
That delight in consciousness is grasping.
With that clinging as condition, existence arises;
with existence as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, [aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise]...pe...
Thus occurs the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
This, monks, is the origination of form;
this is the origination of feeling.
This is the origin of perception;
this is the origin of volitional formations;
this is the origin of consciousness.
And what, bhikkhus, is the passing away of form? What is the passing away of feeling? What is the passing away of perception?
What is the passing away of volitional formations?
What is the passing away of consciousness?
Here, monks, one does not delight in it, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it.
And what is it that one does not delight in, does not welcome, and does not remain clinging to?
One does not delight in form, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it.
For one who does not delight in form, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it, whatever delight there was in form ceases.
With the cessation of that delight, grasping ceases.
With the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence...
[as before] ...in this way there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
One does not delight in feeling, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it.
For one who does not delight in feeling, does not welcome it, and remains without clinging to it, whatever craving there was for feeling ceases.
With the cessation of that craving, grasping ceases; with the cessation of grasping, becoming ceases... [and so on] ...up to the complete cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
In this way there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
One does not delight in perception...
[as before] ...one does not delight in volitional formations, one does not welcome them, and one does not remain clinging to them.
For one who does not delight in, welcome, or cling to volitional formations, whatever delight there was in volitional formations ceases.
With the cessation of that delight, clinging ceases;
with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases... [as before] ...pe...
In this way there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
One does not delight in consciousness, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it.
For one who does not delight in consciousness, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it, whatever craving for consciousness there was ceases.
With the cessation of delight comes the cessation of clinging...
[as before] ...Thus there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.

This, monks, is the passing away of form; this is the passing away of feeling; this is the passing away of perception; this is the passing away of volitional formations; this is the passing away of consciousness.”
The Fifth.

Nakulapituvagga (The Chapter on Nakula’s Father)
The Discourse on Seclusion.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, apply yourselves to seclusion."
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is withdrawn in seclusion understands things as they really are.
And what does he understand as they really are?
He understands the origin and the passing away of form; the origin and the passing away of feeling; the origin and the passing away of perception...”
The arising and passing away of volitional formations; the arising and passing away of consciousness...
[to be expanded as in the first sutta].
This is the sixth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.7 (SN 22.7, PTS SN iii 15) 1. Nakulapituvagga Upādāparitassanāsutta: The Discourse on Clinging and Agitation At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, based on what, does craving arise? “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and take recourse in the Blessed One. It would be good if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it. “Then listen, bhikkhus, and attend closely. I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when there is form, by clinging to form, based on form, craving arises. When there is feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, by clinging to consciousness, based on consciousness, craving arises. When what exists, by clinging to what, based on what, does agitation arise? When there is form, by clinging to form, based on form, agitation arises. When there is feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, by clinging to consciousness, based on consciousness, agitation arises. When what exists, by clinging to what, based on what, do fear and dread arise? When there is form, by clinging to form, based on form, fear and dread arise. When there is feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, by clinging to consciousness, based on consciousness, fear and dread arise. When what exists, by clinging to what, based on what, do sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise? When there is form, by clinging to form, based on form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. When there is feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, by clinging to consciousness, based on consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Without depending on the seen, without depending on the heard, without depending on the sensed, without depending on the cognized, I shall make known sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; or I shall demonstrate the way leading to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair’—that would be impossible. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Without depending on the seen, without depending on the heard, without depending on the sensed, without depending on the cognized, I shall make known pleasure, joy, and liberation; or I shall demonstrate the way leading to pleasure, joy, and liberation’—that would be impossible. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Without depending on the seen, without depending on the heard, without depending on the sensed, without depending on the cognized, I shall make known Nibbāna in this very life; or I shall demonstrate the way leading to Nibbāna in this very life’—that would be impossible. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Without depending on the seen, without depending on the heard, without depending on the sensed, without depending on the cognized, I shall make known the origin of suffering; or I shall demonstrate the way leading to the origin of suffering’—that would be impossible. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Without depending on the seen, without depending on the heard, without depending on the sensed, without depending on the cognized, I shall make known the cessation of suffering; or I shall demonstrate the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—that would be impossible. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Without depending on the seen, without depending on the heard, without depending on the sensed, without depending on the cognized, I shall make known the noble truth of suffering; or I shall demonstrate the way leading to the full understanding of the noble truth of suffering’—that would be impossible. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Without depending on the seen, without depending on the heard, without depending on the sensed, without depending on the cognized, I shall make known the noble truth of the origin of suffering; or I shall demonstrate the way leading to the abandoning of the noble truth of the origin of suffering’—that would be impossible. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Without depending on the seen, without depending on the heard, without depending on the sensed, without depending on the cognized, I shall make known the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; or I shall demonstrate the way leading to the realization of the noble truth of the cessation of suffering’—that would be impossible. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Without depending on the seen, without depending on the heard, without depending on the sensed, without depending on the cognized, I shall make known the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering; or I shall demonstrate the way leading to the development of the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering’—that would be impossible. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Without depending on the seen, without depending on the heard, without depending on the sensed, without depending on the cognized, I shall make known the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One; or I shall demonstrate the way leading to the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One’—that would be impossible. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say:

‘Without depending on the seen, without depending on the heard, without depending on the sensed, without depending on the cognized, I shall make known the Dhamma; or I shall demonstrate the way leading to the Dhamma’—that would be impossible. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Without depending on the seen, without depending on the heard, without depending on the sensed, without depending on the cognized, I shall make known the Saṅgha; or I shall demonstrate the way leading to the Saṅgha’—that would be impossible. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Without depending on the seen, without depending on the heard, without depending on the sensed, without depending on the cognized, I shall make known the Ariyan morality; or I shall demonstrate the way leading to the Ariyan morality’—that would be impossible. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Without depending on the seen, without depending on the heard, without depending on the sensed, without depending on the cognized, I shall make known the Ariyan concentration; or I shall demonstrate the way leading to the Ariyan concentration’—that would be impossible. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Without depending on the seen, without depending on the heard, without depending on the sensed, without depending on the cognized, I shall make known the Ariyan wisdom; or I shall demonstrate the way leading to the Ariyan wisdom’—that would be impossible. Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Without depending on the seen, without depending on the heard, without depending on the sensed, without depending on the cognized, I shall make known the Ariyan liberation; or I shall demonstrate the way leading to the Ariyan liberation’—that would be impossible. But, bhikkhus, when one depends on the seen, when one depends on the heard, when one depends on the sensed, when one depends on the cognized, then sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. And when one depends on the seen, when one depends on the heard, when one depends on the sensed, when one depends on the cognized, then pleasure, joy, and liberation arise. And when one depends on the seen, when one depends on the heard, when one depends on the sensed, when one depends on the cognized, then Nibbāna in this very life is made known. And when one depends on the seen, when one depends on the heard, when one depends on the sensed, when one depends on the cognized, then the noble truth of suffering is made known. And when one depends on the seen, when one depends on the heard, when one depends on the sensed, when one depends on the cognized, then the noble truth of the origin of suffering is made known. And when one depends on the seen, when one depends on the heard, when one depends on the sensed, when one depends on the cognized, then the noble truth of the cessation of suffering is made known. And when one depends on the seen, when one depends on the heard, when one depends on the sensed, when one depends on the cognized, then the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering is made known. And when one depends on the seen, when one depends on the heard, when one depends on the sensed, when one depends on the cognized, then the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One is made known. And when one depends on the seen, when one depends on the heard, when one depends on the sensed, when one depends on the cognized, then the Dhamma is made known. At Sāvatthī.
“Monks, I will teach you agitation through clinging and non-agitation through non-clinging.
Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And how, bhikkhus, does agitation due to clinging come about?
In this case, monks, an uninstructed worldling—unseeing of the noble ones, unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones;

unseeing of true persons, unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form.
That form of his undergoes change and becomes otherwise.
With the change and alteration of that form, consciousness becomes subject to the change and alteration of form.
The agitation born of following the change and alteration of form arises from the emergence of phenomena and remains obsessing the mind.
Due to this obsession of the mind, one becomes fearful, distressed, anxious, and agitated by clinging.
One regards feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling, or feeling as being in self, or self as being in feeling.
That feeling of his changes and becomes otherwise.
Because of that change and alteration of feeling, consciousness becomes preoccupied with the change of feeling.
The agitation born of the transformation and reversal of feeling, arising from the emergence of mental phenomena, persists by seizing the mind.
Because the mind is seized, he becomes anxious, distressed, longing, and agitated through clinging.
He regards perception as self... [and so on].
One regards volitional formations as self, or self as possessing volitional formations, or volitional formations as in self, or self as in volitional formations.
Those volitional formations of his change and become otherwise.
With the change and alteration of those volitional formations, his consciousness becomes preoccupied with the change of volitional formations.
In him, anxiety born of the transformation and reversal of formations, arising from the occurrence of phenomena, persists by seizing the mind.
Because the mind is seized, he becomes agitated, distressed, and expectant, and he trembles with clinging.
He regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as being in self, or self as being in consciousness.
That consciousness of his changes and becomes otherwise.
Due to that change and alteration of consciousness, his consciousness becomes preoccupied with the change of consciousness.
The agitation born from being preoccupied with the change of consciousness arises as a phenomenon and remains obsessing the mind.
Because of the obsession of the mind, one becomes fearful, distressed, expectant, and, through clinging, trembles with anxiety.
Thus, monks, there is trembling with anxiety due to clinging.
And how, monks, is there no trembling with anxiety due to non-clinging?
In this case, monks, the well-taught noble disciple—who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and is well-disciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones;

who has seen true persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and is well-disciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as being in self, nor self as being in form.
That form of his changes and becomes otherwise.

Because his consciousness does not follow after the change and alteration of form, the agitation born of following after the change and alteration of form does not arise and persist, taking possession of his mind.
Because his mind is not possessed by this, he is neither agitated nor distressed, nor does he have expectations; and through non-clinging, he does not tremble.
One does not regard feeling as self, nor self as possessing feeling; nor feeling as being in the self, nor the self as being in feeling.
When that feeling changes and becomes otherwise, because of that change and alteration of feeling, consciousness does not follow after the change of feeling.
In him, no agitation born of following the transformation of feelings arises; the phenomena that emerge do not remain obsessing the mind.
Because the mind is not obsessed, he is neither anxious, nor distressed, nor longing; and by not grasping, he does not tremble.
He does not regard perception... [and so on] ...nor mental formations as self.
Neither the formations in oneself, nor oneself in the formations;
nor oneself as possessing the formations.
Those formations of his undergo change and become otherwise.

Because his consciousness does not follow after the alteration and change of formations, the agitation born from following after the alteration and change of formations does not arise and persist by seizing the mind.
Because the mind is not seized, he is neither agitated, nor distressed, nor longing; and through non-clinging, he does not tremble.
One does not regard consciousness as self, nor does one regard the self as possessing consciousness...
[and so on] ...When that consciousness of his changes and becomes otherwise,
because of that change and alteration of consciousness, his consciousness does not follow after the change of consciousness.
In him, no agitation born of following the transformation of consciousness arises; the states produced by phenomena do not remain obsessing the mind.
Because the mind is not obsessed, he is neither anxious, nor distressed, nor expectant; and being without clinging, he does not tremble.
It is in this way, monks, that there is non-trembling through non-clinging.”
The Seventh.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.8 (SN 22.8, PTS SN iii 18) 1.
Nakulapituvagga (The Chapter on Nakulapitā)
The Second Discourse on Agitation through Clinging.
Setting at Sāvatthī:
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you agitation through clinging and non-agitation through non-clinging.”
Listen to that...
How, monks, does agitation through clinging arise?
Here, monks, the uninstructed worldling regards form as ‘this is mine, this am I, this is my self.’
That form of his changes and becomes otherwise.
From that change and alteration of form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in him.
[He regards] feeling as "this is mine" … [and so on].
One regards perception as ‘This is mine’ ...
one regards volitional formations as ‘This is mine’ ...
one regards consciousness as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’
That consciousness of his changes and becomes otherwise.
With the change and alteration of that consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in him.
It is in this way, monks, that there is agitation due to clinging.
And how, monks, is there non-panic through non-clinging?
Here, monks, the learned noble disciple regards form thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
That form of his changes and becomes otherwise.
With the change and alteration of form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise for him.
"Feeling is not mine... ...
"Perception is not mine..."
He regards volitional formations as "not mine," ...
and consciousness as "not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
That consciousness of his changes and becomes otherwise.
With the change and alteration of that consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise.
It is in this way, monks, that there is non-terror through non-clinging. Thus was the eighth [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.9 (SN 22.9, PTS SN iii 19) 1. Nakulapituvagga Kālattaya-aniccasutta (The Discourse on Impermanence in the Three Times) “Bhikkhus, form is impermanent in the past, impermanent in the future, and impermanent in the present. Feeling is impermanent in the past, impermanent in the future, and impermanent in the present. Perception is impermanent in the past, impermanent in the future, and impermanent in the present. Volitional formations are impermanent in the past, impermanent in the future, and impermanent in the present. Consciousness is impermanent in the past, impermanent in the future, and impermanent in the present. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion towards form, revulsion towards feeling, revulsion towards perception, revulsion towards volitional formations, and revulsion towards consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, form—past and future—is impermanent;
what need is there to mention the present?
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple is indifferent toward past form;
he does not delight in future form;
and he practices for the sake of revulsion toward, the fading away of lust for, and the cessation of present form.
Feeling is impermanent … perception is impermanent … volitional formations, past and future, are impermanent.
What need is there to speak of those of the present?
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple is indifferent toward past formations and does not delight in future formations.
He practices for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of present formations.
Consciousness is impermanent in the past and future;
what need is there to speak of the present?
"Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple is indifferent toward past consciousness;
he does not delight in future consciousness;
and he is practicing for the sake of revulsion toward, the fading away of lust for, and the cessation of present consciousness."
The Ninth.

The First Chapter on Nakulapita.
Its summary verse:

and the two Hāliddikāni;
Samādhi and Paṭisallāna.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.12 (SN 22.12, PTS SN iii 21) 2. Aniccavagga Aniccasutta (The Discourse on Impermanence) “Bhikkhus, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self; what is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Feeling is impermanent... Perception is impermanent... Volitional formations are impermanent... Consciousness is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self; what is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion toward form, revulsion toward feeling, revulsion toward perception, revulsion toward volitional formations, and revulsion toward consciousness. Thus have I heard—at Sāvatthī.
There, [the Blessed One] said: …pe…
“Bhikkhus, form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, volitional formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent.

Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness.

“He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.

Sixth. Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.18 (SN 22.18, PTS SN iii 23) 2.
The Chapter on Impermanence (Aniccavagga)
The Discourse on the Impermanent with Cause. At Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, form is impermanent.”
Whatever cause, whatever condition there is for the arising of form, that too is impermanent.
How, monks, could form born of what is impermanent be permanent?
Feeling is impermanent.
Whatever cause, whatever condition there is for the arising of feeling, that too is impermanent.
Feeling, monks, being born of what is impermanent, how could it be permanent?
Perception is impermanent...
Formations are impermanent.
Whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of formations, that too is impermanent.
Since formations, monks, are born of the impermanent, how could they be permanent?
Consciousness is impermanent.
Whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of consciousness, that too is impermanent.
Since consciousness, monks, is born of what is impermanent, how could it be permanent?
"Seeing thus...
he understands: ‘...there is nothing further beyond this state.
This is the seventh [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.19 (SN 22.19, PTS SN iii 23) 2. Aniccavagga Sahetudukkhasutta – The Discourse on Suffering with its Cause “Bhikkhus, suffering arises with a cause; it does not arise without a cause. And what is that cause? It is craving (*taṇhā*). “Bhikkhus, suffering arises with a condition; it does not arise without a condition. And what is that condition? It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a source; it does not arise without a source. And what is that source? It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a foundation; it does not arise without a foundation. And what is that foundation? It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a basis; it does not arise without a basis. And what is that basis? It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a support; it does not arise without a support. And what is that support? It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a fuel; it does not arise without a fuel. And what is that fuel? “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a flame (*joti*); it does not arise without a flame. And what is that flame? It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a radiance (*āloka*); it does not arise without a radiance. And what is that radiance? It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a heat (*uṇha*); it does not arise without a heat. And what is that heat?
