It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a disappearance (*antaradhāna*); it does not arise without a disappearance. And what is that disappearance? It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a vanishing (*vigama*); it does not arise without a vanishing. And what is that vanishing? It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a separation (*viyoga*); it does not arise without a separation. And what is that separation? It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a parting (*vippayoga*); it does not arise without a parting. And what is that parting? It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a loss (*vināsa*); it does not arise without a loss. And what is that loss? It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a decay (*jarā*); it does not arise without a decay. And what is that decay? It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from an aging (*jarā*); it does not arise without an aging. And what is that aging? It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a decrepitude (*jarasā*); it does not arise without a decrepitude. And what is that decrepitude? It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a senescence (*jarā*); it does not arise without a senescence. And what is that senescence? It is craving. “Bhikkhus, suffering arises from a frailty (*dubbalya*); it does not arise without a frailty. And what is that frailty? It is craving. “Bhikkhus,
At Savatthi.
“Bhikkhus, form is suffering.
Whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of form, that too is suffering.”
“Bhikkhus, since form is produced from suffering, how could it be happiness?
Feeling is suffering… perception is suffering…”
Volitional formations are suffering;
consciousness is suffering.
Whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of consciousness, that too is suffering.
“Bhikkhus, since consciousness is born of suffering, how could it be happy?
Seeing thus … he understands:
‘… there is nothing further beyond this state of being.’”
Eighth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.20 (SN 22.20, PTS SN iii 24) 2.
The Chapter on Impermanence (Aniccavagga)
The Discourse on Being Without Self Due to Having a Cause.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Form, bhikkhus, is not-self.”
Whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of form, that too is non-self.
Since form, monks, is born of what is non-self, how could it be self?
Feeling is non-self...
Perception is non-self;
mental formations are non-self;
consciousness is non-self.
Whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of consciousness, that too is non-self.
Monks, since consciousness is born of what is non-self, how could it be self?
Seeing thus... [as before]...
‘There is nothing further beyond this state of being.
This is the ninth [sutta]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.21 (SN 22.21, PTS SN iii 24).
2. The Chapter on Impermanence, Ānanda Sutta.
At Sāvatthī, in a certain monastery.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, it is said, 'cessation, cessation.
Of what things, venerable sir, is the cessation called 'cessation'?"
“Ānanda, form indeed is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.
Its cessation is called ‘cessation.
Feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.”
Its cessation is called "cessation.
Perceptions...
volitional formations are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.
Their cessation is called "cessation.
Consciousness is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.
Its cessation is called "cessation."
“Ānanda, the cessation of these phenomena is what is called ‘cessation.
The tenth [sutta].
The second chapter on Impermanence.
Its summary verse:
Impermanent, suffering, and non-self;
and the other three that are impermanent.
They were spoken of by way of cause,
and they were ten [spoken of] by Ānanda.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.22 (SN 22.22, PTS SN iii 25).
3. The Chapter on the Burden (Bhāravagga). The Discourse on the Burden (Bhārasutta).
At Sāvatthī… there [the Blessed One] … [dwelt].
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the burden, the bearer of the burden, the taking up of the burden, and the laying down of the burden.
Listen to that.
And what, bhikkhus, is the burden?”
"One should say: 'The five aggregates of clinging.
Which five?

The aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to mental formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness."
This, monks, is called the burden.
And who, monks, is the bearer of the burden?
It should be said: "The person."
“Monks, this venerable one of such a name and such a clan—
this, monks, is called the bearer of the burden.
And what, monks, is the taking up of the burden?”
That craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there—
that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence— this, monks,
is called the taking up of the burden.
"And what, monks, is the laying down of the burden?
It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving—its relinquishing, its renunciation, its liberation, and the absence of attachment.
This, monks, is called the laying down of the burden."
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
"The five aggregates are indeed a burden."
The person who bears the burden;
the taking up of the burden is suffering in the world,
while the laying down of the burden is happiness.
Having laid down the heavy burden and not taking up another burden,
having pulled out craving by its very root—
“Free from craving, he has attained final Nibbāna.
Thus it was said. First.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.23. (SN 22.23, PTS SN iii 26)
3. Bhāravagga:
Pariññāsutta.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
“Monks, I will teach you the phenomena that are to be fully understood and full understanding itself.
Listen to that.
And what, monks, are the phenomena that are to be fully understood?”

“Bhikkhus, form is a phenomenon to be fully understood; feeling is a phenomenon to be fully understood; perception is a phenomenon to be fully understood; volitional formations are phenomena to be fully understood; consciousness is a phenomenon to be fully understood.
These, bhikkhus, are called the phenomena to be fully understood.
And what, bhikkhus, is full understanding?”
“Monks, that which is the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion—
this, monks, is called full understanding. Thus was the second [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.24 (SN 22.24, PTS SN iii 26) 3. Bhāravagga Abhijānasutta (The Discourse on Higher Knowledge) "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you about the burden, the taking up of the burden, the laying down of the burden, and the bearer of the burden. Listen to that and attend closely; I will speak. "Yes, venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: "And what, bhikkhus, is the burden? It is the five aggregates subject to clinging. And what are the five? They are the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. This, bhikkhus, is called the burden. And what, bhikkhus, is the taking up of the burden? It is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for cessation of existence. This, bhikkhus, is called the taking up of the burden. And what, bhikkhus, is the laying down of the burden? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it. This, bhikkhus, is called the laying down of the burden. And what, bhikkhus, is the bearer of the burden? It is this person, the individual, the sentient being, the human being, the man, the woman, the self, the soul, the spirit, the creature, the person, the individual who experiences the result of good and bad deeds. This, bhikkhus, is called the bearer of the burden. Thus, bhikkhus, the burden has been explained, the taking up of the burden has been explained, the laying down of the burden has been explained, and the bearer of the burden has been explained. When a noble disciple has thus seen well with right wisdom as it really is, he is not one who looks for a burden, nor one who takes up a burden, nor one who lays down a burden, nor one who is a bearer of a burden. He is one who has cut off craving, severed the fetter, and, through the complete penetration of conceit, has made an end of suffering. When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple has thus abandoned these four things and possesses these four things, he is one who has reached certainty, one who has reached assurance, and he is incapable of falling away from the supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna."
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, without directly knowing form, without fully understanding it, without becoming dispassionate toward it, and without abandoning it, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering.
Without directly knowing feeling, without fully understanding it, without becoming dispassionate toward it, and without abandoning it, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering.”
Not directly knowing perception...
not directly knowing volitional formations, not fully understanding them, not becoming dispassionate toward them, and not abandoning them, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering;
not directly knowing consciousness, not fully understanding it, not becoming dispassionate toward it, and not abandoning it, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering.
"Monks, by directly knowing form, fully understanding it, fading away toward it, and abandoning it, one is capable of the destruction of suffering.
By directly knowing feeling...
perception..."
“By directly knowing and fully understanding volitional formations… consciousness, by making them fade away and abandoning them, one is capable of the destruction of suffering.
The third.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.25 (SN 22.25, PTS SN iii 27) 3. Bhāravagga Chandarāgasutta (The Discourse on Desire and Lust) “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the burden, the taking up of the burden, the laying down of the burden, and the carrier of the burden. Listen to that, bhikkhus, and attend closely; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “And what, bhikkhus, is the burden? ‘The five aggregates subject to clinging,’ this is the burden. And what are the five? They are: the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. This, bhikkhus, is called the burden. And what, bhikkhus, is the taking up of the burden? It is this personal identity [the six internal bases], namely: the eye-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, the tongue-base, the body-base, and the mind-base. This, bhikkhus, is called the taking up of the burden. And what, bhikkhus, is the laying down of the burden? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that same personal identity, its giving up, its relinquishing, its letting go, and its non-adherence. This, bhikkhus, is called the laying down of the burden. And what, bhikkhus, is the carrier of the burden? It is this person with a name and clan, one who experiences the here and now, the experiencer of the result of good and bad deeds. This, bhikkhus, is called the carrier of the burden. “Thus, bhikkhus, the burden has been shown, the taking up of the burden has been shown, the laying down of the burden has been shown, and the carrier of the burden has been shown by me. In this, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves: ‘We will not cling to anything in the world. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. [Then the Venerable Sāriputta said: “Venerable friends, it is said: ‘Desire and lust. To what extent, venerable friends, is there desire and lust? [The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said: “Friend Sāriputta, it is in whatever is impermanent that there is desire and lust; it is in whatever is suffering that there is desire and lust; it is in whatever is non-self that there is desire and lust. [The Venerable Sāriputta said: “Venerable friend Moggallāna, it is in whatever is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change that there is desire and lust. [The Venerable Mahākaccāna said: “Friends, it is in whatever is the five aggregates subject to clinging—form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness—that there is desire and lust. For whoever, friends, does not abandon desire and lust for these five aggregates subject to clinging, their mind does not incline toward nibbāna; being uninclined, it does not lean toward it; being unleaning, it does not tend toward it. But whoever abandons desire and lust for these five aggregates subject to clinging, their mind inclines toward nibbāna; being inclined, it leans toward it; being leaning, it tends toward it. [The Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita said: “Friends, it is in whatever is the six bases of contact—eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact—that there is desire and lust. For whoever, friends, does not abandon desire and lust for these six bases of contact, their mind does not incline toward nibbāna; being uninclined, it does not lean toward it; being unleaning, it does not tend toward it. But whoever abandons desire and lust for these six bases of contact, their mind inclines toward nibbāna; being inclined, it leans toward it; being leaning, it tends toward it. [The Venerable Mahākappina said: “Friends, it is in whatever is the seven stations of consciousness and the two bases—that there is desire and lust. For whoever, friends, does not abandon desire and lust for these seven stations of consciousness and two bases, their mind does not incline toward nibbāna; being uninclined, it does not lean toward it; being unleaning, it does not tend toward it. But whoever abandons desire and lust for these seven stations of consciousness and two bases, their mind inclines toward nibbāna; being inclined, it leans toward it; being leaning, it tends toward it. [The Venerable Mahācunda said: “Friends, it is in whatever is the nine abodes of beings and the four modes of becoming—that there is desire and lust. For whoever, friends, does not abandon desire and lust for these nine abodes of beings and four modes of becoming, their mind does not incline toward nibbāna; being uninclined, it does not lean toward it; being unleaning, it does not tend toward it. But whoever abandons desire and lust for these nine abodes of beings and four modes of becoming, their mind inclines toward nibbāna;

being inclined, it leans toward it; being leaning, it tends toward it. [The Venerable Anuruddha said: “Friends, it is in whatever is the ten courses of wholesome action and the ten courses of unwholesome action—that there is desire and lust. For whoever, friends, does not abandon desire and lust for these ten courses of wholesome action and ten courses of unwholesome action, their mind does not incline toward nibbāna; being uninclined, it does not lean toward it; being unleaning, it does not tend toward it. But whoever abandons desire and lust for these ten courses of wholesome action and ten courses of unwholesome action, their mind inclines toward nibbāna; being inclined, it leans toward it; being leaning, it tends toward it. [The Venerable Revata said: “Friends, it is in whatever is the twelve bases—that there is desire and lust. For whoever, friends, does not abandon desire and lust for these twelve bases, their mind does not incline toward nibbāna; being uninclined, it does not lean toward it; being unleaning, it does not tend toward it. But whoever abandons desire and lust for these twelve bases, their mind inclines toward nibbāna; being inclined, it leans toward it; being leaning, it tends toward it. [The Venerable Ānanda said: “Friends, it is in whatever is the eighteen mental explorations—that there is desire and lust. For whoever, friends, does not abandon desire and lust for these eighteen mental explorations, their mind does not incline toward nibbāna; being uninclined, it does not lean toward it; being unleaning, it does not tend toward it. But whoever abandons desire and lust for these eighteen mental explorations, their mind inclines toward nibbāna; being inclined, it leans toward it; being leaning, it tends toward it. [The Venerable Rāhula said: “Friends, it is in whatever is the twenty-two faculties—that there is desire and lust. For whoever, friends, does not abandon desire and lust for these twenty-two faculties, their mind does not incline toward nibbāna; being uninclined, it does not lean toward it; being unleaning, it does not tend toward it. But whoever abandons desire and lust for these twenty-two faculties, their mind inclines toward nibbāna; being inclined, it leans toward it; being leaning, it tends toward it. [The Venerable Sāriputta said: “Friends, it is in whatever is the four noble truths—that there is desire and lust. For whoever, friends, does not abandon desire and lust for these four noble truths, their mind does not incline toward nibbāna; being uninclined, it does not lean toward it; being unleaning, it does not tend toward it. But whoever abandons desire and lust for these four noble truths, their mind inclines toward nibbāna; being inclined, it leans toward it; being leaning, it tends toward it. [The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said: “Friends, it is in whatever is the dependent origination—that there is desire and lust. For whoever, friends, does not abandon desire and lust for this dependent origination, their mind does not incline toward nibbāna; being uninclined, it does not lean toward it; being unleaning, it does not tend toward it. But whoever abandons desire and lust for this dependent origination, their mind inclines toward nibbāna; being inclined, it leans toward it; being leaning, it tends toward it. [The Venerable Sāriputta said: “Friends, it is in whatever is the cessation of dependent origination—that there is desire and lust. For whoever, friends, does not abandon desire and lust for this cessation of dependent origination, their mind does not incline toward nib
At Savatthi.
"Bhikkhus, whatever desire and lust there is for form, abandon it.
In this way, that form will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and incapable of arising again in the future."
Abandon whatever desire and lust there is for feeling.
In this way, that feeling will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and incapable of arising again in the future.
Abandon whatever desire and lust there is for perception.
In this way, that perception will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
Abandon whatever desire and lust there is for volitional formations;
in this way, those volitional formations will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
“Whatever desire and lust there is for consciousness, abandon that.
In this way, that consciousness will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and incapable of arising again in the future.
The fourth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.26 (SN 22.26, PTS SN iii 27) 3. Bhāravagga Assādasutta The Discourse on Gratification "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the burden, the taking up of the burden, the laying down of the burden, and the carrier of the burden. Listen to that and attend closely; I will speak. "Yes, venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: "And what, bhikkhus, is the burden? It is the five aggregates subject to clinging. And what are the five? They are: the aggregate of form subject to clinging, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging, the aggregate of volitional formations subject to clinging, and the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging. This, bhikkhus, is called the burden. And what, bhikkhus, is the taking up of the burden? It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, bhikkhus, is called the taking up of the burden. And what, bhikkhus, is the laying down of the burden? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, and non-reliance on it. This, bhikkhus, is called the laying down of the burden. And what, bhikkhus, is the carrier of the burden? It is this person, the individual, the creature, the human being, the man, the mortal, the son of the man, who experiences the arising and passing away of these very five aggregates subject to clinging. This, bhikkhus, is called the carrier of the burden. "Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion towards form, revulsion towards feeling, revulsion towards perception, revulsion towards volitional formations, and revulsion towards consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion [his mind] is liberated. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: 'It is liberated. He understands: 'Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.'"
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened bodhisatta, this thought occurred to me:
‘What now is the gratification in form, what the danger, and what the escape?’”
What is the gratification in feeling? What is the danger? What is the escape?
What is the gratification in perception? What is the danger? What is the escape?
What is the gratification in volitional formations? What is the danger? What is the escape?
“What is the gratification of consciousness, what is the danger, and what is the escape?
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
“The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on form—this is the gratification of form.”
That form which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in form.
The removal of desire and lust for form, the abandoning of desire and lust for form—this is the escape from form.
That pleasure and joy that arise dependent on feeling—this is the gratification in feeling.
That feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in feeling.
The removal of desire and lust for feeling, the abandoning of desire and lust for feeling—this is the escape from feeling.
That perception which arises dependent upon [feeling]... [and so on].
The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on volitional formations: this is the gratification in volitional formations.
That volitional formations are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger in volitional formations.
The removal of desire and lust for volitional formations, the abandoning of desire and lust for them: this is the escape from volitional formations.
The pleasure and joy that arise in dependence on consciousness: this is the gratification in consciousness.
That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger in consciousness.
The removal of desire and lust for consciousness, the abandoning of desire and lust for consciousness: this is the escape from consciousness.’
“Bhikkhus, as long as I did not directly know, as they really are, the gratification in these five aggregates subject to clinging as gratification,
the danger as danger, and the escape as escape, for so long, bhikkhus, I did not claim:
‘In this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, I have attained the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.’”
“I claimed, monks, to have awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
But it was when I had directly known, as they really are, the gratification in these five aggregates of clinging as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape— that I, monks,
claimed to have awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.”
"And knowledge and vision arose in me:
‘My liberation is unshakable; this is my final birth; now there is no further becoming.
Thus ends the fifth [sutta].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.27 (SN 22.27, PTS SN iii 29) 3. Bhāravagga The Second Discourse on Gratification “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the burden, the taking up of the burden, the laying down of the burden, and the carrier of the burden. It is the five aggregates subject to clinging. And what are the five? They are: the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. This, bhikkhus, is called the burden. “And what, bhikkhus, is the taking up of the burden? This, bhikkhus, is called the taking up of the burden. “And what, bhikkhus, is the laying down of the burden? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it. This, bhikkhus, is called the laying down of the burden. “And what, bhikkhus, is the carrier of the burden? It is this person, the so-called individual, comprised of the six sense bases and bound by craving. This, bhikkhus, is called the carrier of the burden. “Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion towards form, revulsion towards feeling, revulsion towards perception, revulsion towards volitional formations, and revulsion towards consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion [his mind] is liberated. When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’”
At Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, I set out seeking the gratification in form.
Whatever gratification there is in form, that I discovered.”
"To whatever extent there is gratification in form, that has been clearly seen by me through wisdom.
Monks, I undertook a search for the danger in form;
I discovered whatever danger there is in form."
"To the extent that there is danger in form, that has been well seen by me with wisdom.
Monks, I practiced the search for escape from form,
and I attained that which is the escape from form."
"To the extent that there is an escape from form, that has been well-seen by me through wisdom.
As for feeling, monks...
as for perception, monks..."
“Bhikkhus, I set out seeking the gratification in volitional formations… in consciousness.
Whatever gratification there is in consciousness, that I discovered.”
"To whatever extent there is gratification in consciousness, that has been clearly seen by me through wisdom.
Monks, I undertook a search for the danger in consciousness;
I discovered whatever danger there is in consciousness."
To whatever extent there is danger in consciousness, that has been clearly seen by me through wisdom. Monks,
I undertook a search for the escape from consciousness,
and I have attained that which is the escape from consciousness.
"To the extent that there is an escape from consciousness, that has been well-seen by me through wisdom.

Monks, as long as I did not directly know, as they really are, the gratification in these five aggregates of clinging as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape … [as before] … I directly knew them."
And knowledge and vision arose in me:
“Unshakable is my liberation; this is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence.
Thus it was for the sixth time.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.28 (SN 22.28, PTS SN iii 29) 3. Bhāravagga Tatiya-assādasutta: The Third Discourse on Gratification “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the burden, the taking up of the burden, the laying down of the burden, and the carrier of the burden. Listen to that and attend closely; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “And what, bhikkhus, is the burden? ‘The five aggregates subject to clinging,’ this is called the burden. And what, bhikkhus, is the taking up of the burden? ‘Craving for existence,’ this is called the taking up of the burden. And what, bhikkhus, is the laying down of the burden? ‘The cessation of craving,’ this is called the laying down of the burden. And what, bhikkhus, is the carrier of the burden? ‘This person, the individual,’ this is called the carrier of the burden. “What five aggregates subject to clinging? They are: the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates subject to clinging. “Whatever, bhikkhus, is the gratification in these five aggregates subject to clinging, that is their gratification. Whatever is the danger in them, that is their danger. Whatever is the escape from them, that is their escape. “And what, bhikkhus, is the gratification in these five aggregates subject to clinging? Whatever pleasure and satisfaction arise in dependence on these five aggregates subject to clinging—this is the gratification in them. “And what, bhikkhus, is the danger in these five aggregates subject to clinging? These five aggregates subject to clinging are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in them. “And what, bhikkhus, is the escape from these five aggregates subject to clinging? The complete dispassion toward these five aggregates subject to clinging, their fading away, and their cessation—this is the escape from them. “Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion toward form, revulsion toward feeling, revulsion toward perception, revulsion toward volitional formations, and revulsion toward consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. Being liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
At Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, if there were no gratification in form, beings would not become infatuated with form.
But because there is gratification in form, beings become infatuated with form."
If, monks, there were no danger in form, beings would not become disenchanted with form.
But because there is danger in form, monks, beings become disenchanted with form.
If, monks, there were no escape from form, beings would not escape from form.
But because, monks, there is an escape from form, therefore beings escape from form.
If, monks, there were no escape from feeling...
[and so on] ...if, monks, there were no escape from perception... [and so on]...
If, monks, there were no escape from volitional formations, beings would not escape from volitional formations.
But because, monks, there is an escape from volitional formations, beings escape from volitional formations.
If, monks, there were no gratification in consciousness, beings would not become infatuated with consciousness.
But because, monks, there is gratification in consciousness, beings are infatuated with consciousness.
If, monks, there were no danger in consciousness, beings would not become disenchanted with consciousness.
But because, monks, there is danger in consciousness, beings become disenchanted with consciousness.
If, monks, there were no escape from consciousness, beings would not escape from consciousness.
But because, monks, there is an escape from consciousness, therefore beings escape from consciousness.
And as long as, monks, beings have not known, as they really are, the gratification in these five aggregates of clinging as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape;

Monks, beings—including devas, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its devas and humans—did not yet dwell having escaped from, become detached from, and liberated from this world, with a mind that had transcended its boundaries.
But when, monks, beings have directly known, as it really is, the gratification in these five aggregates of clinging as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape;

Then, monks, beings—along with the world of devas, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans—dwell having escaped, detached, and liberated from it, with a mind that has transcended all boundaries.
This is the seventh.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.29 (SN 22.29, PTS SN iii 31).
3. Bhāravagga.
Abhinandanasutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, whoever delights in form delights in suffering.
Whoever delights in suffering, I say, is not liberated from suffering.
Whoever delights in feeling …”
Whoever delights in perception...
whoever delights in volitional formations...
whoever delights in consciousness, that person delights in suffering.
"Whoever delights in suffering, I say that person is not liberated from suffering.
But whoever, monks, does not delight in form, he does not delight in suffering.
Whoever does not delight in suffering, I say that person is liberated from suffering."
He who does not delight in feeling...
he who does not delight in perception...
he who does not delight in volitional formations...
"One who does not delight in consciousness does not delight in suffering.
One who does not delight in suffering, I say, is fully released from suffering. Thus it was said.
The eighth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.30 (SN 22.30, PTS SN iii 31) 3. Bhāravagga Uppādasutta: The Discourse on Arising “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, does the arising of form occur? When what exists, by what being present, does the arising of feeling occur? When what exists, by what being present, does the arising of perception occur? When what exists, by what being present, does the arising of volitional formations occur? When what exists, by what being present, does the arising of consciousness occur? “Venerable sir, it is through these things being taught by the Blessed One that we understand: ‘When this exists, by the presence of this, there is the arising of form; when this exists, by the presence of this, there is the arising of feeling; when this exists, by the presence of this, there is the arising of perception; when this exists, by the presence of this, there is the arising of volitional formations; when this exists, by the presence of this, there is the arising of consciousness. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, does the arising of form occur? ... [and so on for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness] ... “Bhikkhus, when there is ignorance, by the presence of ignorance, there is the arising of volitional formations. When there is craving, by the presence of craving, there is the arising of clinging. When there is existence, by the presence of existence, there is the arising of birth. When there is birth, by the presence of birth, there is the arising of aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, does the cessation of form occur? When what exists, by what being present, does the cessation of feeling occur? When what exists, by what being present, does the cessation of perception occur? When what exists, by what being present, does the cessation of volitional formations occur? When what exists, by what being present, does the cessation of consciousness occur? “Venerable sir, it is through these things being taught by the Blessed One that we understand: ‘When this exists, by the presence of this, there is the cessation of form; when this exists, by the presence of this, there is the cessation of feeling; when this exists, by the presence of this, there is the cessation of perception; when this exists, by the presence of this, there is the cessation of volitional formations; when this exists, by the presence of this, there is the cessation of consciousness. “Bhikkhus, when there is no ignorance, by the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations. When there is no craving, by the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging. When there is no existence, by the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth. When there is no birth, by the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.”
At Sāvatthī.

"Bhikkhus, whatever is the arising, the persistence, the production, and the manifestation of form—that is the arising of suffering, the persistence of diseases, and the manifestation of aging and death.
Whatever is the [arising, etc.,] of feeling... [and so on].
Whatever is the arising, the persistence, the production, and the manifestation of perception... [and so on] ...of volitional formations...
[and so on] ...of consciousness: that is the arising of suffering, the persistence of diseases, and the manifestation of aging and death.
But, monks, that which is the cessation, the subsiding, the passing away of form— this is the cessation of suffering, the subsiding of diseases, the passing away of aging and death.
That which is [the cessation] of feeling … of perception … [and so on].

That which is the cessation, the subsiding, the passing away of volitional formations... that which is the cessation, the subsiding, the passing away of consciousness—that is the cessation of suffering, the subsiding of diseases, the passing away of aging and death.
The ninth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.31 (SN 22.31, PTS SN iii 32) 3. Bhāravagga Aghamūlasutta: The Root of Misfortune “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the root of misfortune and the root of good fortune. Listen and pay close attention; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “And what, bhikkhus, is the root of misfortune? Greed is the root of misfortune; hatred is the root of misfortune; delusion is the root of misfortune. This, bhikkhus, is called the root of misfortune. “And what, bhikkhus, is the root of good fortune? Non-greed is the root of good fortune; non-hatred is the root of good fortune; non-delusion is the root of good fortune. This, bhikkhus, is called the root of good fortune.”
At Sāvatthī.
“Monks, I will teach you about suffering and the root of suffering.
Listen to that.”
And what, monks, is misfortune? Form, monks, is misfortune;
feeling is misfortune; perception is misfortune; volitional formations are misfortune; consciousness is misfortune.
This, monks, is called misfortune.
And what, bhikkhus, is the root of misery?
It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there;
namely, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
"This, monks, is called the root of suffering.
Tenth. Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.32 (SN 22.32, PTS SN iii 32)
3. Bhāravagga:
Pabhaṅgu Sutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Monks, I will teach you what is fragile and what is not fragile.
Listen to that.
And what, monks, is fragile, and what is not fragile?
“Bhikkhus, form is fragile.
Its cessation, its subsiding, its passing away—this is non-fragile.
Feeling is fragile.”
That which is its cessation, its subsiding, its passing away—this is the imperishable.
Perception is perishable;
volitional formations are perishable.
That which is their cessation, pacification, and disappearance—this is indestructible.
Consciousness is destructible;
that which is its cessation, pacification, and disappearance—this is indestructible.”
Eleventh. The third chapter, the Chapter on the Burden.
Its summary verse:
Having fully understood the burden and directly known it,
with the fourth being desire and lust;
and the three kinds of gratification have been declared.
Abhinandana is the eighth; Uppāda, Aghamūla,
and Pabhaṅgu are the eleventh.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.33 4. The Chapter on What Does Not Belong to You The Discourse on What Does Not Belong to You “Bhikkhus, form is not yours; abandon it. By abandoning it, there will be freedom from suffering for a long time. Feeling is not yours... Perception is not yours... Formations are not yours... Consciousness is not yours; abandon it. By abandoning it, there will be freedom from suffering for a long time. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But, Bhante, what is form, and to whom does form belong? What is feeling, and to whom does feeling belong? What is perception, and to whom does perception belong? What are formations, and to whom do formations belong? What is consciousness, and to whom does consciousness belong? “Bhikkhu, form is not yours; abandon it. By abandoning it, there will be freedom from suffering for a long time. Feeling is not yours... Perception is not yours... Formations are not yours... Consciousness is not yours; abandon it. By abandoning it, there will be freedom from suffering for a long time. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, when one says, ‘Form is not mine,’ ‘Feeling is not mine,’ ‘Perception is not mine,’ ‘Formations are not mine,’ ‘Consciousness is not mine’—by means of what knowledge does one know this, and by means of what vision does one see this? “Bhikkhu, when one knows as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is suffering,’ and when one knows as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ and when one knows as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and when one knows as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—it is by means of such knowledge and such vision that one knows: ‘Form is not mine,’ ‘Feeling is not mine,’ ‘Perception is not mine,’ ‘Formations are not mine,’ ‘Consciousness is not mine. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, how does one know, and how does one see, so that, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external signs, there is no more I-making, mine-making, or the underlying tendency to conceit? “Bhikkhu, when one knows as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘All phenomena are non-self’—it is by means of such knowledge and such vision that, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external signs, there is no more I-making, mine-making, or the underlying tendency to conceit. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, how does one know, and how does one see, so that, through the destruction of craving, one is liberated, and having been liberated, one knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being’? “Bhikkhu, when one knows as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the origin of suffering’... ‘This is the cessation of suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—it is by means of such knowledge and such vision that, through the destruction of craving, one is liberated, and having been liberated, one knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the full admission. Then that bhikkhu received the going forth under the Blessed One, and he received the full admission. And soon, not long after his full admission, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, that bhikkhu realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having entered upon it, he dwelt therein. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And that venerable one became another of the arahants.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it.
When you have abandoned it, that will lead to your welfare and happiness.”
And what, monks, is not yours?
Form, monks, is not yours; abandon it.
When it is abandoned by you, that will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Feeling is not yours; abandon it.
When it is abandoned, it will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Perception is not yours...
Volitional formations are not yours; abandon them.
When they are abandoned, they will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Consciousness is not yours; abandon it.
"That which has been abandoned by you will lead to your welfare and happiness.

Just as if, monks, someone were to take away, or burn, or do whatever they please with the grass, sticks, branches, and foliage in this Jeta Grove—would it occur to you: [‘This is being taken from us,’ ‘This is being burned,’ or ‘This is being done with us’?]"
“Does anyone carry us away, or burn us, or do with us as they please?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“And for what reason?”
“Indeed not, Bhante; this is neither our self nor what belongs to our self.
“In the same way, monks, form is not yours; abandon it.
When it is abandoned by you, it will lead to your welfare and happiness.”
Feeling is not yours; abandon it.
When it is abandoned by you, it will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Perception is not yours...
“Volitional formations are not yours… consciousness is not yours; abandon it.
Its abandonment will lead to your welfare and happiness.”
First.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.34 (SN 22.34, PTS SN iii 34) 4. The Chapter on What Does Not Belong to You (Natumhāka-vagga)
The Second Discourse on What Belongs to You.
Setting at Sāvatthī:
“Bhikkhus, whatever does not belong to you, abandon that.
That which has been abandoned by you will lead to your welfare and happiness.
And what, monks, is not yours?
Form, monks, is not yours; abandon it.
That being abandoned will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Feeling is not yours… perception is not yours…
Volitional formations are not yours… consciousness is not yours; abandon it.
Its abandonment will lead to your welfare and happiness.
“Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it.
When that has been abandoned, it will lead to your welfare and happiness. This is the second [sutta].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.35 The Discourse to a Certain Bhikkhu (From the Chapter on "Not Yours") At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One said this to a certain bhikkhu: "Bhikkhu, do you regard form as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'? "No, venerable sir. "Bhikkhu, do you regard feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'? "No, venerable sir. "Then, bhikkhu, what is it that you do not regard as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'? "Venerable sir, I do not regard form as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self. I do not regard feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self. "Good, good, bhikkhu! It is good that you do not regard form as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self,' and that you do not regard feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self. For, bhikkhu, if one were to regard form as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self,' then with the change and alteration of form, there would arise in one sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. If one were to regard feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self,' then with the change and alteration of consciousness, there would arise in one sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Therefore, bhikkhu, whatever is not yours, abandon it; abandoning it, it will be for your long-term welfare and happiness. And what, bhikkhu, is not yours? Form is not yours: abandon it. Feeling is not yours: abandon it. Perception is not yours: abandon it. Volitional formations are not yours: abandon them. Consciousness is not yours: abandon it. Abandoning it, it will be for your long-term welfare and happiness. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous how well the Dhamma has been taught by the Blessed One, so that one who has gone forth can truly know: 'I am not, and it is not mine. "Indeed, bhikkhu, it is wonderful, it is marvelous how well the Dhamma has been taught by the Tathāgata, so that one who has gone forth can truly know: 'I am not, and it is not mine. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, I now go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last. "Surely, bhikkhu, those who have gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha for their entire lives are declared to be of right view; they possess a firm foundation. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, that bhikkhu delighted in the Blessed One's words. (This concludes the third discourse in the Chapter on "Not Yours.")
At Sāvatthī.
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief.”
“Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, may I dwell alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, and resolute.
“Bhikkhu, by whatever one is under the influence of a latent tendency, by that one is reckoned;
by whatever one is not under the influence of a latent tendency, by that one is not reckoned.”
“Understood, Blessed One; understood, Sugata.
“But how, monk, do you understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief?
“If, venerable sir, one is obsessed by form, one is reckoned by that [form].”
If one underlies feeling, one is reckoned by that;
if one underlies perception, one is reckoned by that;
if one underlies volitional formations, one is reckoned by that.

If consciousness underlies one, by that one is reckoned. If form, venerable sir, does not underlie one, one is not reckoned by that. If feeling... [does not underlie one... [one is not reckoned by that. ...if consciousness... [does not underlie one... [one is not reckoned by that.]
If one does not underlie perception... if one does not underlie volitional formations...
if one does not underlie consciousness, one does not thereby come to be reckoned by way of that.
“Venerable sir, it is in this way that I understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by the Blessed One in brief.
“Excellent, excellent, monk!
It is well, monk, that you understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief.”
If, bhikkhu, one underlies form, by that one comes to be reckoned [as such].
If one underlies feeling...
if one underlies perception...
If one underlies volitional formations...
or if one underlies consciousness, by that one is reckoned.
But if, bhikkhu, one does not underlie form, one is not reckoned by that.
If feeling...
if perception...
if mental formations...
“If one does not underlie consciousness, one does not thereby come to be reckoned by it.
This, monk, is how the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief should be understood in detail.
Then that monk, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, that bhikkhu, before long,

realized for himself through direct knowledge in this very life that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness; having attained it, he dwelt therein.
“He has understood: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
And that bhikkhu became one of the arahants. Thus ends the third [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.36 (SN 22.36, PTS SN iii 36) 4. Natumhākavagga The Second Discourse to a Certain Bhikkhu At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One said this to a certain bhikkhu: “Bhikkhu, do you regard form as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. “Bhikkhu, do you regard feeling as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. “Bhikkhu, do you regard perception as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. “Bhikkhu, do you regard volitional formations as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. “Bhikkhu, do you regard consciousness as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. “Bhikkhu, since you do not regard these five aggregates subject to clinging in such a way, for what else could there be an ‘I am’? When this was said, that bhikkhu was silent. A second time and a third time, the Blessed One asked him the same question, and a second and a third time, that bhikkhu was silent. Then it occurred to the Venerable Ānanda: “Why does this bhikkhu remain silent? Perhaps he is afraid of the Blessed One. So the Venerable Ānanda said to that bhikkhu: “What do you think, friend bhikkhu? Is form permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, venerable sir. “But is what is impermanent suffering or happiness? “Suffering, venerable sir. “But is what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change fit to be regarded thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. [And so on for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. “What do you think, friend bhikkhu? Since you have seen with right wisdom according to reality as it actually is, that all things are not-self, would it be fitting for you to regard anything as ‘I am’? “No, venerable sir. “Good, good, friend bhikkhu! It is good that you have understood the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in this way. For this, friend, is the teaching of the Blessed One: ‘All things are not-self. When this was said, that bhikkhu asked the Venerable Ānanda: “But, friend Ānanda, where does this ‘I am’ come to be? “‘I am,’ friend, is a mere designation; ‘I am this’ is a mere designation; ‘I am otherwise’ is a mere designation; ‘I am not’ is a mere designation; ‘I shall be’ is a mere designation; ‘I shall not be’ is a mere designation; ‘I shall be possessed of form’ is a mere designation; ‘I shall be formless’ is a mere designation; ‘I shall be percipient’ is a mere designation; ‘I shall be non-percipient’ is a mere designation; ‘I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient’ is a mere designation. These, friend, are merely designations in the world, mere expressions, mere manners of speaking, mere common usage, mere designations in the world, which the Tathāgata uses, without being led by them, knowing their origin, knowing their passing away, knowing their gratification, knowing their danger, and knowing the escape from them. When this was said, that bhikkhu asked the Venerable Ānanda: “But, friend Ānanda, where do these designations cease without remainder? “Here, friend, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Here these designations cease without remainder. “Again, friend, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

Here these designations cease without remainder. When this was said, that bhikkhu asked the Venerable Ānanda: “But, friend Ānanda, where do these perceptions and feelings cease without remainder? “Here, friend, with the complete transcending of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impingement, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] ‘space is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. Here these perceptions and feelings cease without remainder. “Again, friend, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, [perceiving] ‘consciousness is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. Here these perceptions and feelings cease without remainder. “Again, friend, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, [perceiving] ‘there is nothing,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. Here these perceptions and feelings cease without remainder. “Again, friend, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Here these perceptions and feelings cease without remainder. “Again, friend, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. And here these perceptions and feelings cease without remainder. When this was said, that bhikkhu asked the Venerable Ānanda: “But, friend Ānanda, where does this consciousness turn back? “Consciousness turns back, friend, having reached its limit at the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. When this was said, that bhikkhu asked the Venerable Ānanda: “But, friend Ānanda, who is it that turns back? “Friend, it is ‘one who has craving’ who turns back, not ‘one who is without craving. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Venerable Ānanda: “It is wonderful, friend Ānanda, it is marvelous, friend Ānanda, how well this has been stated by the Venerable Ānanda! It is as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry a lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. Just so, the Dhamma has been made clear by the Venerable Ānanda in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, I go for refuge to the Dhamma, I go for refuge to the Saṅgha. May the Venerable Ānanda accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...and sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:

“It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.”
“Bhikkhu, whatever one underlies, that one infers;
what one infers, by that one comes to reckon.
What one does not underlie, one does not infer.”
“That which is not inferred does not fall into reckoning.
“Understood, Blessed One; understood, Sugata.
“But how, monk, do you understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief?”
“If, venerable sir, one underlies form, one is measured by it;
what one is measured by comes to be reckoned as that.
If one underlies feeling …”
If one underlies perception,
or if one underlies volitional formations,
or if one underlies consciousness, one is measured by that.
Whatever is inferred is thereby reckoned.
If, venerable sir, one does not underlie form with a latent tendency, it is not inferred;
what is not inferred is not thereby reckoned.
If one does not underlie feeling...
if one does not underlie perception...
if one does not underlie volitional formations...
“If one does not underlie consciousness, it is not inferred;
what is not inferred does not come to be reckoned by that.
This, venerable sir, is how I understand in detail the meaning of what was stated by the Blessed One in brief.”
“Excellent, excellent, bhikkhu!
It is good that you, bhikkhu, understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief.
If one is obsessed with form, bhikkhu, one is measured by it.”
Whatever is inferred by that comes under the category of "reckoning.
Whether it be feeling, monk,
or perception, monk...
If, bhikkhu, one underlies volitional formations...
or if, bhikkhu, one underlies consciousness, one is measured by that;
by what one is measured, one comes to be reckoned accordingly.
If, bhikkhu, one does not underlie form with a latent tendency, one does not infer it;
what one does not infer does not become reckoned by that.
If one does not underlie feeling with a latent tendency...
If one does not underlie perception, ...
if one does not underlie volitional formations, ...
if one does not underlie consciousness, one is not inferred by that.
"What is not inferred does not enter into reckoning.
This, monk, is how the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief should be understood in detail.
... [and] that certain monk became one of the arahants.
The Fourth.

4. Natumhākavagga.
Second Discourse to Ānanda.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
As the Venerable Ānanda was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Ānanda, if you were asked:
‘Friend Ānanda, of which phenomena was arising discerned, passing away discerned, and alteration while persisting discerned?’”
“Of which phenomena will arising be discerned, passing away be discerned, and change while persisting be discerned?
Of which phenomena is arising discerned, passing away discerned, and change while persisting discerned?
Being asked this, Ānanda, how would you answer?”
“If, venerable sir, they were to ask me thus:
‘Of what things, friend Ānanda, was arising discerned, passing away discerned, and alteration while standing discerned?
Of what things will arising be discerned, passing away be discerned, and alteration while standing be discerned?’”
‘Of which phenomena is arising discerned, passing away discerned, and the alteration of that which persists discerned?
Being asked thus, venerable sir, I would answer:
‘That form, friend, which is past, ceased, and changed;’”
Its arising was discerned, its passing away was discerned, and its alteration while persisting was discerned.
As for that feeling which is past, ceased, and changed:
its arising was discerned, its passing away was discerned, and its alteration while persisting was discerned.
Whatever perceptions… whatever volitional formations have passed away, ceased, and changed:
their arising was discerned, their passing away was discerned, and the alteration of that which stood was discerned.
That consciousness which was past, ceased, and changed:
its arising was discerned, its passing away was discerned, and its alteration while persisting was discerned.
Indeed, friends, it is of these phenomena that their arising was discerned, their passing away was discerned, and their alteration while persisting was discerned.
Friend, whatever form has not been born and has not become manifest—
its arising will be discerned, its passing away will be discerned, and its alteration while persisting will be discerned.
Whatever feeling has not been born and has not become manifest...
Its arising will be discerned, its passing away will be discerned, and its alteration while persisting will be discerned.
As for perception … [and] those volitional formations that are unborn and unmanifested:
Their arising will be discerned, their passing away will be discerned, and the alteration of that which stands will be discerned.
As for that consciousness which is unborn and unmanifested:
its arising will be discerned, its passing away will be discerned, and the alteration of that which stands will be discerned.
"Friends, for these phenomena, arising will be discerned, passing away will be discerned, and change while persisting will be discerned.
Whatever form has been born and has become manifest—
of that, arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, and change while persisting is discerned."
Whatever feeling has arisen and become manifest ...
whatever perception ...
whatever formations have arisen and become manifest;
‘Their arising is discerned, their passing away is discerned, and the alteration of that which stands is discerned.
Of whatever consciousness has been born and manifested, its arising is discerned, its passing away is discerned, and the alteration of that which stands is discerned.
It is of these phenomena, friends, that their arising is discerned, their passing away is discerned, and the alteration of that which stands is discerned.’”
“If asked thus, Bhante, I would answer in this way.
“Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!
For that form, Ānanda, which is past, ceased, and changed;”
Its arising was discerned, its passing away was discerned, and its alteration while persisting was discerned.
This is true of whatever feeling... whatever perception... [there may be].
Those volitional formations … that consciousness which was past, ceased, and changed:
its arising was discerned, its passing away was discerned, and its alteration while persisting was discerned.
“Ānanda, for these phenomena, arising was discerned, passing away was discerned, and change while persisting was discerned.
Ānanda, as for that form which has not yet been born and has not yet become manifest:
its arising will be discerned, its passing away will be discerned, and its change while persisting will be discerned.”
Whatever feeling...
whatever perception...
whatever volitional formations...
That consciousness which is unborn and unmanifested—
its arising will be discerned, its passing away will be discerned, and its alteration while persisting will be discerned. Indeed, Ānanda,
it is of these phenomena that their arising will be discerned, their passing away will be discerned, and their alteration while persisting will be discerned.
Ānanda, whatever form has been born, has become manifest— in that,
arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, and the alteration of that which persists is discerned.
Whatever feeling has been born, has become manifest...
Whatever perception...
whatever volitional formations...
whatever consciousness has been born and has become manifest;
“Arising is discerned for it, passing away is discerned, and the alteration of that which stands is discerned.
It is for these phenomena, Ānanda, that arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, and the alteration of that which stands is discerned.
Being asked thus, Ānanda, you should answer in this way.”
The Sixth.

Natumhākavagga (The Chapter on "Not Yours")
The Discourse on the Dharma in Accordance with the Dharma. Setting at Sāvatthī.
“Monks, for a monk who practices in accordance with the Dharma, this is the practice in accordance with the Dharma.”

One should dwell frequently with disenchantment toward form, one should dwell frequently with disenchantment toward feeling, one should dwell frequently with disenchantment toward perception, one should dwell frequently with disenchantment toward volitional formations, and one should dwell frequently with disenchantment toward consciousness.

One who dwells frequently with disenchantment toward form, and who dwells frequently with disenchantment toward feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness, fully understands form; he fully understands feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness.

“Thus, by fully understanding form, by fully understanding feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness, one is liberated from form, liberated from feeling, liberated from perception, liberated from volitional formations, liberated from consciousness;
one is liberated from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; one is liberated from suffering, I say.
The seventh [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.40 (SN 22.40, PTS SN iii 41) 4. Natumhākavagga Second Discourse on Conformity with the Dhamma (Dutiya-anudhamma-sutta) “Bhikkhus, whatever is not yours, you should abandon it. When you have abandoned it, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. And what, bhikkhus, is not yours? Form is not yours; abandon it. When you have abandoned it, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. Feeling is not yours; abandon it... Perception is not yours; abandon it... Volitional formations are not yours; abandon them... Consciousness is not yours; abandon it. When you have abandoned it, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But, Bhante, what is form, whose is form, from where has form come? “Bhikkhu, form is impermanent; it is not yours, you should abandon it. When you have abandoned it, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. Feeling is impermanent... Perception is impermanent... Volitional formations are impermanent... Consciousness is impermanent; it is not yours, you should abandon it. When you have abandoned it, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But, Bhante, what is form, whose is form, from where has form come? What is feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, whose is consciousness, from where has consciousness come? “Bhikkhu, form arises from ignorance; when ignorance ceases, form ceases. Feeling arises from ignorance... Perception arises from ignorance... Volitional formations arise from ignorance... Consciousness arises from ignorance; when ignorance ceases, consciousness ceases. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, is it the case that form is one thing and the one who knows form is another? Is it the case that feeling is one thing and the one who knows feeling is another? Is it the case that perception is one thing and the one who knows perception is another? Is it the case that volitional formations are one thing and the one who knows volitional formations is another? Is it the case that consciousness is one thing and the one who knows consciousness is another? “Bhikkhu, it is not the case that form is one thing and the one who knows form is another. It is not the case that feeling is one thing and the one who knows feeling is another. It is not the case that perception is one thing and the one who knows perception is another. It is not the case that volitional formations are one thing and the one who knows volitional formations is another. It is not the case that consciousness is one thing and the one who knows consciousness is another. Rather, bhikkhu, it is this very same consciousness that knows form, that knows feeling, that knows perception, that knows volitional formations. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, if it is this very same consciousness that knows form, that knows feeling, that knows perception, that knows volitional formations, then, Bhante, the continuity of consciousness is eternal, and there is no liberation from suffering. “Bhikkhu, it is not the case that the continuity of consciousness is eternal, nor is there no liberation from suffering. For, bhikkhu, when one sees with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—then, bhikkhu, by means of this very same knowledge, one is liberated from suffering. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, if it is by means of this very same knowledge that one is liberated from suffering, then, Bhante, the one who knows is the liberation, and the liberation is the one who knows. “Bhikkhu, it is not the case that the one who knows is the liberation, nor that the liberation is the one who knows. Rather, bhikkhu, it is by means of this very same knowledge that one is liberated from suffering. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, if it is by means of this very same knowledge that one is liberated from suffering, then, Bhante, the one who knows is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the one who knows. “Bhikkhu, it is not the case that the one who knows is the Tathāgata, nor that the Tathāgata is the one who knows. Rather, bhikkhu, it is by means of this very same knowledge that the Tathāgata is liberated from suffering. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, if it is by means of this very same knowledge that the Tathāgata is liberated from suffering, then, Bhante, the Tathāgata is the knowledge, and the knowledge is the Tathāgata. “Bhikkhu, it is not the case that the Tathāgata is the knowledge, nor that the knowledge is the Tathāgata. Rather, bhikkhu, it is by means of this very same knowledge that the Tathāgata is liberated from suffering. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One:

At Sāvatthī.
