4. Natumhākavagga:
The Fourth Discourse on Conformity with the Dhamma.
Setting at Sāvatthī.

“Monks, for a monk who practices in accordance with the Dhamma, this is the practice in accordance with the Dhamma: that he should dwell contemplating non-self in form, and dwell contemplating non-self in feeling … in perception … in volitional formations … in consciousness.
One who dwells contemplating non-self in form … [as before] … fully understands form;
he fully understands feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness. Fully understanding form, feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness…”
“By fully understanding, one is liberated from form; one is liberated from feeling; one is liberated from perception;
one is liberated from volitional formations; one is liberated from consciousness; one is liberated from birth, aging, and death, from sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs.
One is liberated from suffering—so I say. This was the tenth [discourse].
The fourth chapter, "Not Yours," is concluded.
Its summary verse:
Two [verses] were spoken beginning with "Not yours."
Two others were spoken of by the monks; two by Ānanda;
and two difficult [cases] regarding secondary rules (anudhamma).

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.43 (SN 22.43, PTS SN iii 42) 5. Attadīpavagga Attadīpasutta (The Discourse on Being an Island unto Oneself) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, it is by being an island unto oneself, a refuge unto oneself, with no other refuge, that one dwells with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, Bhante, does one dwell as an island unto oneself, a refuge unto oneself, with no other refuge, dwelling with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge? “Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. It is in this way, bhikkhu, that one dwells as an island unto oneself, a refuge unto oneself, with no other refuge, dwelling with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, Bhante, does one dwell contemplating the body in the body? “Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu goes to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, and sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out. Breathing in long, he understands: ‘I breathe in long’; or breathing out long, he understands: ‘I breathe out long. Breathing in short, he understands: ‘I breathe in short’; or breathing out short, he understands: ‘I breathe out short. He trains thus: ‘Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe out. Just as a skilled turner or his apprentice, when making a long turn, understands: ‘I make a long turn,’ or when making a short turn, understands: ‘I make a short turn’; so too, a bhikkhu breathes in long and understands: ‘I breathe in long’... [as above] ...he trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe out. He dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, externally, and both internally and externally; he dwells contemplating its arising factors, its vanishing factors, and both its arising and vanishing factors in the body. Or else, mindfulness that ‘there is a body’ is simply established in him to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. It is in this way, bhikkhu, that one dwells contemplating the body in the body. [The Blessed One continued: “And how, bhikkhu, does one dwell contemplating feelings in feelings? Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu feels a pleasant feeling, and he understands: ‘I feel a pleasant feeling’; he feels a painful feeling, and he understands: ‘I feel a painful feeling’; he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and he understands: ‘I feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. When he feels a pleasant worldly feeling, he understands: ‘I feel a pleasant worldly feeling’; when he feels a pleasant spiritual feeling, he understands: ‘I feel a pleasant spiritual feeling’; when he feels a painful worldly feeling, he understands: ‘I feel a painful worldly feeling’; when he feels a painful spiritual feeling, he understands: ‘I feel a painful spiritual feeling’; when he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant worldly feeling, he understands: ‘I feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant worldly feeling’; when he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant spiritual feeling, he understands: ‘I feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant spiritual feeling. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings internally, externally, and both internally and externally; he dwells contemplating their arising factors, their vanishing factors, and both their arising and vanishing factors in feelings. Or else, mindfulness that ‘there is feeling’ is simply established in him to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. It is in this way, bhikkhu, that one dwells contemplating feelings in feelings. [The Blessed One continued: “And how, bhikkhu, does one dwell contemplating mind in the mind? Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu understands a mind with lust as a mind with lust; he understands a mind without lust as a mind without lust. He understands a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred; he understands a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred. He understands a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion; he understands a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion. He understands a contracted mind as a contracted mind; he understands a distracted mind as a distracted mind. He understands a great mind as a great mind; he understands an immeasurable mind as an immeasurable mind. He understands a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind; he understands an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind. He understands a liberated mind as a liberated mind; he understands an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind. He dwells contemplating mind in the mind internally, externally, and both internally and externally; he dwells contemplating its arising factors, its vanishing factors, and both its arising and vanishing factors in the mind.

Or else, mindfulness that ‘there is mind’ is simply established in him to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. It is in this way, bhikkhu, that one dwells contemplating mind in the mind. [The Blessed One continued: “And how, bhikkhu, does one dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena? Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena in terms of the five hindrances... in terms of the five aggregates subject to clinging... in terms of the six internal and external sense bases... in terms of the seven factors of enlightenment... in terms of the Four Noble Truths. And how, bhikkhu, does one dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena in terms of the Four Noble Truths? Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally, externally, and both internally and externally; he dwells contemplating their arising factors, their vanishing factors, and both their arising and vanishing factors in phenomena. Or else, mindfulness that ‘there are phenomena’ is simply established in him to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. It is in this way, bhikkhu, that one dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena. “It is in this way, bhikkhu, that one dwells as an island unto oneself, a refuge unto oneself, with no other refuge, dwelling with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante! Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. We go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. May we receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may we receive the full admission. Then that bhikkhu received the going forth under the Blessed One, and he received the full admission. And soon, not long after his full admission, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, that bhikkhu realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed consummation of the spiritual life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having entered upon it, he dwelt therein. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And that venerable one became one of the arahants.
At Sāvatthī.
“Monks, dwell with yourselves as an island, with yourselves as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge.
For those who dwell with themselves as an island, with themselves as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge...”
The source of those who have no other refuge should be examined: "Of what nature are sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; what is their origin?
And of what nature, monks, are sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; what is their origin?

Here, monks, the uninstructed worldling—who has no regard for the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has no regard for true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—[is subject to them].
One regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form.
When that form of his changes and becomes otherwise,
then with the change and alteration of that form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in him.
One regards feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling, or feeling as being in self, or self as being in feeling.
That feeling of his changes and becomes otherwise.
With the change and alteration of that feeling, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in him.
One regards perception as self...
one regards mental formations as self...
one regards consciousness as self, or the self as possessing consciousness; or consciousness as being in the self, or the self as being in consciousness.
That consciousness of his changes and becomes otherwise.
With the change and alteration of that consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in him.
But, monks, having understood the impermanence, the change, the fading away, and the cessation of form, [one understands]: "In the past..."
“Whatever form there was in the past, whatever form there will be in the future, and whatever form there is now—all that form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
When one sees this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are abandoned.
With their abandonment, one does not tremble; not trembling, one dwells in happiness. A bhikkhu who dwells in happiness is said to be “extinguished in that respect” (*tadaṅga-nibbuto*).
But, monks, by knowing the impermanence, change, fading away, and cessation of feeling itself,
and seeing it as it really is with right wisdom thus: "Both past feeling and present feeling— all feelings— are impermanent, suffering,
and subject to change," those sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs that arise are abandoned.
With their abandoning, he does not tremble; not trembling, he dwells in happiness. A bhikkhu dwelling in happiness is said to be “extinguished in that respect.
Having understood the impermanence, change, fading away, and cessation of perceptions... and of volitional formations, monks, [he thinks]: "Previously..."
“Both past conditioned phenomena and all present conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
When one sees this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are abandoned.
With their abandonment, one does not tremble; not trembling, one dwells in happiness. A bhikkhu dwelling in happiness is said to be “extinguished in that respect.”
But by understanding the impermanence, change, fading away, and cessation of consciousness itself, monks—

seeing it as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "Both past consciousness and present consciousness, all consciousness, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change"— those sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs are abandoned.
“With their abandonment, he does not tremble; not trembling, he dwells in happiness. A bhikkhu dwelling in happiness is said to be ‘extinguished in that respect.
Thus was the first [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.44. (SN 22.44, PTS SN iii 43)
5. Attadīpavagga:
Paṭipadāsutta.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
“Monks, I will teach you the practice that leads to the arising of identity and the practice that leads to the cessation of identity.
Listen to that.
And what, monks, is the practice that leads to the arising of identity?”

Here, monks, an uninstructed worldling—who has no regard for the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has no regard for true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as being in self, or self as being in form.
He regards feeling as self...

One regards perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception as in self, or self as in perception. One regards volitional formations as self... One regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.
“Monks, this is called ‘the practice leading to the origin of identity; the practice leading to the origin of identity.
Thus, monks, it is said: ‘the contemplation leading to the origin of suffering.
This is precisely the meaning here.”
And what, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of identity?
Here, monks, a well-taught noble disciple—who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and is well-trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones;

who has seen true persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and is well-trained in the Dhamma of true persons—does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as being in self, nor self as being in form.
One does not regard feeling as self… nor perception… nor volitional formations…
One does not regard consciousness as self, nor self as possessing consciousness; nor consciousness as being in self, nor self as being in consciousness.
This, monks, is called ‘the practice leading to the cessation of identity, the practice leading to the cessation of identity.
Thus, monks, this is called ‘the contemplation leading to the cessation of suffering.’
“This is precisely the meaning here.
Second.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.45 (SN 22.45, PTS SN iii 44).
5. Attadīpavagga:
Aniccasutta.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, form is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering;
what is suffering is non-self.”
That which is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
For one who sees this as it really is with correct wisdom, the mind becomes dispassionate and is liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
Feeling is impermanent...
Perception … volitional formations … consciousness are impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering;
what is suffering is non-self;
what is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.”
When one sees this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, the mind becomes dispassionate and is liberated from the taints through non-clinging.

Monks, if a monk’s mind is dispassionate and liberated from the taints through non-clinging regarding the element of form, regarding the element of feeling … [and so on] … regarding the element of perception … [and so on] … [regarding the element of volitional formations … and so on] … regarding the element of consciousness, then his mind is dispassionate and liberated from the taints through non-clinging.

If, monks, a bhikkhu’s mind is dispassionate toward the element of volitional formations … and the element of consciousness, and is liberated from the taints through non-clinging, then because it is liberated, it is steadfast;
because it is steadfast, it is content; because it is content, it does not tremble. Not trembling, he attains final Nibbāna right here within himself.
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being,’ he understands.
Thus it was said. Third. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.46. (SN 22.46, PTS SN iii 45)
5. Attadīpavagga.
Second Discourse on Impermanence.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, form is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering;
what is suffering is non-self.”
That which is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
Feeling is impermanent...
perception is impermanent...
Volitional formations are impermanent… consciousness is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering;
That which is suffering is non-self;
that which is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
For one who sees this as it really is with correct wisdom, views regarding the past do not arise.
When there is no view regarding the past, there are no views regarding the future.
When there are no views regarding the future, there is no stubborn adherence.
When there is no stubborn adherence, [craving] for form...
In feeling … in perception … in volitional formations …
“Consciousness becomes dispassionate toward consciousness and is liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
Because it is liberated, it is steadied; because it is steadied, it is content; because it is content, it does not tremble. Not trembling, one attains final Nibbāna by oneself, realizing:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”
The Fourth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.47 (SN 22.47, PTS SN iii 46) 5. Attadīpavagga (The Chapter on Being One’s Own Island)
The Discourse on Contemplation. At Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins contemplate the self in various ways, they all contemplate the five aggregates of clinging, or one or another of them.”
Which five?

Here, monks, an uninstructed worldling—unseeing of the noble ones, unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; unseeing of true persons, unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form.
Feeling … perception … volitional formations …
One regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.
Thus, this very way of regarding things persists, and the thought "I am" has not yet vanished for him.
Monks, when the thought "I am" has not vanished, there occurs the descent of the five faculties.
There is the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, and the body-faculty.
There is, monks, the mind, there are mental phenomena, and there is the element of ignorance.
When an uninstructed worldling, touched by a feeling born of contact with ignorance, thinks "I am"; that is so for him.
‘This I am’ occurs to him;
‘I shall be’ occurs to him;
‘I shall not be’ occurs to him.
‘I shall be possessed of form’ occurs to him;
‘I shall be formless’ occurs to him;
‘I shall be percipient’ occurs to him.
‘I shall be non-percipient,’ this occurs to him;
‘I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient,’ this occurs to him.
Yet, monks, those very five faculties remain right there.
Then, in this case, for the learned noble disciple, ignorance is abandoned and true knowledge arises.
With the fading away of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge, the thought "I am" does not occur to him,
nor does the thought "This I am" occur to him.
‘I shall be’ … ‘I shall not be’ … ‘possessing form’ …
formless … percipient … non-percipient …
“‘I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient’—even this does not occur to him.
The fifth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.48 (SN 22.48, PTS SN iii 47).
5. Attadīpavagga, Khandhasutta.
Setting at Savatthi.
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the five aggregates and the five aggregates subject to clinging.
Listen to that.
And what, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates?”
“Bhikkhus, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that is called the aggregate of form.
Whatever feeling there is … [and so on] … whatever perception there is …”
Whatever formations there are—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; ... [as before] ... this is called the aggregate of formations.
Whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—this is called the aggregate of consciousness.
These, monks, are called the five aggregates.
"And what, monks, are the five aggregates of clinging?

Whatever form, monks, is past, future, or present ... [as before] ... whether far or near, that which is accompanied by taints (sāsava) and subject to clinging—this is called the form aggregate of clinging.
Whatever feeling ... [as before] ... whether far or near, that which is accompanied by taints and subject to clinging—this is called the feeling aggregate of clinging."

Whatever kind of perception there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—whatever is accompanied by taints (*sāsava*) and subject to clinging (*upādāniya*), this is called the aggregate of clinging to perception (*saññupādānakkhandha*).

Whatever kind of mental formations there are—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—whatever are accompanied by taints and subject to clinging, these are called the aggregate of clinging to mental formations (*saṅkhārupādānakkhandha*).

Whatever kind of consciousness there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—whatever is accompanied by taints and subject to clinging, this is called the aggregate of clinging to consciousness (*viññāṇupādānakkhandha*).
“Monks, these are called the five aggregates subject to clinging.
The sixth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.49 (SN 22.49, PTS SN iii 48).
5. Attadīpavagga, Soṇasutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then Soṇa, the householder’s son, approached the Blessed One...
[as before] ...and sat down to one side. As Soṇa, the householder’s son, was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Whatever recluses or brahmins, Soṇa, regard form— which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change— with the thought,
‘I am superior,’ or regard it with the thought, ‘I am equal,’ or regard it with the thought, ‘I am inferior’— ”
What else is there but the non-seeing of things as they really are?
Regarding feeling—which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—they regard it thus:
"I am superior," or they regard it thus: "I am equal."
Or they regard themselves as "inferior"—
what is this other than a failure to see things as they truly are?
[This applies to] the perception of impermanence...
Regarding conditioned phenomena that are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, they regard them as:
"I am superior," or they regard them as: "I am equal," or they regard them as: "I am inferior."
What else is there but the failure to see things as they really are?
On account of a consciousness that is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, they regard it thus:
"I am superior," or they regard it thus: "I am equal."
Or they regard themselves as "inferior"—
what else could this be but a failure to see things as they truly are?
And yet, Soṇa, there are some ascetics or brahmins who, regarding form— which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change— do not even regard themselves as "superior."
They do not regard themselves as equal,
nor do they regard themselves as inferior;
for what else is there but the seeing of things as they truly are?
In impermanent feeling … in impermanent perception … in impermanent volitional formations …
With regard to consciousness, which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,
they do not regard it as ‘I am better,’ nor do they regard it as ‘I am equal,’ nor do they regard it as ‘I am inferior.’
What else is there than the seeing of things as they really are?
What do you think, Soṇa,
is form permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“Is feeling permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.
… “Perception …”
“Are volitional formations … consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.”
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:”
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“Therefore, Soṇa, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external—”
Whether gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form should be seen as it actually is with right wisdom thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
Whatever feeling there may be...
Whatever perception there is … whatever formations there are … whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle—
Whether inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.

Seeing thus, Soṇa, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness.
“Becoming disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated. One understands:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This is the seventh [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.50 5. Attadīpavagga The Second Discourse on Soṇa At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is one who has made a refuge for himself, who has made an island for himself, who has made a final recourse for himself, and does not seek a refuge other than himself, nor an island other than himself, nor a final recourse other than himself—how is a bhikkhu one who has made a refuge for himself, who has made an island for himself, who has made a final recourse for himself, and does not seek a refuge other than himself, nor an island other than himself, nor a final recourse other than himself? It is, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; when he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... when he dwells contemplating mind in the mind... when he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world—in this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has made a refuge for himself, who has made an island for himself, who has made a final recourse for himself, and does not seek a refuge other than himself, nor an island other than himself, nor a final recourse other than himself. When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has made a refuge for himself, who has made an island for himself, who has made a final recourse for himself, and does not seek a refuge other than himself, nor an island other than himself, nor a final recourse other than himself, then, whether night or day comes, he dwells in comfort, and his mind inclines toward Nibbāna. Just as, bhikkhus, a well-constructed wooden bowl, when placed on a stand, remains steady and does not wobble, so too, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is one who has made a refuge for himself... then, whether night or day comes, he dwells in comfort, and his mind inclines toward Nibbāna. Just as, bhikkhus, a well-trimmed oil lamp, when set in a sheltered place, burns brightly and does not flicker, so too, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is one who has made a refuge for himself... then, whether night or day comes, he dwells in comfort, and his mind inclines toward Nibbāna. Just as, bhikkhus, a mountain peak, rising high above the surrounding plains, remains firm and unshakable by the winds that blow from the four quarters, so too, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is one who has made a refuge for himself... then, whether night or day comes, he dwells in comfort, and his mind inclines toward Nibbāna. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall become those who have made a refuge for themselves, who have made an island for themselves, who have made a final recourse for themselves, and who do not seek a refuge other than themselves, nor an island other than themselves, nor a final recourse other than themselves. Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went into his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, the venerable Soṇa approached the venerable Ānanda and said: “Friend Ānanda, the Blessed One has spoken these verses: ‘One who has made a refuge for oneself, Who has made an island for oneself, Who has made a final recourse for oneself, And does not seek a refuge other than oneself, Nor an island other than oneself, Nor a final recourse other than oneself— Whether night or day comes, He dwells in comfort, And his mind inclines toward Nibbāna. Just as a well-constructed wooden bowl, When placed on a stand, Remains steady and does not wobble, So too, when a bhikkhu is one who has made a refuge for himself... Just as a well-trimmed oil lamp, When set in a sheltered place, Burns brightly and does not flicker, So too, when a bhikkhu is one who has made a refuge for himself... Just as a mountain peak, Rising high above the surrounding plains, Remains firm and unshakable by the winds, So too, when a bhikkhu is one who has made a refuge for himself... Friend Ānanda, I do not understand the full meaning of these verses spoken by the Blessed One in brief. It would be good, friend Ānanda, if you could explain to me the full meaning of these verses spoken by the Blessed One in brief.

“Then listen, friend Soṇa, and attend closely. I will speak. “Yes, friend,” the venerable Soṇa replied to the venerable Ānanda. The venerable Ānanda said this: “Here, friend Soṇa, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. When, friend Soṇa, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, then, whether night or day comes, he dwells in comfort, and his mind inclines toward Nibbāna. When, friend Soṇa, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... when he dwells contemplating mind in the mind... when he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, then, whether night or day comes, he dwells in comfort, and his mind inclines toward Nibbāna. This, friend Soṇa, is the full meaning of these verses spoken by the Blessed One in brief, which I have understood as such. “Excellent, friend Ānanda! Excellent, friend Ānanda! As if one were to set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been explained by the venerable Ānanda in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the venerable Ānanda accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts. “Friend Soṇa, since you have already been converted by the Blessed One, it is fitting for you to go to the Blessed One yourself and say: ‘I am, venerable sir, one who has been converted by the Blessed One; I am, venerable sir, one who has entered the stream of the Dhamma; I am no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, I am firmly established, and I am destined for full enlightenment. “Friend Ānanda, since you have already been converted by the Blessed One, it is fitting for you to go to the Blessed One yourself and say: ‘I am, venerable sir, one who has been converted by the Blessed One; I am, venerable sir, one who has entered the stream of the Dhamma; I am no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, I am firmly established, and I am destined for full enlightenment. “Very well, friend,” the venerable Soṇa replied to the venerable Ānanda. Then, having risen from his seat and paid homage to the venerable Ānanda, keeping him on his right, he departed. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went into his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, the venerable Soṇa attained final Nibbāna. Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.

Then Soṇa, the householder’s son, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As Soṇa, the householder’s son, was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:

“Sonā, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not fully understand form, do not fully understand the origin of form, do not fully understand the cessation of form, and do not fully understand the practice leading to the cessation of form;

who do not fully understand feeling, do not fully understand the origin of feeling, do not fully understand the cessation of feeling, and do not fully understand the practice leading to the cessation of feeling;
who do not fully understand perception … [and so on] …”

They do not understand volitional formations, they do not understand the origin of volitional formations, they do not understand the cessation of volitional formations, and they do not understand the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations.

They do not understand consciousness, they do not understand the origin of consciousness, they do not understand the cessation of consciousness, and they do not understand the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness.
Sonadaṇḍa, those ascetics or brahmins are not ascetics among ascetics, nor are they brahmins among brahmins, in my view.
Yet those venerable ones do not dwell having realized for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, the goal of the ascetic life or the goal of the holy life,

having attained it. But as for those recluses or brahmins, Soṇa, who understand form, understand the origin of form, understand the cessation of form, and understand the way leading to the cessation of form;
They understand feeling … they understand perception … they understand volitional formations …
They understand consciousness; they understand the origin of consciousness; they understand the cessation of consciousness; they understand the way leading to the cessation of consciousness.
And these, Soṇa, whether recluses or brahmins, are reckoned among the recluses as true recluses and among the brahmins as true brahmins;
and those venerable ones, in this very life, have realized the goal of the recluse and the goal of the brahmin.

Setting at Sāvatthī.

Seeing rightly, he becomes disenchanted.
With the destruction of delight comes the destruction of lust; with the destruction of lust comes the destruction of delight.

Attadīpavagga Dutiyanandikkhayasutta (The Second Discourse on the Destruction of Delight) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the destruction of delight, the destruction of delight. To what extent, venerable sir, is there the destruction of delight? “Bhikkhu, form is subject to arising; by comprehending it as it really is with correct wisdom thus, ‘form is subject to arising,’ one becomes disenchanted with form, one detaches from form, and by detaching from form, one is liberated from it. When liberated, one understands: ‘It is liberated. Feeling is subject to arising... Perception is subject to arising... Volitional formations are subject to arising... Consciousness is subject to arising; by comprehending it as it really is with correct wisdom thus, ‘consciousness is subject to arising,’ one becomes disenchanted with consciousness, one detaches from consciousness, and by detaching from consciousness, one is liberated from it. When liberated, one understands: ‘It is liberated. To this extent, bhikkhu, there is the destruction of delight. And what is the destruction of delight? The destruction of delight in form, the destruction of delight in feeling, the destruction of delight in perception, the destruction of delight in volitional formations, the destruction of delight in consciousness. This is called the destruction of delight. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the destruction of desire, the destruction of desire. To what extent, venerable sir, is there the destruction of desire? “Bhikkhu, form is subject to cessation; by comprehending it as it really is with correct wisdom thus, ‘form is subject to cessation,’ one becomes disenchanted with form, one detaches from form, and by detaching from form, one is liberated from it. When liberated, one understands: ‘It is liberated. Feeling is subject to cessation... Perception is subject to cessation... Volitional formations are subject to cessation... Consciousness is subject to cessation; by comprehending it as it really is with correct wisdom thus, ‘consciousness is subject to cessation,’ one becomes disenchanted with consciousness, one detaches from consciousness, and by detaching from consciousness, one is liberated from it. When liberated, one understands: ‘It is liberated. To this extent, bhikkhu, there is the destruction of desire. And what is the destruction of desire? The destruction of desire for form, the destruction of desire for feeling, the destruction of desire for perception, the destruction of desire for volitional formations, the destruction of desire for consciousness. This is called the destruction of desire. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the destruction of craving, the destruction of craving. To what extent, venerable sir, is there the destruction of craving? “Bhikkhu, form is impermanent; by comprehending it as it really is with correct wisdom thus, ‘form is impermanent,’ one becomes disenchanted with form, one detaches from form, and by detaching from form, one is liberated from it. When liberated, one understands: ‘It is liberated. Feeling is impermanent... Perception is impermanent... Volitional formations are impermanent... Consciousness is impermanent; by comprehending it as it really is with correct wisdom thus, ‘consciousness is impermanent,’ one becomes disenchanted with consciousness, one detaches from consciousness, and by detaching from consciousness, one is liberated from it. When liberated, one understands: ‘It is liberated. To this extent, bhikkhu, there is the destruction of craving. And what is the destruction of craving? The destruction of craving for form, the destruction of craving for feeling, the destruction of craving for perception, the destruction of craving for volitional formations, the destruction of craving for consciousness. This is called the destruction of craving. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the destruction of lust, the destruction of lust. To what extent, venerable sir, is there the destruction of lust? “Bhikkhu, form is suffering; by comprehending it as it really is with correct wisdom thus, ‘form is suffering,’ one becomes disenchanted with form, one detaches from form, and by detaching from form, one is liberated from it. When liberated, one understands: ‘It is liberated. Feeling is suffering... Perception is suffering... Volitional formations are suffering... Consciousness is suffering;

by comprehending it as it really is with correct wisdom thus, ‘consciousness is suffering,’ one becomes disenchanted with consciousness, one detaches from consciousness, and by detaching from consciousness, one is liberated from it. When liberated, one understands: ‘It is liberated. To this extent, bhikkhu, there is the destruction of lust. And what is the destruction of lust? The destruction of lust for form, the destruction of lust for feeling, the destruction of lust for perception, the destruction of lust for volitional formations, the destruction of lust for consciousness. This is called the destruction of lust. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the destruction of passion, the destruction of passion. To what extent, venerable sir, is there the destruction of passion? “Bhikkhu, form is non-self; by comprehending it as it really is with correct wisdom thus, ‘form is non-self,’ one becomes disenchanted with form, one detaches from form, and by detaching from form, one is liberated from it. When liberated, one understands: ‘It is liberated. Feeling is non-self... Perception is non-self... Volitional formations are non-self... Consciousness is non-self; by comprehending it as it really is with correct wisdom thus, ‘consciousness is non-self,’ one becomes disenchanted with consciousness, one detaches from consciousness, and by detaching from consciousness, one is liberated from it. When liberated, one understands: ‘It is liberated. To this extent, bhikkhu, there is the destruction of passion. And what is the destruction of passion? The destruction of passion for form, the destruction of passion for feeling, the destruction of passion for perception, the destruction of passion for volitional formations, the destruction of passion for consciousness. This is called the destruction of passion. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the destruction of attachment, the destruction of attachment. To what extent, venerable sir, is there the destruction of attachment? “Bhikkhu, form is empty of self and of what belongs to self; by comprehending it as it really is with correct wisdom thus, ‘form is empty of self and of what belongs to self,’ one becomes disenchanted with form, one detaches from form, and by detaching from form, one is liberated from it. When liberated, one understands: ‘It is liberated. Feeling is empty of self and of what belongs to self... Perception is empty of self and of what belongs to self... Volitional formations are empty of self and of what belongs to self... Consciousness is empty of self and of what belongs to self; by comprehending it as it really is with correct wisdom thus, ‘consciousness is empty of self and of what belongs to self,’ one becomes disenchanted with consciousness, one detaches from consciousness, and by detaching from consciousness, one is liberated from it. When liberated, one understands: ‘It is liberated. To this extent, bhikkhu, there is the destruction of attachment. And what is the destruction of attachment? The destruction of attachment to form, the destruction of attachment to feeling, the destruction of attachment to perception, the destruction of attachment to volitional formations, the destruction of attachment to consciousness. This is called the destruction of attachment. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the destruction of grasping, the destruction of grasping. To what extent, venerable sir, is there the destruction of grasping? “Bhikkhu, form is not mine; by comprehending it as it really is with correct wisdom thus, ‘form is not mine,’ one becomes disenchanted with form, one detaches from form, and by detaching from form, one is liberated from it. When liberated, one understands: ‘It is liberated. Feeling is not mine... Perception is not mine... Volitional formations are not mine... Consciousness is not mine; by comprehending it as it really is with correct wisdom thus, ‘consciousness is not mine,’ one becomes disenchanted with consciousness, one detaches from consciousness, and by detaching from consciousness, one is liberated from it. When liberated, one understands: ‘It is liberated. To this extent, bhikkhu, there is the destruction of grasping. And what is the destruction of grasping? The destruction of grasping after form, the destruction of grasping after feeling, the destruction of grasping after perception, the destruction of grasping after volitional formations, the destruction of grasping after consciousness. This is called the destruction of grasping. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the destruction of the underlying tendencies, the destruction of the underlying tendencies. To what extent, venerable sir, is there the destruction of the underlying tendencies? “Bhikkhu, form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; by comprehending it as it really is
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Monks, attend wisely to form, and contemplate the impermanence of form as it really is.

With the destruction of delight comes the destruction of lust; with the destruction of lust comes the destruction of delight.
Through the destruction of both delight and lust, the mind is said to be liberated, well-liberated.
Monks, attend to feeling thoroughly, and contemplate the impermanence of feeling as it really is.

Upāyavagga (The Chapter on Clinging)
The Discourse on Clinging. At Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, one who clings is unliberated; one who does not cling is liberated."
“Bhikkhus, if consciousness were to persist supported by form, with form as its object and established upon form, nourished by delight, it would come to growth, increase, and abundance.
Or if consciousness were to persist supported by feeling … or supported by perception …” [and so on].

“Or, monks, consciousness might persist by finding a footing in volitional formations, with volitional formations as its object and support, receiving nourishment from delight, and thus come to growth, increase, and abundance.

Monks, if anyone were to say: ‘Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, and apart from volitional formations, I shall describe the coming, the going, the passing away, the arising, the death, the birth, the growth, the increase, or the abundance of consciousness’—that would be impossible.”
‘I shall point out his coming or going, his passing away or rebirth, his growth, increase, or fullness,’ this is impossible.
But if, monks, a bhikkhu has abandoned lust for the form element... [he can do so].”
With the abandoning of lust, the object is cut off and consciousness finds no footing.
If, monks, there is no more clinging to the element of feeling...
if, monks, there is no more clinging to the element of perception... [and so on].
“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu has abandoned lust for the element of volitional formations… and if a bhikkhu has abandoned lust for the element of consciousness,
then with the abandoning of lust, the object is cut off and there is no foundation for the establishing of consciousness.”
When consciousness is thus unestablished, not growing, and unconditioned, it is liberated.
Because it is liberated, it is steady; because it is steady, it is content; because it is content, it does not tremble. Not trembling, one attains final Nibbāna right here, realizing:
"Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
First.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.54 (SN 22.54, PTS SN iii 54) 6.
Upāyavagga (The Chapter on Clinging)
The Discourse on Seeds.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of seeds.”
Which five?
Root-seed, stem-seed, joint-seed, cutting-seed, and seed-seed as the fifth.
Suppose, monks, these five kinds of seeds were unbroken, not rotten, not damaged by wind or heat, fertile, well-preserved, yet there were neither earth nor water; [they would not grow].
“Monks, would these five kinds of seeds attain growth, increase, and abundance?
“No, venerable sir.
“But if, monks, these five kinds of seeds were unbroken … [and so on] … well-stored, and there were both earth and water;”
“Monks, would these five kinds of seeds attain growth, increase, and abundance?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Monks, just as the earth element is, so should the four stations of consciousness be regarded.”
“Bhikkhus, just as the water element is, so should delight and lust be regarded.
Just as there are five kinds of seeds, so should consciousness together with its nutriment be regarded.
Consciousness, bhikkhus, when it persists, persists supported by form, having form as its object, established upon form; it attains growth, increase, and abundance, being moistened by delight.”
“Or, bhikkhus, if consciousness were to persist, it would persist by approaching feeling...
Or, bhikkhus, if consciousness were to persist, it would persist by approaching perception...

Or, bhikkhus, if consciousness were to persist, it would persist by approaching volitional formations; having volitional formations as its object, having volitional formations as its support, and being moistened by delight, it would come to growth, increase, and abundance.”
“Monks, whoever should say:
‘Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, and apart from volitional formations,
I shall point out the coming or going, the passing away or rebirth, the growth, increase, or maturation of consciousness’— ”
This is impossible:
that for a bhikkhu, bhikkhus, lust for the form element has been abandoned.
With the abandoning of lust, the object is cut off; there is no footing for consciousness.
If there were no element of feeling … no element of perception … no element of mental formations …
If, monks, a bhikkhu has abandoned lust for the consciousness element,
then with the abandoning of lust, the object is cut off and there is no foundation for the establishment of consciousness.
Consciousness being unestablished and not growing, it is liberated through non-forming.
"Because of being liberated, it is steadfast. Because of being steadfast, it is content. Because of being content, it does not tremble. Not trembling, it attains final nibbāna right here.
It understands: ‘Birth is exhausted... there is nothing further of this state of being. This is the second [sutta].

Upayavagga Udānasutta At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when it was said: ‘The world is empty,’ in what way has this been said? “Bhikkhus, it is by being empty of self and of what belongs to self that the world has been declared empty by the Tathāgata. “Bhikkhus, it is by being empty of self and of what belongs to self that form has been declared empty by the Tathāgata. It is by being empty of self and of what belongs to self that feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness has been declared empty by the Tathāgata. “It is in this way, bhikkhus, that ‘the world is empty’ has been said by the Tathāgata. [The Buddha then uttered this inspired utterance: “The world is empty; The world is indeed empty. Of what is the world empty? It is empty of self and of what belongs to self. “Empty is the world of the ‘I am’-conceit, Empty is the world of the ‘mine’-conceit; But for one who has fully understood this, There is no more yearning for anything anywhere.”
At Sāvatthī.
There the Blessed One uttered this inspired exclamation:
“‘I might not be, and it might not be for me; it would not come to be, and it will not come to be for me.’”
“A bhikkhu who resolves in this way would cut off the lower fetters.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, Bhante, does one resolve thus:
‘May I not be, and may nothing be mine; may I not come to be, and may nothing be mine in the future’?”
“Is it by resolving thus that a bhikkhu would cut off the lower fetters?
“In this case, bhikkhu, an uninstructed worldling, who has no regard for the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones,
untrained in the Dhamma of true persons, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form.
Feeling … perception … volitional formations …
One regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as being in self, or self as being in consciousness.
Such a person does not understand form, which is impermanent, as it really is: “Form is impermanent”;
they do not understand feeling, which is impermanent, as it really is: “Feeling is impermanent.”
One does not understand impermanent perception as it really is, thinking, ‘Perception is impermanent’;
one does not understand impermanent formations as they really are, thinking, ‘Formations are impermanent’;
one does not understand impermanent consciousness as it really is, thinking, ‘Consciousness is impermanent.’
One does not understand suffering form as it really is, [thinking] ‘suffering form’;
one does not understand suffering feeling … suffering perception …
He does not understand as it really is that conditioned phenomena are suffering … that consciousness is suffering, “consciousness is suffering.
He does not understand as it really is that form is non-self, “form is non-self.”
One does not understand feeling, which is non-self, as it really is: "feeling is non-self";
one does not understand perception, which is non-self, as it really is: "perception is non-self";
one does not understand volitional formations, which are non-self, as they really are: "volitional formations are non-self."
One does not understand consciousness, which is non-self, as it really is: "Consciousness is non-self.
One does not understand conditioned form, which is conditioned, as it really is: "Form is conditioned. One does not understand conditioned feeling...

One does not understand, as it really is, conditioned perception as ‘conditioned perception’; one does not understand conditioned volitional formations as ‘conditioned volitional formations’; one does not understand conditioned consciousness as ‘conditioned consciousness.’
One does not understand as it really is: "Form will cease"; one does not understand as it really is:
"Feeling will cease"; one does not understand as it really is:
"Perception will cease."
He does not understand as it really is: "Formations will cease... consciousness will cease.

But the learned noble disciple, monks, who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, well-trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has seen the true persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of the true persons, well-trained in the Dhamma of the true persons—
One does not regard form as self … nor feeling … nor perception … [and so on].
He does not regard volitional formations as self, nor consciousness as self.
He understands impermanent form, as it really is, to be “impermanent form.”
Feeling is impermanent… perception is impermanent… volitional formations are impermanent…
One understands as it really is that consciousness is impermanent: “Consciousness is impermanent.
One understands as it really is that form is suffering … [and so on] … that consciousness is suffering … that form is non-self … [and so on] … that consciousness is non-self.
He understands conditioned form as it really is: “conditioned form”; …pe… he understands conditioned consciousness as it really is: “conditioned consciousness.
He understands as it really is: “form will cease”; [he understands] feeling … as it really is.
He understands as it really is: "Perception... volitional formations... consciousness will cease."

“Thus, through the dissolution of form, the dissolution of feeling, the dissolution of perception, the dissolution of volitional formations, and the dissolution of consciousness— when a bhikkhu is thus resolved, thinking: ‘May I not be,
may I not have anything, may I not come to be,
may there be nothing for me’— he would cut off the lower fetters.”
“Resolving thus, Bhante, a bhikkhu would cut off the lower fetters.
“But how, Bhante, for one who knows what and sees what, does the immediate destruction of the taints occur?
“Here, bhikkhu, the uninstructed worldling experiences fear in a place that is not fearful.”
For this, O monk, is the fear of the uninstructed worldling:
‘May I not be, may nothing be mine, may I not come to be, may nothing be mine in the future.
But the instructed noble disciple, O monk, does not fall into fear regarding that which is a ground for fearlessness.
“Bhikkhu, this fear does not exist for the learned noble disciple:
‘May I not be, may I not have anything, may I not come to be, may there be nothing for me.
For if consciousness were to persist supported by form, having form as its object, established upon form, and being moistened by delight, it would reach growth, increase, and abundance.”
Or, bhikkhu, if consciousness were to persist by approaching feeling... or by approaching perception...

or by approaching volitional formations, bhikkhu, then—having volitional formations as its object, having volitional formations as its support, and being moistened by delight—it would come to growth, increase, and abundance.
“Bhikkhu, if anyone were to say:
‘Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, and apart from volitional formations,
I shall point out the coming or going, the passing away or rebirth, the growth, increase, or fullness of consciousness,’ [he would be speaking falsely].”
This is impossible.
If, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu has abandoned lust for the form element, then with the abandoning of lust, the object is cut off and there is no foundation for consciousness.
If, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu [has abandoned lust] for the feeling element...
If, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu has abandoned lust for the element of perception… if, bhikkhu,
a bhikkhu has abandoned lust for the element of volitional formations… if,
bhikkhu, a bhikkhu has abandoned lust for the element of consciousness, then with the abandoning of lust, the object is cut off and there is no foundation for the establishing of consciousness.
When consciousness is not established there, it does not grow, and being unconditioned, it is liberated.
Through liberation it is steady; through steadiness it is content; through contentment it does not tremble. Not trembling, one attains final nibbāna right here, realizing:
"Birth is exhausted... there is nothing further of this state of being."
“It is for one who knows thus, bhikkhu, and who sees thus, that the immediate destruction of the taints occurs.
The third.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.56 (SN 22.56, PTS SN iii 58)
6. The Chapter on Skillful Means (Upāyavagga). Discourse on the Turning of Appropriation (Upādānaparivattasutta).
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging.
Which five?

The aggregate subject to clinging of form, the aggregate subject to clinging of feeling, the aggregate subject to clinging of perception, the aggregate subject to clinging of volitional formations, and the aggregate subject to clinging of consciousness.”
“Monks, as long as I did not directly know these five aggregates of clinging in their fourfold cycle as they really are,

I did not, monks, claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.

But when, monks, I directly knew these five aggregates of clinging as they really are through their fourfold cycle, then, monks, I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas... including gods and humans.
And what is the fourfold cycle?
I directly knew form; I directly knew the origin of form; I directly knew the cessation of form; I directly knew the practice leading to the cessation of form. [I directly knew] feeling...
perception...

I directly knew volitional formations... I directly knew consciousness, I directly knew the origin of consciousness, I directly knew the cessation of consciousness, and I directly knew the way leading to the cessation of consciousness.
And what, bhikkhus, is form?
The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements:
this, monks, is called form.
With the arising of nutriment comes the arising of form.
With the cessation of nutriment comes the cessation of form.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of form; that is to say:
right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.
"Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins, having directly known form as it is, having directly known the origin of form as it is,
having directly known the cessation of form as it is, and having directly known the practice leading to the cessation of form as it is,
are practicing for the sake of revulsion toward form, for its dispassion, and for its cessation— they are practicing rightly."
Those who have practiced well find a firm footing in this Dhamma and Discipline.

And as for those recluses or brahmins, monks, who—having directly known such form... having directly known such a path leading to the cessation of form—are liberated through revulsion toward form, through its fading away, through its cessation, and through non-clinging, they are well-liberated.
Those who are well-liberated are perfected ones.
For those who are *kevalins*, there is no cycle of existence to be designated.
And what, monks, is feeling?
There are these six groups of feeling, monks:
Feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact.
This, monks, is called feeling.
With the arising of contact comes the arising of feeling.
With the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of feeling; that is to say:
right view …pe… right concentration.
"Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins, having thus directly known feeling, having thus directly known the origin of feeling,
having thus directly known the cessation of feeling, and having thus directly known the way leading to the cessation of feeling,
are practicing for the sake of disenchantment with feeling, for its fading away, and for its cessation— they are practicing rightly."
Those who have practiced well find a firm footing in this Dhamma and Discipline.

And as for those recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, who have directly known feeling in this way … [and] who have directly known the practice leading to the cessation of feeling in this way … for them there is no further round to be described.
And what, monks, is perception?
There are these six classes of perception, monks:
perception of forms, perception of sounds, perception of odors, perception of tastes, perception of tangibles, and perception of mental phenomena.
This, monks, is called perception.
With the arising of contact there is the arising of perception;
with the cessation of contact there is the cessation of perception.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of perception, namely:
right view … [as above] … right concentration … [as above] … for them there is no cycle to be described.
"And what, bhikkhus, are volitional formations?
There are these six classes of volition, bhikkhus:
volition regarding forms, volition regarding sounds, volition regarding odors, volition regarding tastes, volition regarding tangibles, and volition regarding mental phenomena."
These, monks, are called volitional formations.
With the arising of contact there is the arising of volitional formations;
with the cessation of contact there is the cessation of volitional formations.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations; that is to say:
right view …pe… right concentration.
For whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, have thus directly known volitional formations and the origin of volitional formations …pe… [and their cessation].

Having directly known this, having directly known the cessation of volitional formations in this way, and having directly known the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations in this way,
those who have set out for the disenchantment with, the fading away of lust for, and the cessation of volitional formations are practicing rightly.
Those who practice rightly find their footing in this Dhamma and Discipline.
But those recluses or brahmins, monks, who— having directly known formations thus, having directly known the arising of formations thus,
having directly known the cessation of formations thus, and having directly known the way leading to the cessation of formations thus—
are liberated through non-clinging by means of revulsion toward, dispassion for, and the cessation of formations: they are well-liberated.
Those who are well-liberated are the possessors of the absolute.
For those who possess the absolute, there is no round of existence to be designated.
And what, monks, is consciousness?
“Bhikkhus, there are these six classes of consciousness:
eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
This, bhikkhus, is called consciousness.”
With the arising of name-and-form, there is the arising of consciousness;
with the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of consciousness.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of consciousness, namely: [the eight factors].
Right view ... right concentration.

For whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, have thus directly known consciousness, have thus directly known the arising of consciousness, have thus directly known the cessation of consciousness, and have thus directly known the way leading to the cessation of consciousness—
Those who are practicing for the sake of disenchantment with consciousness, for its fading away, and for its cessation, are practicing rightly.
Those who practice rightly find a firm footing in this Dhamma and Discipline.
And as for those recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, who have thus directly known consciousness and thus [known] the origin of consciousness...

Having directly known this, having directly known the cessation of consciousness in this way, and having directly known the path leading to the cessation of consciousness in this way, they are liberated through non-clinging by means of revulsion toward, dispassion for, and the cessation of consciousness; they are well-liberated.
Those who are well-liberated are perfected ones (kevalinaḥ).
“For those who are *kevalins*, there is no cycle of existence to be designated.
The fourth.
