6. Upāyavagga:
Sattaṭṭhānasutta.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is skilled in seven things and has investigated in three ways is called one who is complete, one who has lived the holy life, a supreme person in this Dhamma and Discipline.
And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu skilled in seven things?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands form, he understands the origin of form, he understands the cessation of form, he understands the way leading to the cessation of form; [he understands feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, he understands the origin of consciousness, he understands the cessation of consciousness, he understands the way leading to the cessation of consciousness].”
One understands the gratification of form, understands the danger of form, and understands the escape from form;
one understands feeling … perception … [and so forth].
He understands volitional formations...
he understands consciousness, he understands the origin of consciousness, he understands the cessation of consciousness, and he understands the way leading to the cessation of consciousness;
he understands the gratification in consciousness, he understands the danger in consciousness, and he understands the escape from consciousness.
And what, monks, is form?
The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
This, monks, is called form.
With the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of form;
with the cessation of nutriment, there is the cessation of form.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of form, namely: [the rest of the eight factors].
Right view … right concentration.
Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on form—
this is the gratification in form.
That form which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—
this is the danger in form.
The removal of desire and lust for form, the abandoning of desire and lust for form— this is the escape from form.
This is the escape from form.

For whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, have directly known form in this way, have directly known the origin of form, have directly known the cessation of form, and have directly known the path leading to the cessation of form;

and have directly known the gratification of form, have directly known the danger of form, and have directly known the escape from form—those who are practicing for the purpose of revulsion toward form, for its fading away, and for its cessation, are practicing rightly.
Those who have practiced well find their footing in this Dhamma and Vinaya.

And as for those recluses or brahmins, monks, who—having directly known form, having directly known the origin of form, having directly known the cessation of form, and having directly known the way leading to the cessation of form;

having directly known the gratification of form, having directly known the danger in form, and having directly known the escape from form—are liberated through disenchantment with form, through dispassion toward it, through its cessation, and through non-clinging: they are well-liberated.
Those who are well-liberated are the possessors of the absolute.
For those who possess the absolute, there is no round of existence to be designated.
And what, monks, is feeling?
There are these six groups of feeling, monks:
feeling born of eye-contact …pe… feeling born of mind-contact.
This, monks, is called feeling.
With the arising of contact there is the arising of feeling;
with the cessation of contact there is the cessation of feeling.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of feeling, namely:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence upon feeling—
This is the gratification in feeling.
That feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—
this is the danger in feeling.
The removal of desire and lust for feeling, the abandoning of desire and lust for feeling—

this is the escape from feeling. For whatever recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, have thus directly known feeling, have thus directly known the origin of feeling, have thus directly known the cessation of feeling, and have thus directly known the way leading to the cessation of feeling;

Thus, having directly known the gratification in feeling, having directly known the danger in feeling, and having directly known the escape from feeling, those who practice for the sake of disenchantment with feeling, for its fading away, and for its cessation, are practicing rightly.
Those who practice rightly find a firm footing in this Dhamma and Discipline.
And as for those recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, who have thus directly known feeling... [and so on].
There is no cycle for them to describe.
And what, bhikkhus, is perception?
There are these six classes of perception, bhikkhus:
Perception of forms, perception of sounds, perception of odors, perception of tastes, perception of tangibles, and perception of mental phenomena.
This, monks, is called perception.
With the arising of contact, there is the arising of perception.
With the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of perception.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of perception;
that is to say: right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration ... [and so on].
There is no cycle for them to describe.
And what, bhikkhus, are volitional formations? These six classes of volition, bhikkhus: [the volitions regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena].
Volition regarding forms …pe… volition regarding mental phenomena. These,
monks, are called volitional formations.
With the arising of contact, there is the arising of volitional formations;
with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of volitional formations.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations, namely: [the rest of the eight factors].
Right view … right concentration.
Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on volitional formations—
this is the gratification in volitional formations.
That formations are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—
this is the danger in formations.
The removal of desire and lust for formations, the abandoning of desire and lust for them— this is the escape from formations.
This is the escape from volitional formations.
For whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, have thus directly known volitional formations, have thus directly known the origin of volitional formations,
have thus directly known the cessation of volitional formations, and have thus directly known the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations—
Those who have practiced for the sake of revulsion toward, dispassion toward, and cessation of formative forces through direct knowledge—those are practicing rightly.
Those who practice rightly find a foothold in this Dhamma and Discipline...
for them there is no cycle of existence to be described.
And what, monks, is consciousness?
There are these six classes of consciousness, monks:
eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
This, monks, is called consciousness.
With the arising of name-and-form there is the arising of consciousness;
with the cessation of name-and-form there is the cessation of consciousness.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of consciousness, namely:
right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.
Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence upon consciousness—
This is the gratification in consciousness.
That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—
this is the danger in consciousness.
The removal of desire and lust for consciousness, the abandoning of desire and lust for consciousness—
this is the escape from consciousness.
For whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, have thus directly known consciousness and thus [known] the origination of consciousness...
Having directly known this, having directly known the cessation of consciousness in this way, having directly known the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness in this way;

having directly known the gratification of consciousness in this way, having directly known the danger in consciousness in this way, and having directly known the escape from consciousness in this way, those who have set out for the disenchantment with, the fading away of lust for, and the cessation of consciousness are practicing rightly.
Those who are practicing rightly find a foothold in this Dhamma and Discipline.
But whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, have thus directly known consciousness,
have thus directly known the origin of consciousness, have thus directly known the cessation of consciousness, and have thus directly known the way leading to the cessation of consciousness;

and have thus directly known the gratification in consciousness, have thus directly known the danger in consciousness, and have thus directly known the escape from consciousness— being liberated through non-clinging by means of disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness— they are well-liberated.
Those who are well-liberated are the possessors of the absolute (kevalin).
For those who are possessors of the absolute, there is no round of existence to be described.
In this way, monks, a monk is skilled in the seven points.
And how, monks, is a monk one who investigates in three ways?
Here, monks, a monk investigates by way of the elements, he investigates by way of the sense bases, and he investigates by way of dependent origination.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who investigates in three ways.

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is skilled in the seven cases and examines things in three ways is called one who is complete, one who has lived the holy life, a supreme person in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Thus was the fifth discourse spoken. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.58.
6. Upāyavagga:
Sammāsambuddhasutta.
Setting at Sāvatthī.

“Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, through disenchantment with form, through dispassion toward it, through its cessation, and through non-clinging, is liberated; thus he is called ‘the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is liberated by wisdom, through disenchantment with form, through dispassion toward it, through its cessation, and through non-clinging, is called ‘one liberated by wisdom.

Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, through disenchantment with feeling, through dispassion toward it, through its cessation, and through non-clinging, is liberated; thus he is called ‘the Perfectly Enlightened One.’”
“Monks, a bhikkhu who is liberated by wisdom, through disenchantment with feeling... is called ‘one liberated by wisdom.
Monks, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, [is liberated] from perception...
from mental formations...”
“Through disenchantment with consciousness, through dispassion toward it, through its cessation, and through non-clinging, one is liberated; such a one is called a ‘Perfectly Enlightened One.
A monk, monks, who is liberated by wisdom, through disenchantment with consciousness, through dispassion toward it, through its cessation, and through non-clinging, is called ‘liberated by wisdom.

In this regard, monks, what is the distinction, what is the difference in meaning, and what is the disparity between a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, and a monk who is liberated by wisdom?”
“Venerable sir, our teachings have the Blessed One as their root, the Blessed One as their guide, and the Blessed One as their resort.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“In that case, bhikkhus, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path; he is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the one skilled in the path.”
“Monks, at present the disciples dwell following the path, having subsequently attained it.
This, monks, is the distinction, this is the specific intention, this is the difference between a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, and a monk liberated by wisdom.
Thus ends the sixth [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.59 (SN 22.59, PTS SN iii 66) 6. The Chapter on Clinging The Discourse on the Characteristic of Non-Self At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form is non-self. If form were self, this body would not be subject to affliction. It would be possible to have it of form: ‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus. But because form is non-self, this body is subject to affliction, and it is not possible to have it of form: ‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus. “Feeling is non-self... Perception is non-self... Volitional formations are non-self... Consciousness is non-self. If consciousness were self, this body would not be subject to affliction. It would be possible to have it of consciousness: ‘Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus. But because consciousness is non-self, this body is subject to affliction, and it is not possible to have it of consciousness: ‘Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus. “Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion toward form, revulsion toward feeling, revulsion toward perception, revulsion toward volitional formations, and revulsion toward consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, those bhikkhus considered: “Friends, the Blessed One taught us the Dhamma in brief without expounding the detailed exposition. As to that, friends, we do not understand the detailed exposition of the Blessed One’s teaching in brief. Let us now go to the bhikkhunīs’ quarters and teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhunīs. Perhaps the bhikkhunīs will understand the detailed exposition of the Blessed One’s teaching in brief. Then those bhikkhus went to the bhikkhunīs’ quarters and taught the Dhamma to the bhikkhunīs as they had heard it and as they had memorized it. Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported everything that had occurred, adding: “Venerable sir, when we heard this Dhamma, our hairs stood on end. Venerable sir, please teach us the Dhamma further in detail. “Bhikkhus, if anyone should speak thus: ‘Apart from material form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from volitional formations, I make known the coming and going of beings, their passing away and reappearance, their growth, increase, and maturation in this or that state of existence’—that would be a mere empty boast on his part. If the mind of such a person is not concentrated, he cannot know or see things as they really are. “But, bhikkhus, if anyone should speak thus: ‘I make known the coming and going of beings, their passing away and reappearance, their growth, increase, and maturation in this or that state of existence, by directly knowing and fully understanding material form, by developing dispassion toward it and abandoning it; by directly knowing and fully understanding feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, by developing dispassion toward it and abandoning it’—that would be a fitting statement for him. If the mind of such a person is concentrated, he can know and see things as they really are. “What do you think, bhikkhus, is material form permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, venerable sir. “But is what is impermanent suffering or happiness? “Suffering, venerable sir. “But is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. “Is feeling permanent or impermanent?... Is perception permanent or impermanent?... Are volitional formations permanent or impermanent?... Is consciousness permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, venerable sir. “But is what is impermanent suffering or happiness? “Suffering, venerable sir. “But is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. “Therefore, bhikkhus, any kind of material form whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all material form should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Any kind of feeling whatsoever... Any kind of perception whatsoever... Any kind of volitional formations whatsoever...

Any kind of consciousness whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion toward material form, revulsion toward feeling, revulsion toward perception, revulsion toward volitional formations, and revulsion toward consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. And while this discourse was being spoken, the minds of sixty bhikkhus were liberated from the taints by non-clinging, and the hairs on the bodies of many other bhikkhus stood on end. Those bhikkhus, with their bodies covered in a thrill of joy, paid homage to the Blessed One and departed. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
There the Blessed One addressed the monks of the group of five: “Monks!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Form, bhikkhus, is not-self.”
“Bhikkhus, if this form were self, this form would not lead to affliction, and one could exercise mastery over it, saying:
‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus.
But because form is not-self, bhikkhus, therefore form leads to affliction, and one cannot exercise mastery over it:”
‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus.
Feeling is non-self.
For if, monks, feeling were self, this feeling would not lead to affliction, and one could exercise mastery over feeling: [“Let my feeling be thus; let my feeling not be thus”].
‘May my feeling be thus; may my feeling not be thus.
But because feeling is non-self, monks, therefore feeling leads to affliction, and it is not possible regarding feeling:
‘May my feeling be thus; may my feeling not be thus.’
Perception is non-self...
volitional formations are non-self.
For if, monks, these volitional formations were self, then these volitional formations would not lead to affliction, and it would be possible regarding volitional formations:
‘May my volitional formations be thus; may my volitional formations not be thus.
But because, monks, volitional formations are non-self, therefore volitional formations lead to affliction, and it is not possible regarding volitional formations:
‘May my volitional formations be thus; may my volitional formations not be thus.’
Consciousness is non-self.
For if this consciousness, monks, were the self, then this consciousness would not lead to affliction, and one could exercise mastery over consciousness, saying:
"Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus."
But because, monks, consciousness is non-self, therefore consciousness leads to affliction, and it is not possible regarding consciousness:
"Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus.
What do you think, monks?
“Is form permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, Bhante.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Feeling … perception …”
“Are volitional formations … consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.”
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:”
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“Therefore, bhikkhus, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external—”
Whether gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form should be seen as it actually is with right wisdom thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
Whatever feeling there is—past, future, or present; internal or external … [and so on] … far or near.
Or whatever feeling there may be: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus should it be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Whatever perception there may be... [and so on].
Whatever formations there are—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior;
far or near—all formations should be seen as they really are with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
Whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."

"Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness.
Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there arises the knowledge:
‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’"
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The group of five monks were uplifted and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
And while this exposition was being spoken, the minds of the group of five monks were liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
The Seventh.

The Mahālisutta:
Thus have I heard—
on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Then Mahāli the Licchavi approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...and sitting to one side, Mahāli the Licchavi said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa says thus:
‘There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings;’”
“Beings become defiled without cause, without condition.
There is no cause, there is no condition for the purification of beings;
beings are purified without cause, without condition.”
"What does the Blessed One say about this?
"Mahāli, there is a cause, there is a condition for the defilement of beings;
with cause and with condition, beings become defiled."
“There is, Mahāli, a cause, there is a condition for the purification of beings;
with cause and with condition, beings are purified.
“But what, Bhante, is the cause, what is the condition for the defilement of beings?”
"How, with what causes and conditions, do beings become defiled?
"If this form, Mahāli, were exclusively suffering—overwhelmed by suffering, immersed in suffering, and not touched by pleasure—then beings would not become infatuated with form.
But because form, Mahāli, is pleasant, overwhelmed by pleasure, immersed in pleasure, and not touched by suffering, therefore beings become infatuated with form."
Those who have passion are fettered; through fetters they become defiled.
This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the defilement of beings;
thus, with cause and with condition, beings become defiled.
If feeling here, Mahāli, were exclusively painful—overcome by pain, entered by pain, and not entered by pleasure—then beings would not become infatuated with feeling.
But because feeling, Mahāli, is pleasant, overcome by pleasure, entered by pleasure, and not entered by pain, therefore beings become infatuated with feeling;
through infatuation, they become fettered.
Through conjunctions they become defiled.
This, Mahāli, is a cause, this is a condition for the defilement of beings.
Thus it is that beings are defiled with a cause and with a condition.
“Mahāli, if perception here...
[and] if formations here, Mahāli, were exclusively painful—overwhelmed by pain, beset by pain, and not touched by pleasure—then beings would not become infatuated with formations.
But because, Mahāli, formations are pleasant—overwhelmed by pleasure, beset by pleasure, and not touched by pain—therefore beings become infatuated with formations.”
Those who are full of lust become fettered;
through fetters they become defiled.
This, Mahāli, is a cause, this is a condition for the defilement of beings.
Thus, with causes and conditions, beings become defiled.
Furthermore, Mahāli, if this consciousness were exclusively suffering—overcome by suffering, beset by suffering, and not joined with happiness—beings would not be infatuated with consciousness.
But because, Mahāli, consciousness is pleasure—joined with pleasure, beset by pleasure, and not joined with suffering—therefore beings are infatuated with consciousness.
“Those who are full of lust become fettered; through fetters they become defiled.
This, Mahāli, is a cause, this is a condition for the defilement of beings.
Thus, with cause and with condition, beings become defiled.”
“But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition for the purification of beings;
how is it that beings, having a cause and a condition, become purified?

“Mahāli, if this form here were exclusively pleasant, immersed in pleasure, steeped in pleasure, and not steeped in pain, beings would not experience revulsion toward form. But because form is subject to change and transformation, beings experience revulsion toward form.”
But because, Mahāli, form is suffering, beset by suffering, overwhelmed by suffering, and not joined with happiness, therefore beings become disenchanted with form;
through disenchantment they become dispassionate; through dispassion they are purified.
This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the purification of beings.
Thus, with causes and conditions, beings are purified.
For if, Mahāli, feeling here were exclusively pleasant … [and so on] … if, Mahāli, perception here were exclusively pleasant … [and so on].
If, Mahāli, volitional formations were exclusively pleasant here...

[and so on] ...and if consciousness here, Mahāli, were exclusively pleasant—pervaded by pleasure, steeped in pleasure, and not steeped in suffering—then beings would not experience revulsion toward consciousness.
But because consciousness, Mahāli, is suffering—pervaded by suffering, steeped in suffering, and not steeped in pleasure—therefore beings experience revulsion toward consciousness.
“Becoming disenchanted, they become dispassionate; through dispassion, they are purified.
This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the purification of beings.
Thus it is that beings are purified with a cause and with a condition.”
The Eighth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.61 (SN 22.61, PTS SN iii 71) 6.
Upāyavagga (The Chapter on Clinging)
The Discourse on the Burning:
The Setting is at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, form is burning; feeling is burning; perception is burning; volitional formations are burning; consciousness is burning.”

"Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, and he becomes disenchanted with feeling... with perception... with volitional formations... and he becomes disenchanted with consciousness.
Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there arises the knowledge: 'It is liberated. He understands:
'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.'"
The Ninth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.62 (SN 22.62, PTS SN iii 71) 6.
Upāyavagga (The Chapter on Clinging)
The Discourse on the Modes of Expression. At Sāvatthī.

“Monks, there are these three modes of expression, modes of designation, and modes of description that are unmixed, have never been mixed, are not being mixed, and will not be mixed; they are not censured by wise recluses and brahmins.”
Which three?
That form, monks, which is past, ceased, and changed, is reckoned as "it was," designated as "it was," and described as "it was";
it is not reckoned as "it exists," nor is it reckoned as "it will be."
Any feeling that is past, ceased, and changed is reckoned as “it was,” designated as “it was,” and described as “it was”;
it is not reckoned as “it exists,” nor is it reckoned as “it will exist.
Any perception...
Those formations that are past, ceased, and changed are reckoned as ‘they were,’ designated as ‘they were,’ and described as ‘they were’;
they are not reckoned as ‘they exist,’ nor are they reckoned as ‘they will be.
That consciousness which is past, ceased, and changed is reckoned as ‘it was,’ designated as ‘it was,’ and described as ‘it was.’
There is no designation for it as "it exists," nor is there a designation for it as "it will exist.
Monks, that form which is unborn and unmanifested: the designation "it will exist" is its designation, "it will exist" is its conventional term, "it will exist" is its description;
there is no designation for it as "it exists," nor is there a designation for it as "it has been."
Whatever feeling has not yet arisen and is not yet manifest, it is designated as "it will be," it is termed "it will be," and it is described as "it will be";
there is no designation for it as "it exists," nor is there any designation for it as "it was.
Whatever perception...
Those formations that have not been born and have not become manifest: “they will be” is their reckoning, “they will be” is their designation, “they will be” is their description;
it is not their reckoning that “they exist,” nor is it their reckoning that “they have been.
That consciousness which has not been born and has not become manifest: “it will be” is its reckoning, “it will be” is its designation, “it will be” is its description.
For him there is no designation "it exists," nor for him the designation "it was.

Monks, whatever form has been born and manifested, for that there is the designation "it exists," the conventional term "it exists," and the description "it exists"; for it there is no designation "it was," nor for it the designation "it will be."

Whatever feeling has arisen and become manifest, for it there is the designation ‘it exists,’ for it there is the convention ‘it exists,’ for it there is the description ‘it exists’; for it there is no designation ‘it was,’ nor is there a designation for it ‘it will be.
Whatever perception...

Those formations that have arisen and become manifest are reckoned as “they exist,” they are designated as “they exist,” and they are described as “they exist”; it is not their reckoning that “they were,” nor is it their reckoning that “they will be.
That consciousness which has arisen and become manifest is reckoned as “it exists,” it is designated as “it exists,” and it is described as “it exists.”
There is no such conception for him as "it was," nor is there any such conception for him as "it will be.

These, monks, are the three pathways of language, pathways of designation, and pathways of description; they are unmixed, never before mixed, are not being mixed, and will not be mixed; they are not censured by wise recluses and brahmins.
Even those, monks, who were the Ukkalāvassabhajñas—proponents of causelessness, proponents of non-action, and proponents of nihilism—[did not censure these].
They did not think that they should criticize or reject those three ways of expression, those three ways of designation, those three ways of description.
Why was that? Out of fear of censure, confrontation, reproach, and attack.”
The first chapter of the Majjhimapaṇṇāsaka, the Upaya-vagga.
Its summary verse (uddāna) is: Upaya, Bīja, Udāna.
The turning of clinging, the sevenfold basis,
and the five great fires burning— thus did the Sambuddha teach, O Mahāli.
The Chapter on the Path of Language.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.63 (SN 22.63, PTS SN iii 73).
7. The Chapter on Arahants.
The Discourse on Clinging.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
“Bhikkhu, one who grasps is bound by Māra.”
“Not grasping, he is freed from the Evil One.
“Understood, Blessed One; understood, Sugata.
“But how, monk, do you understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief?”
“Venerable sir, one who clings to form is bound by Māra;
one who does not cling to it is freed from the Evil One.
One who clings to feeling is bound by Māra...”
Not grasping, he is freed from the Evil One.
[He does not grasp at] perception … volitional formations …
“Grasping at consciousness, one is bound by Māra;
not grasping at it, one is freed from the Evil One.
This, venerable sir, is how I understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by the Blessed One in brief.”
“Excellent, excellent, bhikkhu!
It is excellent that you, bhikkhu, understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief.
For, bhikkhu, one who clings to form is bound by Māra.”
Not grasping, he is liberated from the Evil One. [He is liberated from] feeling...
perception...
One who grasps at volitional formations … consciousness is bound by Māra;
one who does not grasp is freed from the Evil One.
“Bhikkhu, the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief should be understood in detail in this way.
Then that bhikkhu, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed.
Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, in no long time—that for which one lives the holy life...

Noble sons go forth from the household life into homelessness rightly, and having realized for themselves through direct knowledge in this very life the supreme goal of the holy life, they enter and abide in it.
He directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
And that monk became one of the arahants.
Thus ends the first [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.64. (SN 22.64, PTS SN iii 74)

“Venerable sir, one who conceives of form is bound by Māra;
one who does not conceive of it is freed from the Evil One.
[The same applies to] feeling...”
One who conceives of perception … of volitional formations … of consciousness is bound by Māra.
“Not conceiving [of them], he is freed from the Evil One.
It is in this way, Bhante, that I understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by the Blessed One in brief.
“Excellent, excellent, monk!”
"It is good, bhikkhu, that you understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief.
For, bhikkhu, one who conceives of form is bound by Māra;
one who does not conceive of it is freed from the Evil One."
Feeling … perception … volitional formations …

not conceiving it, one is freed from the Evil One.

Abhinandamānasutta.

Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One... and having sat down to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:

“Bhikkhu, one who delights is bound by Māra.”

one who does not delight in it is freed from the Evil One.

Delighting in perception … in volitional formations … in consciousness, one is bound by Māra.
“Not relishing it, he is freed from the Evil One.

“Excellent, excellent, monk!”

one who does not delight in it is freed from the Evil One."
Feeling … perception … volitional formations …

not delighting in it, one is freed from the Evil One.
This, monk, is how the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief should be understood in detail. …pe…

Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.67 (SN 22.67, PTS SN iii 77) 7. Arahantavagga Dukkhasutta (The Discourse on Suffering) “Bhikkhus, form is suffering. Feeling is suffering. Perception is suffering. Volitional formations are suffering. Consciousness is suffering. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion toward form, revulsion toward feeling, revulsion toward perception, revulsion toward volitional formations, and revulsion toward consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
At Sāvatthī.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.70 (SN 22.70, PTS SN iii 79) 7. The Chapter on Arahants The Discourse on Being Established in What is Seductive "Bhikkhus, whatever is of a nature to be seductive, therein one should not take a stand. And what, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive? The eye is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. The ear... the nose... the tongue... the body... the mind is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. "And why, bhikkhus, should one not take a stand in what is of a nature to be seductive? Because, bhikkhus, the mind is bound up with what is of a nature to be seductive. "Whatever, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive, therein one should not take a stand. And what, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive? Visible objects are of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. Sounds... odors... tastes... tangibles... mental phenomena are of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. "And why, bhikkhus, should one not take a stand in what is of a nature to be seductive? Because, bhikkhus, the mind is bound up with what is of a nature to be seductive. "Whatever, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive, therein one should not take a stand. And what, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive? Eye-consciousness is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. Ear-consciousness... nose-consciousness... tongue-consciousness... body-consciousness... mind-consciousness is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. "And why, bhikkhus, should one not take a stand in what is of a nature to be seductive? Because, bhikkhus, the mind is bound up with what is of a nature to be seductive. "Whatever, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive, therein one should not take a stand. And what, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive? Eye-contact is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. Ear-contact... nose-contact... tongue-contact... body-contact... mind-contact is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. "And why, bhikkhus, should one not take a stand in what is of a nature to be seductive? Because, bhikkhus, the mind is bound up with what is of a nature to be seductive. "Whatever, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive, therein one should not take a stand. And what, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive? Feeling born of eye-contact is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. Feeling born of ear-contact... feeling born of nose-contact... feeling born of tongue-contact... feeling born of body-contact... feeling born of mind-contact is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. "And why, bhikkhus, should one not take a stand in what is of a nature to be seductive? Because, bhikkhus, the mind is bound up with what is of a nature to be seductive. "Whatever, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive, therein one should not take a stand. And what, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive? Perception of visible objects is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. Perception of sounds... perception of odors... perception of tastes... perception of tangibles... perception of mental phenomena is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. "And why, bhikkhus, should one not take a stand in what is of a nature to be seductive? Because, bhikkhus, the mind is bound up with what is of a nature to be seductive. "Whatever, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive, therein one should not take a stand. And what, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive? Volition regarding visible objects is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. Volition regarding sounds... volition regarding odors... volition regarding tastes... volition regarding tangibles... volition regarding mental phenomena is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. "And why, bhikkhus, should one not take a stand in what is of a nature to be seductive? Because, bhikkhus, the mind is bound up with what is of a nature to be seductive. "Whatever, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive, therein one should not take a stand. And what, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive? Craving for visible objects is of a nature to be seductive;

therein one should not take a stand. Craving for sounds... craving for odors... craving for tastes... craving for tangibles... craving for mental phenomena is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. "And why, bhikkhus, should one not take a stand in what is of a nature to be seductive? Because, bhikkhus, the mind is bound up with what is of a nature to be seductive. "Whatever, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive, therein one should not take a stand. And what, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive? The form aggregate is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. The feeling aggregate... the perception aggregate... the volitional formations aggregate... the consciousness aggregate is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. "And why, bhikkhus, should one not take a stand in what is of a nature to be seductive? Because, bhikkhus, the mind is bound up with what is of a nature to be seductive. "Whatever, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive, therein one should not take a stand. And what, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive? The earth element is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. The water element... the fire element... the air element... the space element... the consciousness element is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. "And why, bhikkhus, should one not take a stand in what is of a nature to be seductive? Because, bhikkhus, the mind is bound up with what is of a nature to be seductive. "Whatever, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive, therein one should not take a stand. And what, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive? The eye base is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. The ear base... the nose base... the tongue base... the body base... the mind base is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. "And why, bhikkhus, should one not take a stand in what is of a nature to be seductive? Because, bhikkhus, the mind is bound up with what is of a nature to be seductive. "Whatever, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive, therein one should not take a stand. And what, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive? The visible-object base is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. The sound base... the odor base... the taste base... the tangible-base... the mental-phenomena base is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. "And why, bhikkhus, should one not take a stand in what is of a nature to be seductive? Because, bhikkhus, the mind is bound up with what is of a nature to be seductive. "Whatever, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive, therein one should not take a stand. And what, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive? Eye-consciousness element is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. Ear-consciousness element... nose-consciousness element... tongue-consciousness element... body-consciousness element... mind-consciousness element is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. "And why, bhikkhus, should one not take a stand in what is of a nature to be seductive? Because, bhikkhus, the mind is bound up with what is of a nature to be seductive. "Whatever, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive, therein one should not take a stand. And what, bhikkhus, is of a nature to be seductive? Eye-contact element is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. Ear-contact element... nose-contact element... tongue-contact element... body-contact element... mind-contact element is of a nature to be seductive; therein one should not take a stand. "And why, bhikkhus
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One... [and] sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
"It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell... [as previously described].
“Bhikkhu, whatever is established as a basis for passion, therein you must abandon desire.
“It is understood, Blessed One; it is understood, Sugata.
“But how, bhikkhu, do you understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief?”
“Form, venerable sir, is established as something that arouses passion; therein my desire must be abandoned.
Feeling … perception …”
“Volitional formations… consciousness is established as something provocative of lust; therein my desire must be abandoned.
This, venerable sir, is how I understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by the Blessed One in brief.”
“Excellent, excellent, bhikkhu!
It is good that you understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief.
Form, bhikkhu, is established as something provocative of passion; therein, you should abandon desire.”
Feeling … perception … volitional formations …
“Consciousness is established upon what is provocative of lust; therein, your desire must be abandoned.
This, monk, is how the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief should be understood in detail.
… [as before] … And that certain monk became one of the Arahants.
The Eighth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.71 (SN 22.71, PTS SN iii 79) 7.
The Chapter on Arahants.
The Rādhasutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then the Venerable Rādha approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, for one who knows what and sees what do the underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ and conceit not arise with regard to this conscious body and all external signs?
“Rādha, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all form is to be seen as: ‘This is not mine…’”
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus one sees this as it really is with correct wisdom.
Whatever feeling there is...
whatever perception there is...

“Whatever formations there are … whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness should be seen with right wisdom, as it really is, thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
It is for one who knows thus and sees thus, Rādha, that in regard to this conscious body and all external signs, the underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ and conceit do not exist. …pe…
And furthermore, the Venerable Rādha became one of the Arahants.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.72.
7. The Chapter on Arahants.
Surādhasutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then the Venerable Surādha said this to the Blessed One:

“In what way, venerable sir, for one who knows what and sees what does the mind become free from the notions of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ and from the conceit ‘I am,’ regarding both this conscious body and all external signs, having transcended differentiation?”
“Is he peaceful and well-liberated?
“Surādha, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior;
far or near—all form should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’”
Having seen this, one is liberated through non-clinging.
Whatever feeling there may be… whatever perception there may be…
Whatever formations there are ...
whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all feeling ...
all perception ... [and so on].
"All formations...
all consciousness: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—having seen this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one is liberated through non-clinging.
It is for one who knows thus and sees thus, Surādha, regarding this body with its consciousness and all external signs, that [this occurs]."
“His mind becomes free from the notions of ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ transcending all diversity, peaceful, and well-liberated. ...
And so it was that the Venerable Surādha became one of the Arahants.
The tenth [discourse].
The second chapter: The Chapter on Arahants.
Its summary verse:
"Appropriating," "conceiving another,"...
And then, while still rejoicing,
one perceives what is impermanent, suffering, and non-self,
as well as that which is not one's own, yet appears fixed in its attractiveness.
Rādha, you will give to those who deserve it.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.73 (SN 22.73, PTS SN iii 81) 8.

“Bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling does not understand, as it really is, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to form.”
Of feeling … of perception … of volitional formations …
He does not understand, as they really are, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding consciousness.
But, monks, the learned noble disciple understands, as they really are, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding form;
[and] regarding feeling...

First.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.74 (SN 22.74, PTS SN iii 82) 8.
Khajjanīyavagga (The Chapter on Edibles)
The Discourse on Origination. At Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling does not understand, as it really is, the origination, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding form."
Of feeling … of perception … of volitional formations …
He does not understand, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding consciousness.

But, monks, the learned noble disciple understands, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding form. [He understands these] regarding feeling...

Of feeling … of perception … of volitional formations …
