*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.76. (SN 22.76, PTS SN iii 82)
8. Khajjanīyavagga, Arahantasutta.
Setting at Savatthi.
“Bhikkhus, form is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering;
what is suffering is non-self.”
That which is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Feeling... perception... [should be seen in the same way].
Volitional formations … consciousness is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering;
Whatever is suffering is non-self;
whatever is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.

Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness.
“Through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated. One understands:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Monks, as far as the abodes of beings extend, as far as the peak of existence, these are the foremost, these are the best in the world: namely, the Arahants.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
"Happy indeed are the Arahants."
Craving does not exist for them;
the conceit "I am" is utterly severed,
and the net of delusion has been torn asunder.
They have attained the unshakable;
their minds are undisturbed;
they are unsullied in the world.
Become Brahmas, free from taints;
having fully understood the five aggregates,
they dwell among the seven true Dhammas.
The sons of the Buddha, born of his breast, are praiseworthy true men,
endowed with the seven treasures.
Trained in the three trainings,
the great heroes wander about,
having abandoned fear and terror.
Endowed with these ten factors,
these great beings are concentrated;
indeed, they are the most excellent in the world.
Craving does not exist for them.
The knowledge of the one beyond training has arisen;
this is the final body.
In that which is the essence of the holy life,
they are independent of others;
they do not waver amidst various speculative views.
Completely liberated from renewed existence,
having reached the stage of the tamed,
they are victors in the world.
Above, across, and behind,
no delight is found in them;
they roar the lion’s roar.
“The Buddhas are unsurpassed in the world.
The fourth [sutta].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.77. (SN 22.77, PTS SN iii 84)
8. Khajjanīyavagga, Second Discourse on the Arhats.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, form is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering;
what is suffering is non-self.”
"What is non-self, that should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.

… Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness.
Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’"
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being,’ he understands.
To whatever extent, monks, there are abodes of beings, as far as the peak of existence, these are the foremost, these are the best in the world, namely, the Arahants.
This is the fifth [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.78 (SN 22.78, PTS SN iii 84) 8. Khajjanīyavagga Sīhasutta (The Lion) “Bhikkhus, just as the lion, the king of beasts, roars his lion’s roar out of a mountain cave, so too, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has understood form as it really is, its origin as it really is, its cessation as it really is, and the way leading to its cessation as it really is; when he has understood feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as it really is, its origin as it really is, its cessation as it really is, and the way leading to its cessation as it really is—then he is called a bhikkhu who is a lion, a great lion. He roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and he does not tremble when questioned by wanderers of other sects. “What, bhikkhus, is form? Whatever kind of form there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near: this is called form. “And what, bhikkhus, is the origin of form? It is craving, which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that; that is, craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, and craving for extermination. This is called the origin of form. “And what, bhikkhus, is the cessation of form? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the abandoning of it, the relinquishing of it, the liberation from it, and the non-attachment to it. This is called the cessation of form. “And what, bhikkhus, is the way leading to the cessation of form? It is simply this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view … right concentration. This is called the way leading to the cessation of form. “Feeling … Perception … Volitional formations … Consciousness: whatever kind of consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near: this is called consciousness. “And what, bhikkhus, is the origin of consciousness? It is craving, which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that; that is, craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, and craving for extermination. This is called the origin of consciousness. “And what, bhikkhus, is the cessation of consciousness? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the abandoning of it, the relinquishing of it, the liberation from it, and the non-attachment to it. This is called the cessation of consciousness. “And what, bhikkhus, is the way leading to the cessation of consciousness? It is simply this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view … right concentration. This is called the way leading to the cessation of consciousness. “When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has thus understood form as it really is, its origin as it really is, its cessation as it really is, and the way leading to its cessation as it really is; when he has thus understood feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as it really is, its origin as it really is, its cessation as it really is, and the way leading to its cessation as it really is—then he is called a bhikkhu who is a lion, a great lion. He roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and he does not tremble when questioned by wanderers of other sects.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, in the evening time the lion, the king of beasts, emerges from his lair; having emerged from his lair, he stretches himself;
having stretched himself, he surveys the four quarters all around; having surveyed the four quarters all around, three times..."
He lets out a lion’s roar; having roared his lion’s roar three times, he sets out for his range.
For whatever creatures belonging to the animal realm, monks, hear the sound of the lion, the king of beasts, roaring, they for the most part fall into fear, agitation, and terror;
those who dwell in holes enter their holes, and those who dwell in water [enter the water].
They enter [the forest]; out of a desire for the forest, they enter the forest; birds resort to the sky.

Even those royal elephants, monks, who are bound by strong leather thongs in villages, market towns, and royal capitals—even they, having cut through and shattered those bonds, flee here and there in fear, voiding urine and dung.
“Monks, so great is the psychic power of Sīha, the king of beasts, among animals of the animal realm; so great is his influence, so great is his majesty.

In the same way, monks, when a Tathāgata arises in the world—an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Well-Gone One, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One—he teaches the Dhamma:”
‘Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away;
such is feeling … such is perception …’
“Such is volitional formations...
such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away.

Monks, even those gods who are long-lived, beautiful, abundant in happiness, and dwell for long periods in lofty palaces, upon hearing the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, for the most part fall into fear, a sense of urgency, and terror:
‘Alas, sirs, though we were indeed impermanent, we imagined ourselves to be permanent;
though we were indeed unstable, we imagined ourselves to be stable;
though we were indeed non-eternal, we imagined ourselves to be eternal.’
"Indeed, sir, we too are impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and included within identity.
"In this way, monks, the Tathāgata is of such great psychic power in the world with its devas, of such great authority, and of such great majesty.
Thus spoke the Blessed One... [as before]...
The Teacher said this:
“When the Buddha, having attained direct knowledge,
set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma;”
The Teacher, peerless in the world with its devas,
[taught] both personal existence and its cessation.
And the origin of personal existence;
and the Noble Eightfold Path that leads to the stilling of suffering.
Even those long-lived deities,
radiant and glorious,
fell into terror and were seized with fear.
Like other animals to a lion,
we have not transcended personal existence;
indeed, O sir, we are impermanent!
Having heard the words of the Arahant,
the one who is completely liberated and poised in equanimity.
Thus ends the sixth [verse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.79 (SN 22.79, PTS SN iii 86) 8. Khajjanīyavagga: The Discourse on the Edible (Khajjanīyasutta) “Bhikkhus, whatever is subject to being devoured, that is subject to suffering. And what, bhikkhus, is subject to being devoured? The eye is subject to being devoured; therefore it is subject to suffering. The ear is subject to being devoured; therefore it is subject to suffering. The nose is subject to being devoured; therefore it is subject to suffering. The tongue is subject to being devoured; therefore it is subject to suffering. The body is subject to being devoured; therefore it is subject to suffering. The mind is subject to being devoured; therefore it is subject to suffering. Whatever is subject to being devoured, bhikkhus, that is subject to suffering. And what, bhikkhus, is subject to being devoured? The eye is subject to being devoured; therefore it is subject to suffering. The ear... the nose... the tongue... the body... the mind is subject to being devoured; therefore it is subject to suffering. Whatever is subject to being devoured, bhikkhus, that is subject to suffering.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.

"Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins recollect their manifold past abodes, they all recollect these five aggregates of clinging, or one or another of them. Which five? [The five aggregates of clinging...]"
‘I was such-and-such in form in the past’—
thus, monks, when recollecting, one recollects only form.
‘I was such-and-such in feeling in the past’— thus...
For in this way, monks, when recollecting, one recollects feeling itself:
‘I had such a perception in the past’ … ‘I had such a volitional formation in the past. …
‘I had such a consciousness in the past’—
in recollecting thus, bhikkhus, one recollects only consciousness.
And what, bhikkhus, do you say is form?
"It is deformed, monks, therefore it is called 'form' (rūpa).
By what is it deformed?
It is deformed by cold, it is deformed by heat, it is deformed by hunger, it is deformed by thirst, and it is deformed by contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things."
“It is deformed, monks, therefore it is called ‘form.
And what, monks, do you call ‘feeling’?
It feels, monks, therefore it is called ‘feeling.’”
And what does it feel?
It feels pleasure, it feels pain, and it feels neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
Monks, because it feels, therefore it is called "feeling."
And why, monks, do you call it perception?
It is called ‘perception,’ monks, because one perceives. And what does one perceive?
One perceives blue, one perceives yellow, one perceives red, and one perceives white.
It is called “perception” (saññā), monks, because one perceives.
And what, monks, do you call “formations” (saṅkhārā)?
“Monks, they construct the conditioned; therefore, they are called ‘volitional formations.
And what is it that they construct as conditioned?
They construct form as form-ness; they construct feeling as feeling-ness.”
They construct the conditioned as perception for the sake of perception; they construct the conditioned as volitional formations for the sake of volitional formations;
they construct the conditioned as consciousness for the sake of consciousness.
"They construct the conditioned," monks, therefore it is called "volitional formations" (*saṅkhārā*).
And why, monks, do you call it consciousness?
It is called “consciousness,” monks, because it cognizes.
And what does it cognize?

It cognizes what is sour, it cognizes what is bitter, it cognizes what is pungent, it cognizes what is sweet, it cognizes what is salty, it cognizes what is unsalty, it cognizes what is salty-sour, and it cognizes what is not salty-sour.
It is called “consciousness” (viññāṇa), bhikkhus, because it cognizes.
Therein, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple reflects thus:
‘I am indeed being devoured by form at present.
In the past, too, I was devoured by form in exactly the same way as I am now being devoured by present form.
And if I were to delight in future form, then in the future, too, I would be devoured by form in exactly the same way as I am now being devoured by present form.’
Having reflected thus, he is indifferent toward past form;
he does not delight in future form;
and he practices for the sake of revulsion toward, dispassion toward, and the cessation of present form.
‘I am indeed being consumed by feeling at present.
In the past, too, I was consumed by feeling in exactly the same way as I am now being consumed by present feeling.
And if I were to delight in future feeling, [the same would happen].’
‘In the future time as well, I shall be devoured by feeling in exactly the same way that I am now being devoured by present feeling.
Having reflected thus, he becomes indifferent toward past feeling and does not delight in future feeling.
He practices for disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of present feeling.
‘I am indeed being devoured by perception at this time...
I am indeed being devoured by volitional formations at this time.’
"In the past, too, I was devoured by formations in just this same way, just as I am now being devoured by present formations.
And if I were to delight in future formations, then in the future, too,
I would be devoured by formations in just this same way, just as I am now being devoured by present formations."
Having reflected thus, he becomes indifferent toward past formations,
does not delight in future formations,
and practices for the sake of disenchantment with, the fading away of lust for, and the cessation of present formations.
‘I am indeed being devoured by consciousness at present.
In the past, too, I was devoured by consciousness in exactly the same way as I am now being devoured by present consciousness.
And if I were to delight in future consciousness;’
‘In the future time as well, I shall be devoured by consciousness in this very same way, just as I am being devoured by consciousness now in the present.
Having reflected thus, he becomes indifferent toward past consciousness and does not delight in future consciousness.
He practices for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of present consciousness.
What do you think, monks,
is form permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“Feeling … perception … volitional formations …”
“Is consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Therefore, bhikkhus, whatever kind of form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external;
gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form [should be regarded as it actually is with right wisdom]:”
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’— thus should this be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Whatever feeling there is… whatever perception there is…
Whatever formations there are...

whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present... far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
This, monks, is called a noble disciple who dismantles and does not accumulate.
He abandons, he does not grasp;
he removes, he does not heap up;
he shakes off, he does not blow upon.
And what does one diminish, not accumulate?
One diminishes form, not accumulating it; one diminishes feeling...
He diminishes perception,
volitional formations,
and consciousness; he does not accumulate them.
And what does one abandon and not cling to?
One abandons form and does not cling to it; one abandons feeling...
One abandons perception,
volitional formations,
and consciousness; one does not cling to them.
And what does he bury and not heap up?
He buries form and does not heap it up; he buries feeling … [and so on for the remaining aggregates].
He suppresses perception,
volitional formations,
and consciousness; he does not exalt them.
And what does he shake off, rather than blowing upon?
He shakes off form, rather than blowing upon it; he shakes off feeling …
He shakes off perception,
volitional formations,
and consciousness; he does not blow them up.

Seeing thus, monks, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, and he becomes disenchanted with feeling... with perception... with volitional formations... and he becomes disenchanted with consciousness.
Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated. He understands:
"Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
This, monks, is called a monk who neither accumulates nor dismantles, but stands having dismantled;
who neither abandons nor grasps, but stands having abandoned; who neither lowers nor raises, but stands having lowered;
who neither fans away nor fans toward, but stands having fanned away.
And what is it that neither accumulates nor diminishes, but stands having been diminished?
Form neither accumulates nor diminishes, but stands having been diminished; feeling ... [neither accumulates nor diminishes, but stands having been diminished].
He neither accumulates nor dismantles perception, volitional formations, and consciousness; having dismantled them, he stands firm.
And what is it that he neither abandons nor clings to, but stands having abandoned?
He neither abandons nor clings to form, but stands having abandoned it; he neither abandons nor clings to feeling...
He neither abandons nor clings to perception, volitional formations, or consciousness; having abandoned them, he stands firm.
And what is it that he neither rejects nor retains, but remains having rejected?
He neither rejects nor retains form, remaining having rejected it; [he neither rejects nor retains] feeling...
He neither suppresses nor exalts perception, volitional formations, and consciousness; having suppressed them, he remains established.
And what is it that he neither shakes off nor fans into flame, but stands having shaken it off?
He neither shakes off nor fans into flame form, but stands having shaken it off; [he neither shakes off nor fans into flame] feeling...
He neither disperses nor intensifies perception, volitional formations, and consciousness; having dispersed them, he remains established.
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus liberated, the gods together with Indra, Brahmā, and Pajāpati pay homage to him from afar, saying:
‘Homage to you, O noble among men!
Homage to you, O supreme among men!’”
“Of that which we do not know,
nor even that upon which you meditate.
Thus ends the seventh [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.80 (SN 22.80, PTS SN iii 91) 8. Khajjanīyavagga Piṇḍolyasutta “Bhikkhus, whatever is found, obtained, sought after, and accumulated by a bhikkhu through alms-gathering—that is his own, that is his personal possession, that is his very self; it is not the property of others, nor will it be taken away by others. Just as whatever is found, obtained, sought after, and accumulated by a man who has gone begging for food—that is his own, that is his personal possession, that is his very self; it is not the property of others, nor will it be taken away by others—so too, bhikkhus, whatever is found, obtained, sought after, and accumulated by a bhikkhu through alms-gathering—that is his own, that is his personal possession, that is his very self; it is not the property of others, nor will it be taken away by others. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will seek our own welfare, not the welfare of others.’”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.
Then, on a certain occasion, the Blessed One dismissed the community of monks and, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Kapilavatthu for alms.
Having walked for alms in Kapilavatthu, after his meal, returning from his almsround, he went to the Great Forest for his midday rest.
Having entered deep into the Great Forest, he sat for his midday rest at the foot of a *veluva* sapling.
Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
"I have indeed dismissed the community of monks."
There are some monks here who are new, recently gone forth, having only lately come to this Dhamma and Discipline.
In their absence from me, there may be a change in them, there may be a transformation.
Just as, for example, a young calf, not seeing its mother, might undergo a change and experience a transformation.
In the same way, there may be change and transformation for those monks here who are new, recently gone forth, and have only lately come to this Dhamma and Vinaya, should they not see me.
Just as young seedlings, if they do not receive water, may undergo change and transformation; even so, there may be change and transformation for those monks here... [as before].
"If they were unable to see me, there might be distress in them; there might be change;
there might be transformation. What if I were now to favor the community of monks just as I previously favored the community of monks?
Then Brahmā Sahampati, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Blessed One's mind—just as if...
Just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, even so, having vanished from the Brahma world,
he appeared before the Blessed One.
Then Brahmā Sahampati, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and extending his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One:
“So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
The Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been left behind by the Blessed One, venerable sir.
Among them are bhikkhus who are new, recently gone forth, having only lately arrived at this Dhamma and Discipline.”
Not seeing the Blessed One, there might be a change in them, there might be a transformation.

Just as a young calf, not seeing its mother, would undergo a change and a transformation, even so, there are here monks who are new, recently gone forth, having only lately come to this Dhamma and Discipline; not seeing the Blessed One, there might be a change in them, there might be a transformation.

"Just as young seeds, if they do not receive water, might undergo alteration and transformation, even so, there are here monks who are new, recently gone forth, and have only lately come to this Dhamma and Vinaya; for them, if they do not obtain a sight of the Blessed One, there might be alteration and transformation.
May the Blessed One, venerable sir, take delight in the Saṅgha of bhikkhus."
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One pay homage to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Just as the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was formerly favored by the Blessed One, so may he favor the Saṅgha of bhikkhus now.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then Brahmā Sahampati, having understood the Blessed One’s consent, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and vanished right there.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the Nigrodha Monastery; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Once seated, the Blessed One performed such a feat of supernormal power that those monks, feeling a sense of longing, would come to him every day or every other day.
Then those bhikkhus, feeling somewhat embarrassed, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, the Blessed One said to those bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, this is the lowest of livelihoods, namely, living on alms."
“Monks, this is a curse in the world: ‘You wander about like a beggar, with bowl in hand!
Yet, monks, it is for the sake of a purpose, and depending on a purpose, that sons of good family enter [the homeless life];
they are not driven by kings, nor driven by thieves, nor oppressed by debt, nor oppressed by fear, nor reduced to such a state by lack of livelihood.”

Moreover, monks, this clansman has gone forth thinking: "We have indeed descended into birth, aging, and death; into sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. We are immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering.
Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.
It is thus, monks, that this clansman has gone forth.

Yet he is covetous regarding sense pleasures, with intense lust, a mind full of ill will, corrupt in his mental intentions, muddled in mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind, and with unguarded faculties. Monks,
just as a brand of wood burning at both ends and smeared with excrement in the middle serves no purpose as firewood either in the village or in the forest—
just so, monks, do I say of this person that he has fallen away from the enjoyments of a householder and does not fulfill the goal of recluseship.
“Bhikkhus, there are three kinds of unwholesome thoughts:
thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty.
And where, bhikkhus, do these three kinds of unwholesome thoughts cease without remainder?”
Or for one who dwells with a mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, developing signless concentration:
to this extent, monks, it is indeed sufficient to develop signless concentration.
Monks, signless concentration, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit.
“Bhikkhus, there are these two views:
the view of existence and the view of non-existence.
In this regard, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple reflects thus:”
‘Is there anything in this world such that, by clinging to it, I would not be blameworthy?
He understands thus:
‘There is indeed nothing in this world such that, by clinging to it, I would not be blameworthy.’
For I would only be grasping if I were grasping at form;
I would only be grasping if I were grasping at feeling... perception... volitional formations... or consciousness.
For me, with clinging as condition, existence would come to be;
with existence as condition, birth;
and with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would arise.
"Thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
"What do you think, monks,
is form permanent or impermanent?"
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Feeling … perception … volitional formations …”
Consciousness … [and so on] … Therefore, bhikkhus,
seeing thus …
“He understands: ‘There is nothing further beyond this state of being.
Thus it was said.
The eighth. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.81. (SN 22.81, PTS SN iii 94)
8. The Chapter on Edibles:
The Pālileyya Discourse.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Kosambī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Kosambī, after his meal and returning from his almsround, he himself arranged his lodging, took his bowl and robe,
and set out on a walking tour alone, without a companion, without informing his attendants and without taking leave of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, a certain bhikkhu approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him:

“Friend Ānanda, the Blessed One has himself put his lodging in order, taken his bowl and robe, and set out on a walking tour alone, without a companion, without taking leave of his attendants and without informing the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“Friend, at the time when the Blessed One has himself put his lodging in order, taken his bowl and robe, and [set out] without taking leave...”
“Without taking leave of his attendants, he sets out on tour alone, without a companion,
because at that time the Blessed One wishes to dwell by himself;
at that time, the Blessed One is not to be followed by anyone.”
Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages on his tour, arrived at Pārileyyaka.
There, the Blessed One stayed near Pārileyyaka at the foot of the Bhaddasāla tree.
Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those bhikkhus said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Friend Ānanda, it has been a long time since we have heard a discourse on the Dhamma from the presence of the Blessed One.
We wish, friend Ānanda, to hear a discourse on the Dhamma from the presence of the Blessed One."

Then the Venerable Ānanda, together with those bhikkhus, approached Pālileyyaka, the foot of the Bhaddasāla tree, where the Blessed One was staying. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As those bhikkhus were seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dhamma.
At that time, a certain bhikkhu had this reflection arise in his mind:
“How indeed must one know, how must one see, for the immediate destruction of the taints to occur?
Then the Blessed One, having known with his own mind the reflection in the mind of that bhikkhu, addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been taught by me through analysis;”
The four foundations of mindfulness are taught by way of investigation;
the four right efforts are taught by way of investigation;
the four bases of psychic power are taught by way of investigation.
The five faculties have been taught by way of investigation;
the five powers have been taught by way of investigation;
the seven factors of enlightenment have been taught by way of investigation.
The Noble Eightfold Path has been taught by me through analysis.
Thus, monks, has the Dhamma been taught by me through analysis.
Now, monks, when the Dhamma has been taught by me through analysis, there arose in the mind of a certain monk this reflection:
‘How is it that for one who knows what, and sees what, there is the immediate destruction of the taints?
And how, monks, is it that for one who knows what, and sees what, there is the immediate destruction of the taints?

Here, monks, an uninstructed worldling—who has no regard for the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has no regard for true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—[perceives things thus].”
One regards form as self.
Now, monks, that regarding is a mental formation (*saṅkhāra*).
What is the source of that formation, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance?
“Bhikkhus, when an uninstructed worldling is touched by a feeling born of contact with ignorance, craving arises in him;
from that, volitional formations are born.
Thus, bhikkhus, those volitional formations are also impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.”
That craving, too, is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
That feeling, too, and that contact, too, are impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
That ignorance, too, is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
In this way too, monks, for one who knows thus and sees thus, there is the destruction of the taints in this very life.
One does not regard form as self,
yet one regards self as possessing form.
Furthermore, monks, that which is contemplation is a volitional formation (*saṅkhāra*).
Now, what is the source of that volitional formation? What is its origin? What is its birth?
What is its provenance? It is the craving that arises, monks, in the uninstructed worldling who has been touched by a feeling born of contact with ignorance.
And that volitional formation is likewise.
Thus, monks, that volitional formation too is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
That craving too...
That feeling as well...
that contact as well...
that ignorance as well is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
In this way too, monks, for one who knows thus and sees thus, there is the immediate destruction of the taints.
It is not that one regards form as self, nor that one regards the self as possessing form;
rather, one regards form as being within the self.
Furthermore, monks, that contemplation is a mental formation (*saṅkhāra*).
Now, what is the source of that formation, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance?
It is the craving that arises, monks, in the uninstructed worldling who has been touched by a feeling born of contact with ignorance.
And that volitional formation as well.
Thus, monks, that volitional formation too is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
And that craving as well...
That feeling as well...
that contact as well...
that ignorance as well is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
In this way too, monks, for one who knows thus and sees thus, there is the immediate destruction of the taints.
It is not that one regards form as self, nor regards self as possessing form, nor regards form as being in self;
rather, one regards self as being in form.
Now, monks, that contemplation is a volitional formation.
And what is the source of that volitional formation, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its arising?
It is the craving that arises in the uninstructed worldling who has been touched by a feeling born of contact with ignorance.
And that volitional formation is likewise.
Thus, monks, that volitional formation is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
And that craving is likewise...
That feeling as well...
that contact as well...
that ignorance as well is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
In this way too, monks, for one who knows thus... there comes to be the destruction of the taints.
It is not that one regards form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as being in self, nor self as being in form;
yet one regards feeling as self, or regards self as possessing feeling, or regards feeling as being in self, or regards self as being in feeling.
Furthermore, one regards perception as self; or one regards self as possessing perception; or one regards perception in self; or one regards self in perception.
Furthermore, one regards consciousness as self; or one regards self as possessing consciousness; or one regards consciousness in self; or one regards self in consciousness.
Now, monks, that contemplation is a formation.
And what is the source of that formation? ... What is its origin?
Monks, craving arises in the uninstructed worldling who has been touched by a feeling born of contact with ignorance.
And that volitional formation is likewise.
Thus, monks, that volitional formation is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
That craving is likewise...
That feeling as well...
that contact as well...
that ignorance as well is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
It is for one who knows thus and sees thus, monks, that the immediate destruction of the taints occurs.
One does not regard form as self,
nor does one regard feeling as self.
One does not regard perception as self, nor volitional formations as self, nor consciousness as self.
Moreover, one holds such a view as this:
‘That self, that world, shall exist after death—eternal, stable, everlasting, not subject to change.
Now, monks, whatever is this eternalist view, it is a conditioned formation.
But what is that volitional formation conditioned by?
... In this way too, monks, for one who knows thus and sees thus, there is the immediate destruction of the taints.
Yet he does not regard form as self.
not feeling … not perception … not volitional formations …
One does not regard consciousness as self,
nor does one hold such a view as:
"That self, that world, shall become after death permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change."
Moreover, one holds such a view as this:
‘I shall not be, and it shall not be mine; I will not exist, and it will not be mine.
Now, monks, that which is the annihilationist view is itself a conditioned formation.
But what is that volitional formation (saṅkhāra) conditioned by, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its source?
Monks, craving arises in the uninstructed worldling who is touched by a feeling born of contact with ignorance;
from that, that volitional formation is born.
"Thus, monks, that formation as well is impermanent...
In this way, monks, for one who knows thus and sees thus, there is the immediate destruction of the taints.
One does not regard form as self, nor feeling..."
He does not regard perception as self... nor volitional formations... nor consciousness as self... [and so on]...
One does not regard consciousness as self, nor does one hold such a view as:
"That is the self, that is the world; after death I shall become permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change";
nor does one hold such a view as:
‘May I not be, and may nothing be mine;
may I not come to be, and may nothing be mine in the future’—yet he remains doubtful, perplexed, and undecided regarding the true Dhamma.
For whatever doubt, perplexity, and indecision there is regarding the true Dhamma, monks, that is a conditioned formation.
But what is that volitional formation (saṅkhāra) rooted in, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its source?
Monks, craving arises in the uninstructed worldling who is touched by a feeling born of contact with ignorance;
that volitional formation is born from that.
Thus, monks, that volitional formation is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
That craving is also impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
That feeling is also impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
That contact too is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
That ignorance too is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.
It is for one who knows thus and sees thus, monks, that the immediate destruction of the taints occurs.
The Ninth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.82 (SN 22.82, PTS SN iii 100) 8.
The Chapter on Edibles (Khajjanīyavagga)
The Full Moon Discourse.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother, together with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Now on that occasion—the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, during the full moon night—the Blessed One was seated in the open air, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Then a certain bhikkhu rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I would ask the Blessed One about a certain point, if the Blessed One would grant me the opportunity for an answer to my question.
“In that case, bhikkhu, sit down on your own seat and ask whatever you wish,” [the Blessed One replied].
“Yes, venerable sir,” that bhikkhu replied to the Blessed One. Sitting on his own seat, he said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, are these the five aggregates subject to clinging? That is to say:

the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging?”
“Monk, these are the five aggregates subject to clinging:
namely, the aggregate of form subject to clinging … [as before] … the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging.
“Excellent, Bhante,” that monk, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, asked the Blessed One a further question:
“But, Bhante, what is the root of these five aggregates subject to clinging?
“Monk, these five aggregates subject to clinging have desire as their root.
… [as before] … “Bhante, is that very clinging the same as those five aggregates subject to clinging, or is clinging something apart from the five aggregates subject to clinging?”

“Monk, clinging is neither identical to those five aggregates of clinging, nor is clinging something apart from the five aggregates of clinging; rather, whatever desire and lust there is for them, that is the clinging therein.
“Excellent, Bhante,” that monk said... [and] asked a further question:
“But could there be, Bhante, a distinction in the desire and lust for the five aggregates of clinging?”
“It may be so, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said.
“In this case, bhikkhu, it occurs to a certain person:

‘May I be of such form in the future; may I be of such feeling in the future; may I be of such perception in the future; may I be of such volitional formations in the future; may I be of such consciousness in the future.’”
“In this way, bhikkhu, there may be a diversity of desire and lust regarding the five aggregates of clinging.
“Very well, Bhante,” that bhikkhu replied, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat down at one side and asked a further question:
“In what way, Bhante, is there the designation ‘aggregates’ for the aggregates?”
“Bhikkhu, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that is called the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha).
Whatever feeling there is… whatever perception there is…”
“Whatever formations...
whatever consciousness, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—this is called the aggregate of consciousness.
To this extent, monk, there is the designation ‘aggregate’ for the aggregates.”
“Excellent, Bhante,” that bhikkhu replied … and he asked:
“What, Bhante, is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the form aggregate;
what is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the feeling aggregate?”
What is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of perception?
What is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of volitional formations?
What is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of consciousness?”
“Bhikkhu, the four great elements are the cause, the four great elements are the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of form.
Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of feeling.
Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of perception.”
“Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of volitional formations.
Name-and-form is the cause, name-and-form is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of consciousness.
“Excellent, Bhante,” that bhikkhu said, and he asked further:
“Venerable sir, how does identity view come to be?
“In this case, bhikkhu, an uninstructed worldling—who has no regard for the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones;

who has no regard for true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form.
feeling … perception … volitional formations …
“One regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.
In this way, bhikkhu, there is identity view.
“Excellent, Bhante,” that bhikkhu replied, and he questioned him further:
“But how, venerable sir, does personality-view not come to be?
“Here, bhikkhu, the well-taught noble disciple—who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and is well-disciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones;

who has seen true persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and is well-disciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as in self, nor self as in form.
not feeling … not perception … not volitional formations …
“He does not regard consciousness as self, nor the self as possessing consciousness; nor consciousness as being in the self, nor the self as being in consciousness.
In this way, bhikkhu, personality-view does not exist.
“Excellent, Bhante,” that bhikkhu said, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat down at one side and asked:
“Venerable sir, what is the gratification in form, what is the danger, and what is the escape? What is the gratification in feeling … what is the gratification in perception …”
“What, monk, is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape regarding volitional formations … regarding consciousness?
“Monk, whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on form— that is the gratification of form.”
That form which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in form.
The removal of desire and lust for form, the abandoning of desire and lust for form—this is the escape from form.
That feeling which is dependent on... [and so forth].
The pleasure and joy that arise in dependence on perception … in dependence on volitional formations … in dependence on consciousness: this is the gratification in consciousness.
“That consciousness which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in consciousness.
The removal of desire and lust for consciousness, the abandoning of desire and lust for consciousness—this is the escape from consciousness.
“Excellent, Bhante! that bhikkhu, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, asked the Blessed One a further question:
“Venerable sir, for one who knows what and sees what do the underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ and conceit not arise regarding this conscious body and all external signs?
“Bhikkhu, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all form is to be seen thus: ‘This is not mine...’”
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus one sees this as it really is with correct wisdom.
Whatever feeling there is...
whatever perception there is...
Whatever formations...
whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness is: "This is not mine, this I am not."
‘This is not my self’—thus one sees this as it really is with correct wisdom.

It is for one who knows thus and sees thus, bhikkhu, that in regard to this conscious body and all external signs, there are no underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ or the conceit ‘I am.
At that time, a reflection arose in the mind of a certain bhikkhu:
“Thus, indeed, friends, form is not-self; feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness is not-self.
How will actions performed by what is not-self affect the self?
Then the Blessed One, having known with his own mind the reflection in the mind of that bhikkhu, addressed the bhikkhus:
“It is possible, monks, that some foolish person here, being ignorant and immersed in ignorance, with a mind dominated by craving, might think the Teacher’s instruction should be overstepped:
‘So, indeed, sirs, form is not-self; feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness is not-self.
How can actions performed by what is not-self affect the self?’”
“Bhikkhus, you have been trained by way of cross-questioning regarding various matters here and there.
What do you think, bhikkhus,
is form permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“Feeling … perception …”
“Are volitional formations … consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.”
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”—
“Suffering, venerable sir.”—
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change— is it fitting to regard it thus:”
“‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”—
“Certainly not, Bhante. Therefore, in this regard … [as before] …
“Seeing thus...
he understands: ‘There is nothing further beyond this state.
“The two aggregates would be that very same thing.”
And by means of a designation and a cause;
two are spoken of by way of personality-view (sakkāya) and by way of the consciousness that experiences gratification.
"These ten kinds have been declared;
thus is a bhikkhu [defined] by way of inquiry. Tenth.
The Third Chapter on Things to be Chewed.
Its summary verse:
Delight and two origins.
Two others were Arahants:
Sīha, who lived on scraps from a food-remnant,
and Puṇṇa by Pālileyya.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.83 (SN 22.83, PTS SN iii 105) 9. Theravagga Ānandasutta Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Ānanda, you have been instructed by me through many discourses on the theme: ‘This is suffering. You have been instructed by me through many discourses on the theme: ‘This is the origin of suffering. You have been instructed by me through many discourses on the theme: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. You have been instructed by me through many discourses on the theme: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “But, venerable sir, how should I understand in detail the meaning of what was stated in brief by the Blessed One? “Ānanda, form is suffering. This, Ānanda, is the detailed meaning of what was stated in brief by me thus: ‘This is suffering. Feeling is suffering... Perception is suffering... Volitional formations are suffering... Consciousness is suffering. This, Ānanda, is the detailed meaning of what was stated in brief by me thus: ‘This is suffering. “Form is impermanent. This, Ānanda, is the detailed meaning of what was stated in brief by me thus: ‘This is the origin of suffering. Feeling is impermanent... Perception is impermanent... Volitional formations are impermanent... Consciousness is impermanent. Theravagga (The Chapter on Elders)
The Tissa Sutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Now on that occasion the Venerable Tissa, the Blessed One’s paternal cousin, announced this to a number of bhikkhus:
“Friends, my body feels as if it has become heavy; the directions are no longer clear to me; the teachings do not occur to me;
sloth and torpor persist, consuming my mind; I live the holy life without delight;
and doubt regarding the teachings arises within me.”

Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the Venerable Tissa, the Blessed One’s paternal cousin, has informed a number of bhikkhus thus:
‘Friends, my body feels as if it has become numb; the directions are not clear to me; even the teachings do not [occur] to me.’”
“[The teachings] do not appear to me; sloth and torpor persist, seizing my mind;
I live the holy life without delight; and I have doubt regarding the Dhammas.
Then the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu:
“Come, bhikkhu, address the bhikkhu Tissa in my name.
“Yes, venerable sir,” that bhikkhu replied to the Blessed One. He then approached the Venerable Tissa and said to him:
“Friend Tissa, the Teacher calls for you.”
“Yes, friend,” the Venerable Tissa replied to that bhikkhu.
He then approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As the Venerable Tissa was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Is it true, Tissa, that you told a number of bhikkhus:
‘Friends, my body feels as if it has become numb... and there is doubt in me regarding the teachings’?
“Yes, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Tissa? For one who has not departed from lust for forms,
who has not departed from desire for them, who has not departed from affection for them, who has not departed from thirst for them, who has not departed from fever for them,
who has not departed from craving for them— does sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise due to the change and alteration of those forms?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Excellent, excellent, Tissa!
It is indeed so, Tissa.”
Just as it is for one who has not abandoned lust for form,
so too for feeling … for perception … [and for volitional formations].
“Is it not the case, bhikkhus, that for one who has not abandoned lust for volitional formations,
sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise with the change and alteration of those volitional formations?”—
“It is so, Bhante.”
“Excellent, excellent, Tissa! It is just so, Tissa;

for this is how it is for one who has not transcended lust for volitional formations, who has not transcended lust for consciousness, and who has not transcended desire, affection, and longing for it.”
“For one whose thirst has not been abandoned, whose fever has not been abandoned, and whose craving has not been abandoned, with the change and alteration of that consciousness,
sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise?”— “Yes, venerable sir.”
“Excellent, excellent, Tissa!
It is so, Tissa; for it is so for one who has not yet become free from lust for consciousness.”
"What do you think, Tissa, for one who is free from lust for form,
free from desire for form, free from affection for form, free from thirst for form, free from fever for form,
and free from craving for form— do sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise due to the change and alteration of that form?"
“No, Bhante.
“Excellent, excellent, Tissa!
For it is so, Tissa, that this is how it is.”
Just as it is for one who is free from lust for form,
so too for feeling… for perception… [and so on].
“...for one who is free from lust for volitional formations ...
for one who is free from lust for consciousness, free from desire, free from affection, free from thirst, free from fever, and free from craving—
do sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in them due to the change and alteration of that consciousness?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Excellent, excellent, Tissa!
For it is so, Tissa, that it is.”
Just as it is for one who is free from lust for consciousness.
What do you think, Tissa,
is form permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“Feeling … perception …”
“Are volitional formations … consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.”
“Therefore, bhikkhus,
… seeing thus … he understands:
‘… there is no more for this state of being.’”
"Just as, Tissa, there might be two men—
one man unskilled in the way and one man skilled in the way—
and that man unskilled in the way were to ask that man skilled in the way about the way."
Then one might say this:
‘Come, good man, this is the path;
go along it for a moment.’
Having gone a short distance from there, you will see a forked path; there, leave the left and take the right.
Go for a short distance by that way.
Having gone a short distance from there, you will see a dense forest thicket.
Go for a moment.
Having gone for a moment, you will see a large, low-lying marsh.
Go for a moment.
“Having gone a short distance from there, you will see a precipice and a chasm.
Go for a short while.
Having gone a short distance from there, you will see a level stretch of ground, delightful.”
This simile, Tissa, has been given by me for the purpose of making the meaning clear.
And this is the meaning here:
"A man unskilled in the path," Tissa, is a designation for the worldling.
‘A man skilled in the path,’ Tissa, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
‘A forked road,’ Tissa, is a designation for doubt.

‘The wrong path to the left,’ Tissa, is a designation for the eightfold wrong path, namely: [the eight factors of wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration].”
“Of wrong view... [and so on] ...of wrong concentration.
‘The right path,’ Tissa, is a designation for this Noble Eightfold Path, namely:
right view... [and so on] ...right concentration.”
“‘The thicket of forest’ (tibbo vanasaṇḍo), Tissa, is a designation for ignorance.
‘The great low-lying marshland’ (mahantaṁ ninnaṁ pallalaṁ), Tissa, is a designation for sensual pleasures.
‘The pit and precipice’ (sobbho papāto), Tissa, is a designation for anger and despair.”
“‘A level stretch of ground, delightful,’ Tissa, is a designation for Nibbāna.
Rejoice, Tissa! Rejoice, Tissa!
Through my instruction, through my assistance, and through my guidance.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Tissa, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.

On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
Now at that time, a pernicious view had arisen in a bhikkhu named Yamaka:
“As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body; he does not exist after death.”
A number of bhikkhus heard that a certain bhikkhu named Yamaka had developed such an evil speculative view as this:
“As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body; he does not exist after death.
Then those bhikkhus approached the Venerable Yamaka and exchanged greetings with him.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, those bhikkhus said to the Venerable Yamaka:
“Is it true, friend Yamaka, that such an evil speculative view has arisen in you:
‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body; he does not exist after death’?”
“Indeed, friend, this is how I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One:
‘With the breakup of the body, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes; he does not exist after death.
“Do not say that, friend Yamaka! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not speak in such a way.”
“A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body; he does not exist after death.
Even though the Venerable Yamaka was addressed by those bhikkhus in this way, he stubbornly and dogmatically adhered to that evil view and continued to assert:
“As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body; he does not exist after death.”
When those bhikkhus were unable to detach the Venerable Yamaka from that evil course of view,
they rose from their seats and approached the Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached,
they said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Friend Sāriputta, such an evil speculative view has arisen in the bhikkhu named Yamaka:
‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body; he does not exist after death.
It would be well if the Venerable Sāriputta would approach the bhikkhu Yamaka out of compassion.”
The Venerable Sāriputta consented by remaining silent.
