“If you were asked this, friend Yamaka, how would you answer?
“If they were to ask me, friend, ‘Friend Yamaka,
what becomes of that bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, with the breakup of the body, after death?’”
Being asked thus, friends, I would answer thus:
"Form, friends, is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering."
Whatever is suffering has ceased; that has come to an end. Feeling … perception … [has ceased; that has come to an end].
Volitional formations ...
consciousness is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering;
“Whatever was suffering has ceased; it has come to an end.
If I were asked thus, friend, I would answer in this way.
“Excellent, excellent, friend Yamaka!”
Therefore, friend Yamaka, I will give you a simile to further clarify this very point.
Suppose, friend Yamaka, there were a householder or a householder’s son, wealthy, affluent, and of great fortune,
who was also well-protected.
Suppose some man were to appear who was desirous of his harm, desirous of his ruin, desirous of his lack of security from bondage, and desirous of depriving him of life.
He would think:
"This householder or householder’s son is wealthy, with great riches and great possessions."
"He is well-guarded;
it is not easy to deprive him of life by force.
What if I were to deprive him of life by stealth?"
Then, having approached that householder or householder’s son, one would say:
“Venerable sir, may I attend upon you?
And that householder or householder’s son would have him attend upon them.
Thus he should attend upon him— rising before him, retiring after him, being responsive to his needs, acting with agreeable conduct,
and speaking kindly. Then that householder or householder’s son would trust him as a friend and trust him as a close companion.
And one might place trust in him. But when that man thinks,
"This householder or householder’s son has placed his confidence in me," then, knowing him to be alone, he might deprive him of life with a sharp sword.
"What do you think, friend Yamaka?
When that man approaches that householder or householder’s son and says,
‘I would serve you, venerable sir,’ even then he is still a murderer."
Moreover, while the executioner was present, he did not recognize him as such,

thinking, "He is my executioner. Even when he attended upon him— rising before him, retiring after him, being obedient to his every command, acting with kindness, and speaking pleasant words— even then, he remained an executioner.
Moreover, while the executioner was present, he did not recognize him,
thinking, "This is my executioner. Even when,
having seen him gone into solitude, he deprives him of life with a sharp blade, even then he is indeed the executioner.
"And yet he did not recognize that his executioner was present, thinking:
'My executioner is here.
"It is so, friend," [he replied].
“In the same way, friend, the uninstructed worldling—who has no regard for the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones;

who has no regard for true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. He regards feeling as self….”

One regards perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception as in self, or self as in perception. One regards volitional formations as self... One regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.
Thus, one does not understand as it really is impermanent form as ‘impermanent form’;
one does not understand as it really is impermanent feeling as ‘impermanent feeling’;
one does not understand as it really is impermanent perception as ‘impermanent perception’.
One does not understand conditioned phenomena as they really are: "Conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
One does not understand consciousness as it really is: "Consciousness is impermanent.
One does not understand form as it really is: "Form is suffering."
Painful feeling … painful perception … painful volitional formations …
One does not understand suffering consciousness as it really is, as “suffering consciousness.
One does not understand non-self form as it really is, as “non-self form.
One does not understand non-self feeling…
One does not understand as it really is impermanent perception... impermanent volitional formations... and impermanent consciousness as ‘impermanent consciousness.’
One does not understand conditioned form as it really is, as "conditioned form. One does not understand conditioned feeling...
conditioned perception... [as they really are].
One does not understand conditioned formations as they really are, as "conditioned formations"; one does not understand conditioned consciousness as it really is, as "conditioned consciousness.
One does not understand murderous form as it really is, as "murderous form."
One does not understand as it really is murderous feeling as ‘murderous feeling’;
one does not understand murderous perception as ‘murderous perception’;
one does not understand murderous volitional formations as ‘murderous volitional formations.’
One does not understand consciousness, which is a murderer, as it really is: ‘Consciousness is a murderer.
Thus one approaches form, clings to it, and resolves upon it, thinking, ‘This is my self. One [does the same] with feeling...
One approaches perception,
volitional formations,
and consciousness, clings to them, and resolves upon them as "this is my self."
These five aggregates of clinging, when approached and clung to, lead for a long time to harm and suffering.
But, friends, the well-taught noble disciple, who has vision of the noble ones...
being well-trained in the Dhamma of the true person, does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as in self, nor self as in form.
Not feeling...
not perception...
not volitional formations...
He does not regard consciousness as self, nor self as possessing consciousness,
nor consciousness as being in self, nor self as being in consciousness.
He understands impermanent form, as it really is, to be "impermanent form."
Feeling is impermanent… perception is impermanent… volitional formations are impermanent…
One understands as it really is that consciousness is impermanent: "Consciousness is impermanent.
One understands as it really is that form is suffering: "Form is suffering. One understands as it really is that feeling is suffering...
One understands as it really is: "Suffering perception... suffering volitional formations... suffering consciousness is suffering consciousness."
One understands form, which is non-self, as it really is: "Form is non-self. One understands feeling, which is non-self... perception, which is non-self... [as it really is:
"Perception is non-self"].
He understands as it really is that volitional formations are non-self… that consciousness is non-self, ‘consciousness is non-self.
He understands as it really is that conditioned form is conditioned, ‘conditioned form.’
Conditioned feeling … conditioned perception … conditioned volitional formations …
One understands conditioned consciousness as it really is: "Conditioned consciousness.
One understands murderous form as it really is: "Murderous form.
One understands murderous feeling...
One understands as it really is murderous perception as ‘murderous perception’; one understands murderous volitional formations as ‘murderous volitional formations’;
one understands murderous consciousness as ‘murderous consciousness.’
Thus one does not approach form, does not cling to it, and does not resolve upon it as "this is my self. [One does not do so with] feeling...
perception...
One does not enter into volitional formations... nor into consciousness; one does not cling to them, nor does one resolve upon them as ‘this is my self.
For one who does so, these five aggregates of clinging—being neither entered into nor clung to—lead to welfare and happiness for a long time.”
“It is so, friend Sāriputta, for those venerable ones who have such compassionate fellow-celibates who desire their welfare, who exhort and instruct them.
And now, having heard this Dhamma teaching from the venerable Sāriputta, my mind is liberated through non-clinging from the taints. Thus it was said.
The third [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.86 (SN 22.86, PTS SN iii 116) 9. Theravagga Anurādhasutta At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Anurādha approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, does form constitute the Tathāgata? “No, Anurādha. “Does feeling constitute the Tathāgata? “No, Anurādha. “Does perception constitute the Tathāgata? “No, Anurādha. “Do volitional formations constitute the Tathāgata? “No, Anurādha. “Does consciousness constitute the Tathāgata? “No, Anurādha. “Then, venerable sir, does the Tathāgata exist apart from form? “No, Anurādha. “Does the Tathāgata exist apart from feeling? “No, Anurādha. “Does the Tathāgata exist apart from perception? “No, Anurādha. “Does the Tathāgata exist apart from volitional formations? “No, Anurādha. “Does the Tathāgata exist apart from consciousness? “No, Anurādha. “Then, venerable sir, is the Tathāgata neither form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor volitional formations, nor consciousness? “No, Anurādha. “When asked, ‘Venerable sir, does form constitute the Tathāgata? you replied, ‘No, Anurādha. When asked, ‘Does feeling constitute the Tathāgata? you replied, ‘No, Anurādha. When asked, ‘Does perception constitute the Tathāgata? you replied, ‘No, Anurādha. When asked, ‘Do volitional formations constitute the Tathāgata? you replied, ‘No, Anurādha. When asked, ‘Does consciousness constitute the Tathāgata? you replied, ‘No, Anurādha. When asked, ‘Then, venerable sir, does the Tathāgata exist apart from form? you replied, ‘No, Anurādha. When asked, ‘Does the Tathāgata exist apart from feeling? you replied, ‘No, Anurādha. When asked, ‘Does the Tathāgata exist apart from perception? you replied, ‘No, Anurādha. When asked, ‘Does the Tathāgata exist apart from volitional formations? you replied, ‘No, Anurādha. When asked, ‘Does the Tathāgata exist apart from consciousness? you replied, ‘No, Anurādha. When asked, ‘Then, venerable sir, is the Tathāgata neither form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor volitional formations, nor consciousness? you replied, ‘No, Anurādha. Now, venerable sir, I am at a loss; my mind is perplexed by this matter. It would be good if the Blessed One would clarify this to me in such a way that I might no longer be at a loss and my mind would not be perplexed. “Anurādha, when it was said: ‘Form is self,’ that would be an eternalist view. When it was said: ‘Feeling is self… Perception is self… Volitional formations are self… Consciousness is self,’ that would be an eternalist view. When it was said: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ that would be an eternalist view. When it was said: ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death… both exists and does not exist after death… neither exists nor does not exist after death,’ that would be an eternalist view. When it was said: ‘Form is not self,’ that would be an annihilationist view. When it was said: ‘Feeling is not self… Perception is not self… Volitional formations are not self… Consciousness is not self,’ that would be an annihilationist view. When it was said: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ that would be an eternalist view. When it was said: ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death… both exists and does not exist after death… neither exists nor does not exist after death,’ that would be an eternalist view. Anurādha, when it was said: ‘Form is self,’ that would be an eternalist view. When it was said: ‘Feeling is self… Perception is self… Volitional formations are self… Consciousness is self,’ that would be an eternalist view. When it was said: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ that would be an eternalist view. When it was said: ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death… both exists and does not exist after death… neither exists nor does not exist after death,’ that would be an eternalist view. When it was said: ‘Form is not self,’ that would be an annihilationist view. When it was said: ‘Feeling is not self… Perception is not self… Volitional formations are not self… Consciousness is not self,’ that would be an annihilationist view. When it was said: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ that would be an eternalist view. When it was said: ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death… both exists and does not exist after death… neither exists nor does not exist after death,’ that would be an eternalist view. But, Anurādha, when it is seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self,’ one becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion [the mind] is liberated. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. One understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. When this was said, the Venerable Anurādha said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Now on that occasion the Venerable Anurādha was dwelling in a forest hut not far from the Blessed One.
Then a number of wanderers of other sects approached the Venerable Anurādha and exchanged greetings with him.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, those wanderers of other sects said this to the Venerable Anurādha:
"Friend Anurādha, regarding that Tathāgata, the supreme person, the highest person, who has attained the highest attainment—that Tathāgata, when describing him, describes him in these four ways:..."

“‘Does the Tathāgata exist after death? or ‘Does the Tathāgata not exist after death? or ‘Does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death? or ‘Does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death?
When this was said, the Venerable Anurādha said this to those wanderers of other sects:
“Friends, when one describes that Tathāgata—the supreme person, the highest person, who has attained the ultimate attainment—by means other than these four positions, he describes him thus:”

“‘Does the Tathāgata exist after death? or ‘Does the Tathāgata not exist after death? or ‘Does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death? or ‘Does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death?
When this was said, the wanderers of other sects said to the Venerable Anurādha:
“This monk must be a newcomer, one who has recently gone forth; or else he is an elder who is ignorant and incompetent.”
Then those wanderers of other sects, having disparaged the Venerable Anurādha with words of "newness" and words of "foolishness," rose from their seats and departed.
Not long after those wanderers of other sects had left, it occurred to the Venerable Anurādha:
"If those wanderers of other sects were to ask me further questions..."
"How might I answer those wanderers of other sects so that I would be speaking in accordance with what the Blessed One has said,
not misrepresenting the Blessed One with what is false, answering in conformity with the Dhamma,
and such that no legitimate criticism could be brought against me as a ground for reproach?"
Then the Venerable Anurādha approached the Blessed One; having approached, ... [as before] ... while sitting to one side, the Venerable Anurādha said this to the Blessed One:
"Here, Bhante, I was dwelling not far from the Blessed One in a forest hut.
Then, Bhante, a number of wanderers of other sects approached me ... [as before] ... and said this to me:"
“Friend Anurādha, when a Tathāgata— a supreme person, a foremost person, one who has attained the highest attainment— is described by a Tathāgata in these four ways:

‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’— is he described by a Tathāgata in these four ways?”
When they had spoken thus, Bhante, I said this to those wanderers of other sects:
"Friends, when a Tathāgata—a supreme person, a highest person, one who has attained the highest attainment—is described by a Tathāgata, he describes him apart from these four positions:
'The Tathāgata exists after death,' or... [and so on]."
“‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death,’ so they say.
When this was said, Bhante, those wanderers of other sects said this to me:
“And this bhikkhu will be either one who has not long gone forth, or else an elder who is foolish and incompetent.”
Then, venerable sir, after those wanderers of other sects had disparaged me with the term “newcomer” and the term “fool,” they rose from their seats and departed.
Not long after those wanderers of other sects had left, venerable sir, this thought occurred to me:
"If those wanderers of other sects were to ask me further questions..."
"How might I answer those wanderers of other sects so that I would be speaking the word of the Blessed One,
not misrepresenting the Blessed One with what is false, answering in accordance with the Dhamma,
and such that no legitimate criticism could find ground for reproach?"

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.87 (SN 22.87, PTS SN iii 119) 9. Theravagga Vakkali Sutta At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. Then the Venerable Vakkali approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Vakkali, where is your mind directed? “My mind, Bhante, is directed toward the Tathāgata. “But, Vakkali, what do you see in the Tathāgata that makes your mind directed toward him? “I see, Bhante, that the Tathāgata is free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion; I see that the Tathāgata has abandoned birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I see that the Tathāgata has transcended all suffering. “Vakkali, it is not because of seeing this body that one who sees the Dhamma sees the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata, Vakkali, is the Dhamma; the Dhamma is the Tathāgata. Seeing the Dhamma, one sees the Tathāgata; seeing the Tathāgata, one sees the Dhamma. But enough of this, Vakkali. What is the use of seeing this foul body? He who sees the Dhamma sees me; he who sees me sees the Dhamma. For, Vakkali, it is by seeing the Dhamma that one sees me; it is by seeing me that one sees the Dhamma. Suppose, Vakkali, there were a man with good eyesight who, standing on the bank of a river, were to see people on the far bank gathering firewood, carrying water-pots, and building a hut. He might think: ‘Those people are surely fools, for they are gathering firewood, carrying water-pots, and building a hut on the far bank. Having thrown it away, he would cross over the mountain crag, the sheer cliff, the precipice, and the deep abyss. Having crossed over, he would stand on level ground. Standing on that level ground, he would look back upon
On one occasion, a number of elder bhikkhus were dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Now at that time, the Venerable Khemaka was staying at the Badarika Monastery, afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
Then, in the evening, the elder bhikkhus emerged from seclusion and addressed the Venerable Dāsaka:
“Come, friend Dāsaka, go to where the bhikkhu Khemaka is; having approached him, say this to the bhikkhu Khemaka:
‘The elders, friend Khemaka, say this to you:
“We hope you are bearing up, friend, we hope you are getting by; we hope that your painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing, and that their subsiding is apparent, not their increase.”’”
“Very well, friends,” the Venerable Dāsaka replied to the elder bhikkhus. He then approached the Venerable Khemaka and said to him:
“The elders, friend Khemaka, ask you this:
‘I hope you are bearing up, friend... [as before] ...is there no improvement?’”
“Friends, I am not getting well, I am not enduring; ...pe... for me, deterioration is apparent, not improvement.
Then the Venerable Dāsaka approached the elder bhikkhus; having approached, he said this to the elder bhikkhus:
“Friends, the bhikkhu Khemaka says this:”
“‘Friend, I am not getting well... [as before] ...no improvement is apparent, only deterioration.
“Come, friend Dāsaka, go to where the bhikkhu Khemaka is; having approached him, say this to the bhikkhu Khemaka:
‘The elders, friend Khemaka, say this to you:’”
“Friend, these five aggregates subject to clinging have been spoken of by the Blessed One; that is to say:

the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.
Does the Venerable Khemaka perceive anything as a self or as belonging to a self within these five aggregates subject to clinging?”
“Yes, friends,” the Venerable Dāsaka replied to the elder bhikkhus. He approached the Venerable Khemaka; having approached him...
[the elders said: “Friend Khemaka, the Blessed One has spoken of these five aggregates subject to clinging, namely:”
“The aggregate of form subject to clinging …pe… the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging.
Does the Venerable Khemaka perceive anything as a self or as belonging to a self within these five aggregates subject to clinging?
“Friend, these five aggregates subject to clinging have been spoken of by the Blessed One; that is to say:”
"The aggregate of form subject to clinging …pe… the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging.
In these five aggregates subject to clinging, friends, I do not perceive anything as self or belonging to self.
Then the Venerable Dāsaka approached the elder bhikkhus; having approached, he said this to the elder bhikkhus:
“Friend, the bhikkhu Khemaka says this:
‘Friends, these five aggregates subject to clinging have been spoken of by the Blessed One; that is to say:
the form aggregate subject to clinging ... [and so on] ... the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.’”
“Indeed, friends, among these five aggregates of clinging, I do not perceive anything as self or as belonging to a self.
“Come, friend Dāsaka, go to where the bhikkhu Khemaka is; having approached him, speak thus to the bhikkhu Khemaka:
‘The elders, friend Khemaka, say this to you—’”
"Friend, these five aggregates subject to clinging have been spoken of by the Blessed One; that is to say:
the form aggregate subject to clinging ... [and so on] ... the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.
Now, it seems that the Venerable Khemaka does not regard anything within these five aggregates subject to clinging as self or as belonging to a self."
“Then, friend, the venerable Khemaka is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed.
“So it is, friends,” the venerable Dāsaka replied to the elder bhikkhus, and he went to the venerable Khemaka...
[and so on] ...The elders said this to you, friend Khemaka:
“Friend, these five aggregates subject to clinging have been spoken of by the Blessed One:
namely, the form aggregate subject to clinging … [and so on] … the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.

Since, friend Khemaka, you do not perceive anything as self or as belonging to self among these five aggregates subject to clinging, then, friend Khemaka, you are an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed.”
“Friends, these five aggregates subject to clinging have been spoken of by the Blessed One:
namely, the form aggregate subject to clinging … [and so on] … the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.
Among these five aggregates subject to clinging, friends, I do not perceive anything as self or as belonging to self; yet I am not an arahant whose taints are destroyed.”
"Moreover, friends, regarding the five aggregates of clinging, the realization 'I am' has been attained by me, yet I do not regard [them] as 'this I am'.
Then the Venerable Dāsaka went to where the elder bhikkhus were...
[and] said this to the elder bhikkhus:
“Friend, the bhikkhu Khemaka says this:
‘Friends, these five aggregates subject to clinging have been spoken of by the Blessed One; that is to say:
the form aggregate subject to clinging ... [and so on] ... the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.’”
"Friends, among these five aggregates of clinging, I do not perceive anything as self or belonging to self. Yet, friends, I am not an arahant whose taints are destroyed;
rather, friends, regarding these five aggregates of clinging, the notion 'I am' has been reached by me, though I do not perceive 'this I am'.
"Come, friend Dāsaka, go to where the bhikkhu Khemaka is; having approached him, speak thus to the bhikkhu Khemaka:"
“Friends, the elders say this to you, Khemaka:
‘Friend Khemaka, when you say “I am,” what is it that you say “I am”?
Do you say “I am” in reference to form? Or do you say “I am” apart from form?’”
Feeling … perception … volitional formations …
“You say, ‘I am consciousness,’ or you say, ‘I am apart from consciousness.
Friend Khemaka, regarding this which you say, ‘I am’: what is it that you say, ‘I am’?
“Yes, friend,” the Venerable Dāsaka replied to the elder bhikkhus. He then approached the Venerable Khemaka and said to him:
The elders said this to you, friend Khemaka:
"Friend Khemaka, when you say 'I am,' what is it that you say is 'I am'?
Do you say 'I am' in reference to form, or do you say 'I am' apart from form?"
Feeling … perception … volitional formations …
"Do you say 'I am' with regard to consciousness, or do you say 'I am' apart from consciousness?
Friend Khemaka, regarding this 'I am' that you say, what is it that you say 'I am'?
"Enough, friend Dāsaka, what is the use of this running around?"
“Bring a staff, friend;
I myself will go to where the elder bhikkhus are.
Then the Venerable Khemaka, leaning on a staff, approached the elder bhikkhus; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the elder bhikkhus.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Khemaka was sitting there, the elder bhikkhus said to him:
"Friend Khemaka, when you say 'I am,' what is it that you say, 'I am'?
Do you say 'I am' in reference to form? Or do you say 'I am' apart from form?"
Feeling … perception … volitional formations …
"Do you say 'I am' with regard to consciousness, or do you say 'I am' apart from consciousness?
Friend Khemaka, as for this 'I am' that you say, what is it that you say 'I am'?
"Friend, I do not say 'I am' with regard to form, nor do I say 'I am' apart from form."
Not feeling … not perception … not volitional formations …
I do not say of consciousness, "I am"; nor do I say of anything apart from consciousness, "I am.
Yet, friend, regarding the five aggregates of clinging, the realization "I am" has occurred to me, and I do not regard it as "this I am.
It is, friend, just like the fragrance of a blue lotus, a red lotus, or a white lotus.
“If someone were to say: ‘The fragrance belongs to the bowl,’ or ‘The fragrance belongs to the color,’ or ‘The fragrance belongs to the pollen,’ would he be speaking correctly?
“No indeed, friend.
“But how, friend, should one answer correctly?”
“‘The fragrance of a flower,’ friend, is how one would rightly answer.
“In the same way, friend, I do not say ‘I am form,’ nor do I say ‘I am apart from form.
I do not [say this] of feeling….”
I do not say of perception...
nor of volitional formations...
nor of consciousness, "I am"; nor do I say of anything apart from consciousness, "I am."
Moreover, friends, regarding the five aggregates of clinging, I have realized "I am," yet I do not perceive "this I am.
Although, friends, for a noble disciple the five lower fetters have been abandoned,
there still remains in him a residual conceit of "I am," a desire of "I am" regarding the five aggregates of clinging.
The underlying tendency "I am" has not been eradicated.
At a later time, he dwells contemplating the arising and passing away in the five aggregates of clinging:
"Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form."
Thus is feeling...
thus is perception...
thus are volitional formations...
‘Such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.
As he dwells thus contemplating the rise and fall of these five aggregates of clinging, whatever underlying tendency of “I am” that accompanies the five aggregates of clinging—
the conceit “I am,” the desire “I am,” and the latent tendency “I am”— which has not yet been eradicated, [is abandoned].
That too goes to complete eradication.
It is just as if, friends, there were a cloth that was soiled and stained; its owners would hand it over to a dyer.
The dyer would scrub it with alkaline salt, or lye, or cow dung, and then wash it in clear water.
Even though that cloth may be pure and bright, there still remains within it an underlying smell of ammonia, lye, or cow dung that has not yet been removed.
The dyer returns it to its owners, and the owners place it in a casket perfumed with fragrant scents.
Then even that underlying smell of ammonia, lye, or cow dung which had not been removed goes away.
In the same way, friends, although the noble disciple has abandoned the five lower fetters,
there still remains within him, as a residual accompaniment to the five aggregates of clinging,
the conceit "I am," the mind-state "I am," and the underlying tendency "I am" that has not yet been eradicated.
Then, at a later time, he dwells contemplating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging:
"Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away;
such is feeling..."
‘Such is perception...
such are volitional formations...
such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’”
“As he dwells contemplating the arising and passing away of these five aggregates of clinging,
whatever underlying tendency of ‘I am’— the conceit ‘I am,’ the desire ‘I am’— that was not yet eradicated among those five aggregates of clinging,
that too goes to its utter destruction.”
When this was said, the elder bhikkhus said to the Venerable Khemaka:
"We did not ask the Venerable Khemaka out of a desire to trouble him;
rather, the Venerable Khemaka was capable of explaining, teaching, proclaiming, establishing, revealing, and elucidating in detail that teaching of the Blessed One."
"To analyze, to clarify.
Thus this teaching of the Blessed One has been fully explained, taught, made known, established, disclosed, analyzed, and clarified by the Venerable Khemaka.
This is what the Venerable Khemaka said.
The elder bhikkhus were uplifted and rejoiced in the words spoken by the Venerable Khemaka.

And while this exposition was being delivered, the minds of about sixty elder bhikkhus, as well as that of the Venerable Khemaka, were liberated from the taints through non-clinging. This is the seventh [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.90 (SN 22.90, PTS SN iii 132) 9. Theravagga Channa Sutta At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. At that time, the Venerable Channa was sick, afflicted, and gravely ill. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: “Venerable sir, the Venerable Channa is sick, afflicted, and gravely ill. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would visit the Venerable Channa out of compassion. The Blessed One consented by silence. Then the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the dwelling of the Venerable Channa. When he arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Channa: “Channa, how are you bearing up? How are you enduring? What is your ailment? And do you have the necessary strength to live, or not? “I am not bearing up, venerable sir; I am not enduring. My ailment is severe. I have no strength to live, nor do I have the strength to die. “Channa, there are these four kinds of nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be or for the support of those seeking a new existence. What four? They are: physical food as nutriments, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These are the four kinds of nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be or for the support of those seeking a new existence. Now, Channa, where there is the cessation of physical food as nutriment, the cessation of craving for it, the cessation of delight in it, and the cessation of attachment to it—there is the cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death cease, as do sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. Where there is the cessation of contact as nutriment... the cessation of mental volition as nutriment... the cessation of consciousness as nutriment, the cessation of craving for it, the cessation of delight in it, and the cessation of attachment to it—there is the cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death cease, as do sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. Channa, do you see any basis for the view: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. “Channa, since you do not see any basis for the view: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self,’ and since you have fully understood it through direct knowledge, what further clinging could there be to this body composed of the four great elements, which is subject to impermanence, suffering, and change? “Venerable sir, I do not see any basis for the view: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self. And since I have fully understood it through direct knowledge, there is no further clinging to this body composed of the four great elements, which is subject to impermanence, suffering, and change. However, venerable sir, I have a certain longing for the Blessed One’s presence. “Channa, whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the nature of ceasing. Give up what is subject to clinging; do not take hold of it again. Then the Venerable Channa, having understood the meaning of the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and circumambulated him three times, keeping him to his right. He then entered his own dwelling and sat down cross-legged on the bed, remaining there without moving for seven days.

It would be good if we were to go and see the Venerable Channa. “Friends, the Venerable Channa is a powerful person. If we go to see him now, he might become agitated. “I attained it, friend Ānanda. “Friend Channa, when you attained the destruction of the taints, did you not declare: ‘I have attained the destruction of the taints’? “I declared it, friend Ānanda. “Friend Channa, when you declared it, did you not understand: ‘My deliverance is unshakable; this is my last birth; there is no more renewed existence’? “I understood it, friend Ānanda. “Friend Channa, when you understood it, did you not attain final Nibbāna? “I attained final Nibbāna, friend Ānanda. “Friend Channa, when you attained final Nibbāna, did you not declare: ‘I have attained final Nibbāna’? “I attained final Nibbāna, friend Ānanda. “Friend Channa, when you attained final Nibbāna, did you not declare: ‘I have attained final Nibbāna’? “I declared it, friend Ānanda. “Friend Channa, when you declared it, did you not understand: ‘My deliverance is unshakable; this is my last birth; there is no more renewed existence’? “I understood it, friend Ānanda. “Friend Channa, when you understood it, did you not attain final Nibbāna? “I attained final Nibbāna, friend Ānanda. “Friend Channa, when you attained final Nibbāna, did you not declare: ‘I have attained final Nibbāna’? On one occasion, a number of elder bhikkhus were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Channa emerged from seclusion, took his key, and went from one dwelling to another, saying this to the elder bhikkhus:
"May the venerable elders exhort me; may the venerable elders instruct me; may the venerable elders give me a Dhamma talk, so that I might see the Dhamma."
When this was said, the elder bhikkhus said to the Venerable Channa:
"Form, friend Channa, is impermanent;
feeling is impermanent."
Perception is impermanent;
volitional formations are impermanent;
consciousness is impermanent.
Form is not-self;
feeling … perception … [is not-self].
Volitional formations … consciousness is non-self.
All volitional formations are impermanent;
“All phenomena are non-self.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Channa:
“This is indeed my own thought as well:”
‘Form is impermanent; feeling … perception … volitional formations …’
Consciousness is impermanent;
form is non-self, feeling is non-self, perception is non-self...
“Volitional formations are non-self… consciousness is non-self.
All formations are impermanent; all phenomena are non-self.”

And yet, my mind does not leap forward, does not find confidence, does not settle, and does not resolve upon the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nibbāna.
Anxiety and clinging arise;
the mind turns back.
‘Then what indeed is my self?
But this does not occur to one who sees the Dhamma in this way. ‘Who then might teach me the Dhamma such that I might see the Dhamma?’”
Then it occurred to the Venerable Channa:
"This Venerable Ānanda dwells at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Monastery, praised and esteemed by the Teacher and by his wise fellow-celibates;
the Venerable Ānanda is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might see the Dhamma."
"I have such great confidence in the Venerable Ānanda that I should now go to where the Venerable Ānanda is.
Then the Venerable Channa, having tidied his lodging, took his bowl and robe and set out for Kosambī, to Ghosita’s Monastery.
He approached the Venerable Ānanda and exchanged greetings with him...
Sitting to one side, the Venerable Channa said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Once, friend Ānanda, I was staying at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana."
Then, friends, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, I took my key and went from dwelling to dwelling, where I said to the elder bhikkhus:
"May the venerable elders exhort me; may the venerable elders instruct me; may the venerable elders give me a Dhamma talk such that I might see the Dhamma."
When this was said, friends, the elder bhikkhus said to me:
“Form, friend Channa, is impermanent; feeling is impermanent…”
Perception … volitional formations … consciousness is impermanent;
“Form is not-self … consciousness is not-self.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all phenomena are not-self.”
Then, friends, this occurred to me:
"It occurs to me too that form is impermanent... [and so on]..."
Consciousness is impermanent; form is non-self; feeling … perception … volitional formations … [are non-self].
“Consciousness is non-self;
all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all things are non-self.

Yet, my mind does not leap forward, does not find confidence, does not settle, and does not resolve upon the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nibbāna.
Agitation arises as clinging;
the mind turns back, thinking:
"But who, indeed, is my self?"
But even as I saw the Dhamma in this way, it did not occur to me:
"Who indeed might teach me the Dhamma such that I might see the Dhamma?
Then, friends, this thought occurred to me:
‘This venerable Ānanda is staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park, praised and esteemed by the Teacher and by his wise fellow-celibates;
the venerable Ānanda is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might see the Dhamma.
And I have sufficient confidence in the venerable Ānanda.’
"What if I were now to approach the Venerable Ānanda?
Let the Venerable Ānanda exhort me;
let the Venerable Ānanda instruct me."
“Venerable Ānanda, may you give me a Dhamma talk such that I might see the Dhamma.
“We are pleased with the Venerable Channa for this much alone, that he has indeed revealed himself and cut through his inner obstruction.
Listen, friend Channa, lend an ear;”
“You are capable of understanding the Dhamma.
Then, at that very moment, a sublime rapture and joy arose in the Venerable Channa:
“I am indeed capable of understanding the Dhamma!”
“Friend Channa, I heard this directly from the Blessed One and received it from his own lips as he was instructing the bhikkhu Kaccānagotta:
‘Kaccāna, this world generally relies on a duality: existence and non-existence.

But for one who sees the origin of the world as it really is with correct wisdom, there is no non-existence regarding the world. For one who sees the cessation of the world as it really is with correct wisdom, there is no existence regarding the world.’”
“Kaccāna, for one who sees the cessation of the world as it really is with correct wisdom, that which is called ‘existence in the world’ does not exist.
For this world, Kaccāna, is generally bound by its attachment to acquisitions, its adherence, and its bondage.

But this person does not approach, does not acquire, and does not adhere to those acquisitions, nor to the mental fixation, adherence, and underlying tendency [toward them], thinking: ‘This is my self.’”
"One does not doubt or hesitate that it is only suffering that arises when arising, and only suffering that ceases when ceasing;
rather, one possesses direct knowledge here independent of others.
To this extent, Kaccāna, there is right view."
"‘Everything exists,’ Kaccāna, is one extreme.
‘Nothing exists’ is the second extreme.
Without approaching either of these two extremes, Kaccāna, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle."
With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise;
with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises...
[and so on] ...in this way there is the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
"But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations...
[and so on] ...in this way there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
"It is so, friend Ānanda; it is so for those venerable ones who have such compassionate fellow-celibates who desire their welfare, who exhort and instruct them."
“Moreover, having heard this Dhamma teaching from the Venerable Ānanda, the Dhamma has been fully realized by me.
The eighth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.91 (SN 22.91, PTS SN iii 135).
9. The Chapter on Elders (Theravagga):
The Discourse to Rāhula (Rāhulasutta).
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then the Venerable Rāhula approached the Blessed One; having approached, ... [he sat down] to one side. While seated to one side, the Venerable Rāhula said this to the Blessed One:
"How, venerable sir, for one who knows what and sees what, do the underlying tendencies of 'I-making,' 'mine-making,' and conceit not arise regarding this conscious body and all external signs?
"Rāhula, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle..."
Whether gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form, one sees it as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
Whatever feeling there is...
Whatever perception there is … whatever formations there are … whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external … [and so on] …
"All consciousness: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus one sees it as it really is with correct wisdom.

It is for one who knows thus and sees thus, Rāhula, that regarding this body with its consciousness and all external signs, there are no underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ or the conceit ‘I am.
(The Ninth)

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.92 (SN 22.92, PTS SN iii 136) 9. Theravagga The Second Discourse to Rāhula At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Rāhula approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit? “Rāhula, when one sees all phenomena as they really are with correct wisdom as ‘not self,’ it is in this way that one should know, in this way that one should see, so that, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit. “But, venerable sir, how does one see all phenomena as they really are with correct wisdom as ‘not self’? “Rāhula, form is not self; seeing it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with form. Feeling is not self... Perception is not self... Volitional formations are not self... Consciousness is not self; seeing it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with consciousness. When one is disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness, one becomes dispassionate toward them. Through dispassion, one is liberated. Through liberation, there is the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. One understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. When this was said, the Venerable Rāhula said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what was overturned, to reveal what was hidden, to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry a lamp into the dark so that those with eyes could see forms, in the same way, the Blessed One has made the Dhamma clear in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the full admission. “You are a clansman, Rāhula; you are a clansman’s son. It is not easy for one who has recently gone forth to obtain the full admission. Wait four years, Rāhula; after four years, if you wish, you may receive the full admission. “Venerable sir, if one who has recently gone forth must wait four years to obtain the full admission, then let me wait eight years; after eight years, may I receive the full admission. Then the Venerable Rāhula received the going forth under the Blessed One and the full admission. And soon after his full admission, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Rāhula, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. And the Venerable Rāhula became one of the arahants.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
While seated to one side, the Venerable Rāhula said this to the Blessed One:
“How, venerable sir, for one who knows what and sees what, regarding this body with consciousness and external [objects]...”
"And how, Rāhula, does the mind become free from the notions of 'I' and 'mine' and from conceit regarding all signs; how does it transcend diversity and become peaceful and well-liberated?
"Rāhula, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; low or exalted;
far or near—all form should be seen as it actually is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'"
Having seen it as it truly is with correct wisdom, one is liberated through non-clinging.
Whatever feeling there may be...
whatever perception there may be...
Whatever formations...
whatever consciousness, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness is "not mine, this I am not."
‘This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self. Having seen this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one is liberated through non-clinging.

It is for one who knows thus and sees thus, Rāhula, that the mind becomes free from the notions of ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ free from conceit regarding this conscious body and all external signs; it transcends differentiation and is peaceful and well-liberated. Thus ends the tenth [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.93 (SN 22.93, PTS SN iii 137) 10. Pupphavagga Nadīsutta The River Discourse “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a river flowing full of water, slanting, sloping, and inclining towards the east. A man would come along, wishing to cross over from this shore to the far shore. He would not think, ‘How can I make this river flow back towards the west? Rather, he would think, ‘I will simply make an effort to cross over from this shore to the far shore. “So too, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple, it is not the case that it has occurred to him: ‘May these five aggregates subject to clinging, which are the basis for attachment and clinging, cease in me! May other aggregates subject to clinging not arise in me! Rather, by seeing with right wisdom as it really is the origination and passing away of these five aggregates subject to clinging, his mind is liberated from the taints by non-clinging. When it is liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth has been eradicated, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
At Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, suppose there were a mountain river flowing downward, extending far, with a swift current.
On both its banks, if *kāsa* grass were growing, it would overhang it; if *kusa* grass were growing, it would overhang it."
If *pabbaja* grass were growing there, they would hang down over it; if *bīraṇa* grass were growing there, they would hang down over it;
if trees were growing there, they would hang down over it. A man being carried along by the current, if he were to grasp at those [reeds], they would break off.
He would thereby meet with misfortune and disaster. If he were to grasp at *kusa* grass...
If he were to take hold of them—whether he takes hold of grass, or takes hold of reeds, or takes hold of trees—they would break off, and because of that, he would meet with misfortune and disaster.

In the same way, monks, the uninstructed worldling, who has no regard for the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has no regard for true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons.
One regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as being in self, or self as being in form.
When that form of his decays,
he undergoes ruin and disaster on that account.
Feeling … perception … volitional formations …
One regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as being in self, or self as being in consciousness.
That consciousness of his disintegrates.
On that account, he encounters ruin and disaster.
“What do you think, bhikkhus,
is form permanent or impermanent?”—
“Impermanent, Bhante.”
"Feeling ...
perception ... "
“Are volitional formations … consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.”
“Therefore, bhikkhus, ...
seeing thus ...
he understands: ‘... there is no more for this state of being.’”

Pupphavagga (The Chapter on Flowers)
The Flower Discourse.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, I do not dispute with the world; rather, it is the world that disputes with me."
“Monks, one who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma does not dispute with anyone in the world.
Whatever is agreed upon as non-existent by the wise in the world, monks, that I also say is ‘non-existent.
Whatever is agreed upon as existent by the wise in the world, monks, that I also say is ‘existent.’”
And what, bhikkhus, is regarded as non-existent by the wise in the world, which I also declare to be ‘non-existent’?
Form, bhikkhus, if it were permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change—regarded as non-existent by the wise in the world—I too would declare that to be ‘non-existent.
Feeling…
Perception...
volitional formations...
consciousness—if it were permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change, it would be considered as "non-existent" by the wise in the world; and I too say of it: "It does not exist."
“Monks, this is what is agreed upon as ‘non-existent’ in the world by the wise; I too say of it: ‘It does not exist.
And what, monks, is agreed upon as ‘existent’ in the world by the wise, which I also say ‘exists’?
Form, monks—impermanent, suffering, subject to change—is agreed upon as ‘existent’ in the world by the wise; I too say of it: ‘It exists.’”
“Feeling is impermanent...
consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is agreed upon as existing by the wise in the world, and I too say that it exists.
This, monks, is agreed upon as existing by the wise in the world, and I too say that it exists.”
“There is, monks, a worldly condition in the world that the Tathāgata fully awakens to and fully realizes;
having fully awakened to and fully realized it, he declares it, teaches it, proclaims it, establishes it, discloses it, analyzes it, and makes it plain.

And what, monks, is that worldly condition in the world which the Tathāgata fully awakens to and fully realizes, and having fully awakened to and fully realized it, declares, teaches, proclaims, establishes, discloses, analyzes, and makes plain?”
“Form, monks, is the world; it is the nature of the world that the Tathāgata fully awakens to and fully realizes.
Having fully awakened to and fully realized it, he declares it, teaches it, proclaims it, establishes it, reveals it, analyzes it, and makes it plain.
Monks, when the Tathāgata thus declares, teaches, proclaims, and establishes it...”
When it is being opened up, analyzed, and made clear, he does not know and does not see it.
Monks, what can I do for that foolish worldling, blind and sightless, who neither knows nor sees?
Feeling, monks, is the world; the nature of the world is feeling... [and so on].
"Perception, monks...
volitional formations, monks...
consciousness, monks, is the world and the nature of the world; that the Tathāgata fully awakens to and fully realizes."
Having fully awakened to it and realized it, he declares it, teaches it, proclaims it, establishes it, discloses it, analyzes it,
and makes it plain. Monks, when the Tathāgata is thus declaring, teaching, proclaiming, establishing, disclosing, analyzing, and making plain [the Dharma],
whoever does not know it and does not see it— that person, monks, I [declare]...
"What can I do for a foolish worldling who is blind, without vision, unknowing, and sightless?
Monks, just as a blue lotus, a red lotus, or a white lotus, born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsullied by the water;
even so, monks, the Tathāgata, born in the world and grown in the world, dwells having overcome the world, unsullied by the world."
The Second.

Pupphavagga (The Chapter on Flowers)
The Discourse on the Simile of the Lump of Foam.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Ayujjhā on the bank of the river Gaṅgā.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, suppose this river Ganges were to carry along a great mass of foam.
A man with good sight might look at it, contemplate it, and examine it thoroughly.
As he looked at it, contemplated it, and examined it thoroughly, it would appear to him as empty, hollow, and substanceless.
"For what substance could there be, monks, in a lump of foam?
In the same way, monks, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior;
far or near—a monk sees it, contemplates it, and examines it thoroughly with wisdom. As he sees it, contemplates it..."
When examined thoroughly, it appears as empty, as hollow, and as substanceless.
For what essence could there be, monks, in form?
It is just like, monks, a bubble on the water when the rain falls in heavy drops during the autumn season.
It arises and it ceases. A man with good sight might look at it, contemplate it, and examine it thoroughly.
As he looks at it, contemplates it, and examines it thoroughly, it would appear to him as empty, hollow, and devoid of essence. For what essence, monks, could there be in a bubble of water?
In the same way, monks, whatever feeling there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
low or exalted; far or near—a monk sees it, contemplates it, and examines it thoroughly.
As he sees it, contemplates it, and examines it thoroughly, it appears to him as empty, as hollow, and as substanceless.
For what, monks, could there be any essence in feeling?
Just as, monks, in the last month of summer, at midday when the heat stands high, a mirage flickers;
a man with good eyesight might look at it, contemplate it, and examine it thoroughly. As he looks at it...
To one who reflects wisely and examines it thoroughly, it would appear as empty and as hollow...
What essence, monks, could there be in a mirage?
Even so, monks, whatever perception there may be... [and so on].
“Monks, it is just as if a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to take a sharp axe and enter a forest.
There he would see a large plantain trunk, straight, fresh, and not yet crooked.
He would cut it at the base; having cut it at the base, he would cut it at the top; having cut it at the top,”
One might peel away the bark of that tree. While peeling away its bark, one would not find even the softwood, let alone the heartwood.
A man with good eyesight might look at it, contemplate it, and examine it thoroughly;
as he looks, contemplates, and examines it thoroughly, it would appear to him as nothing but hollow and empty.
One would perceive it as pithless; one would perceive it as having no core. For what core could there be, monks, in the trunk of a plantain tree?
Even so, monks, whatever formations there are—past, future, or present... far or near—a monk sees them, contemplates them, and examines them thoroughly with wisdom.
As he sees them, contemplates them... [he perceives them as empty, hollow, and insubstantial].
When one examines them thoroughly, they appear as empty, they appear as hollow, and they appear as substanceless.
For what substance could there be, monks, in volitional formations?
It is just as if, monks, a magician or a magician’s apprentice were to display an illusion at a crossroads.
A man with good eyesight might look at it, contemplate it, and examine it thoroughly.
As he looks at it, contemplates it, and examines it thoroughly, it would appear to him as empty, hollow, and devoid of essence.
For what essence, monks, could there be in an illusion?
In the same way, bhikkhus, whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—a bhikkhu sees it, contemplates it, and examines it thoroughly with wisdom.
As he sees it, contemplates it, and examines it thoroughly with wisdom, it appears to him as empty, as hollow, and as substanceless.
It appears [unsubstantial]. For what essence could there be, monks, in consciousness?

Seeing thus, monks, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, and he becomes disenchanted with feeling… with perception… with volitional formations… and he becomes disenchanted with consciousness.
Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated. …pe…
“He understands: ‘There is nothing further beyond this state of being.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further spoke these words:
“Form is like a lump of foam,
feeling is like a bubble;
perception is like a mirage.”
Formations are like a plantain tree;
consciousness is like an illusion—
thus has it been taught by the Kinsman of the Sun.
In whatever way one contemplates it and examines it thoroughly with wisdom,
it proves to be empty and hollow.
Whoever sees this with proper wisdom,
concerning this body,
as taught by the one of vast insight;
When the three things have been abandoned,
behold the form cast off:
vitality, heat, and consciousness.
When one abandons this body, then,
cast aside, it lies insentient,
like food left for another.
Such is this continuity;
this is a deception, a prattle of fools;
it is declared to be a murderer.
No core is found here.
Thus should a bhikkhu of aroused energy contemplate the aggregates.
Whether by day or by night,
being clearly comprehending and mindful,
one should abandon all fetters.
One should make oneself one's own refuge;
one should walk as if with one's head on fire,
aspiring for the deathless state.
Third.

Then the Blessed One took up a small lump of cow dung with his hand and said this to that bhikkhu:

“Bhikkhu, if this acquisition of a personal existence were permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change, then the living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering would not be discerned.

But because, bhikkhu, even such an acquisition of a personal existence is not permanent, stable, eternal, or not subject to change, therefore the living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering is discerned.
Once upon a time, bhikkhu, I was a consecrated Khattiya king.”

Bhikkhu, while I was that consecrated khattiya king, I had eighty-four thousand gabled halls, with the Mahābyūha Gabled Hall as the chief.”
“Bhikkhu, when I was a head-anointed kṣatriya king, I had eighty-four thousand couches made of ivory,
made of heartwood, and made of gold; they were spread with woolen covers, embroidered covers, and fine cotton covers,
furnished with excellent blankets of antelope hide, provided with canopies above, and equipped with red pillows at both ends.”

Bhikkhu, when I was a consecrated khattiya king, I had eighty-four thousand horses adorned with gold, bearing golden banners, covered with nets of gold, headed by the royal horse Valāhaka.”
“Bhikkhu, while I was a consecrated Khattiya king, I had eighty-four thousand chariots adorned with gold, bearing golden banners, covered with nets of gold, headed by the Vejayanta chariot.
Bhikkhu, while I was a consecrated Khattiya king, I had eighty-four thousand jewels, headed by the jewel-treasure.
Bhikkhu … [and so on] … I had eighty-four thousand women, headed by Queen Subhaddā.”
“Monk, for me at that time... there were eighty-four thousand kshatriyas who followed me, headed by the jewel of the commander-in-chief.
Monk, for me at that time... there were eighty-four thousand milch cows with cloths for their halters and bronze vessels for their udders.
Monk, for me at that time... there were eighty-four thousand million pieces of fine cloth: fine linen, fine silk, fine wool, and fine cotton.”
“Monk, at that time I had eighty-four thousand vessels of cooked rice; food was brought to me every morning and evening.
Of those eighty-four thousand cities, monk, there was only one city where I resided at that time—the royal capital, Kusāvatī.
And of those eighty-four thousand palaces, monk, there was only one palace where I resided at that time—the Palace of Dhamma.”
“Furthermore, bhikkhu, among those eighty-four thousand gabled chambers, there was only one single gabled chamber that I inhabited at that time—the Mahābyūha gabled chamber.
And among those eighty-four thousand couches, there was only one single couch that I used at that time—one made of ivory, or of heartwood, or of gold, or of silver.”
“Furthermore, bhikkhu, among those eighty-four thousand elephants, there was only one elephant that I would mount on that occasion—the royal elephant Uposatha.
Among those eighty-four thousand horses, there was only one horse that I would mount on that occasion—the royal horse Valāhaka.
Among those eighty-four thousand chariots, there was only one chariot that I would mount on that occasion—the Vejayanta chariot.”
“Furthermore, bhikkhu, among those eighty-four thousand women, there was only one woman who attended upon me at that time—
a khattiya lady or a velāmikā. Furthermore, bhikkhu, among those eighty-four thousand million pairs of garments,
there was only one pair of garments that I wore at that time— either fine linen, or fine silk, or fine wool.”
or fine cotton cloth.
Yet, monk, of those eighty-four thousand servings of rice, there is only that one single serving of rice from which I eat at most a handful of boiled rice along with a suitable curry.
Thus, monk, all those conditioned phenomena are past, ceased, and changed.
"Thus, bhikkhu, conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
thus, bhikkhu, conditioned phenomena are unstable;
thus, bhikkhu, conditioned phenomena are not a source of consolation."
“To this extent, bhikkhu, it is indeed enough to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, enough to become dispassionate toward them, enough to be liberated from them.

“Bhikkhu, there is not even so much as this much feeling that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and which will remain exactly as it is for all eternity.

What do you think, monk,

“Impermanent, Bhante. …pe…

10. Pupphavagga.
Gaddulabaddhasutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning.
A first point is not discerned of beings roaming and wandering on, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving.
There comes a time, bhikkhus, when the great ocean dries up and evaporates and no longer exists; but there is no end to the suffering, vexation, despair, and fever of those who have experienced it.”
"But I do not say, monks, that there is an end to suffering for beings who wander and transmigrate, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving.
There comes a time, monks, when Sineru, the king of mountains, burns up, perishes, and no longer exists;
yet I do not say, monks, that there is an end to suffering for beings who wander and transmigrate, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving."
"There comes a time, monks, when the great earth is consumed and destroyed and no longer exists.
Yet, monks, I do not say that there is an end to suffering for beings who wander and transmigrate, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving.
Just as a dog tied with a leash to a firm post or stake runs and circles around that very post or stake,"
In the same way, monks, the uninstructed worldling, who has no regard for the noble ones … [as before] … and is undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons,
regards form as self … [as before] … regards feeling as self … [as before].
One regards perception as self...
one regards volitional formations as self...
one regards consciousness as self, or a self possessed of consciousness; or consciousness in the self, or a self in consciousness.
Thus he runs along and circles around form alone; he runs along and circles around feeling alone... perception alone... volitional formations alone... consciousness alone.
Running along and circling around form, running along and circling around feeling... perception... volitional formations...
consciousness, he is not liberated from form, he is not liberated from feeling, he is not liberated from perception.
One is not liberated from volitional formations, one is not liberated from consciousness, one is not liberated from birth,
aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
"One is not liberated from suffering," I say.
But, monks, the learned noble disciple, who has seen the noble ones... [and] is well-trained in the Dhamma of the true person, does not regard form as self...
nor feeling... [nor perception, volitional formations, or consciousness].

One does not regard perception as self, nor self as possessing perception; nor perception in self, nor self in perception. One does not regard volitional formations as self... nor consciousness as self, nor self as possessing consciousness; nor consciousness in self, nor self in consciousness.
Thus he does not run after form, does not circle around form; he does not run after feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, does not circle around consciousness.

Not running after form, not circling around form; not running after feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, not circling around consciousness, he is liberated from form, liberated from feeling, liberated from perception, liberated from volitional formations, liberated from consciousness.

One is liberated from perception, liberated from volitional formations, liberated from consciousness; one is liberated from birth, from aging and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
“One is liberated from suffering,” I say.
