The Vāsijaṭa Sutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Monks, I declare that the destruction of the taints occurs for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see.”
And what, bhikkhus, is it that one who knows and sees thus experiences the destruction of the taints?
“Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away;
such is feeling …”
‘Such is perception...
such are volitional formations...
such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’”
"It is for one who knows thus, monks, and who sees thus, that the destruction of the taints occurs.
For a monk who dwells without being devoted to the practice of development, even though such a wish might arise as:
'O, may my mind be liberated from the taints through non-clinging,' yet his mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging."
For what reason?
It should be said: "Because of its lack of development.
Because of the lack of development of what?
Because of the non-cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness, because of the non-cultivation of the four right endeavors,
because of the non-cultivation of the four bases for psychic power, because of the non-cultivation of the five faculties, because of the non-cultivation of the five powers,
because of the non-cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment, and because of the non-cultivation of the noble eightfold path.
"Suppose, monks, there were eight, ten, or twelve eggs laid by a hen.

If those eggs were not properly incubated by the hen, not properly warmed, and not properly nurtured, even though the wish might arise in that hen: [that her chicks might break out of their shells with their claws or beaks and hatch safely]."
‘Oh, that my chicks might pierce their eggshells with the points of their claws or with their beaks and hatch out safely!’—
even so, those chicks would still be incapable of piercing their eggshells with the points of their claws or with their beaks and hatching out safely. Why is that?
For it is just as if, monks, there were eight, ten, or twelve eggs laid by a hen;
yet those eggs had not been properly incubated by her, nor properly warmed, nor properly brooded over.
In the same way, monks, for a monk who dwells without being devoted to the practice of development, even though such a wish might arise:
‘Oh, that my mind might be liberated from the taints through non-clinging!’—yet his mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
For what reason?
It should be said: ‘Because it has not been developed.’”
Because of what being undeveloped?
Because of the four foundations of mindfulness... [and so on] ...the eightfold path being undeveloped.
For a bhikkhu, monks, who dwells devoted to the practice of development, even if no such desire should arise:
‘Oh, that my mind might be liberated from the taints through non-clinging!’—then indeed his mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
For what reason?
It should be said: ‘Because it has been developed.’”
Through the cultivation of what?
Through the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness, through the cultivation of the four right endeavors,
through the cultivation of the four bases for psychic power, through the cultivation of the five faculties, and through the cultivation of the five powers.
Because of having cultivated the seven factors of enlightenment, and because of having cultivated the noble eightfold path.
Just as if, monks, there were a hen with eight, ten, or twelve eggs;
and those eggs were properly incubated by the hen, properly moistened, and properly nurtured.
Even though it might not occur to that hen: “Oh,
may my chicks break out of their shells safely by means of their claw-tips or their beaks,” nevertheless,
those chicks are indeed capable of breaking out of their shells safely by means of their claw-tips or their beaks.
For what reason? Because, monks, suppose there were eight, ten, or twelve eggs from a hen,
and those eggs had been properly incubated by the hen, properly warmed, and properly nurtured.
In the same way, monks, when a monk dwells devoted to the practice of development, even if no such wish arises in him as,
‘O, may my mind be liberated from the taints through non-clinging,’ nevertheless his mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging. Why is that?
"It should be said: 'Because of his having cultivated [the mind]. Because of having cultivated what?
Because of having cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness... [and so on] ...because of having cultivated the Noble Eightfold Path."
“Just as, monks, when a carpenter or a carpenter’s apprentice looks at his chisel, the marks of the fingers are visible and the mark of the thumb is visible;
yet he does not have the knowledge:
‘So much of my chisel has been worn away today, so much yesterday, and so much in previous days.’”
Then, when they are exhausted, there is knowledge of their exhaustion.
In the same way, monks, for a monk who dwells devoted to the practice of development, even though such knowledge does not arise as:
"So much indeed of my taints has been exhausted today, so much yesterday, so much in the past," yet when they are exhausted, there is simply knowledge of their exhaustion.

“Just as, monks, when a sea-going ship has been bound with cordage for many months at sea, and having spent the rainy season, is hauled onto dry land during the winter, its cordage is parched by wind and sun.

When it is rained upon by a rain-bearing cloud, those cords easily slacken and become rotten; even so, monks, when a bhikkhu’s mind is well-liberated through the destruction of the taints, his fetters are easily loosened and become rotten.”
“In the same way, monks, for a monk who dwells devoted to the practice of development, the fetters are easily stilled and become rotten.
Thus was the ninth [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.102.
10. The Chapter on Flowers: The Discourse on the Perception of Impermanence.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Monks, the perception of impermanence, when developed and cultivated, exhausts all lust for sensual pleasures,
exhausts all lust for form, exhausts all lust for existence, exhausts all ignorance,
and uproots all the conceit ‘I am.’”
“Just as, monks, in the autumn season a farmer, while plowing with a large plowshare, plows away all the root-creepers,
tearing them up completely; even so, monks, when the perception of impermanence is developed and cultivated, it exhausts all lust for sensual pleasures,
exhausts all lust for form, exhausts all lust for existence, and exhausts all ignorance.”
It uproots all conceit of "I am.
Just as, monks, a reed-cutter, having cut a reed, takes it by the tip and shakes it out, winnows it, and threshes it;
even so, monks, the perception of impermanence, when developed and cultivated, consumes all lust for sensual pleasures... [and so on] ...uproots all conceit of "I am."
“Bhikkhus, just as when a cluster of mangoes has been cut from its stalk, whatever mangoes there are that were attached to the stalk all follow along with it;
even so, bhikkhus, when the perception of impermanence is developed … it uproots all conceit ‘I am.
“Bhikkhus, just as in a peaked-roof house, whatever rafters there are all go toward the peak, incline toward the peak, converge at the peak, and the peak is declared to be their chief;”
In the same way, monks, when the perception of impermanence is developed … it uproots all conceit of "I am.
Just as, monks, among all fragrant roots, the fragrance of black sandalwood is declared the foremost;
even so, monks, the perception of impermanence … uproots all conceit of "I am."
“Just as, monks, among all fragrant heartwoods, red sandalwood is declared to be the foremost;
even so, monks, the perception of impermanence … [as before] … eradicates all conceit ‘I am.
Just as, monks, among all flower-fragrances, the vassika jasmine is declared to be the foremost;”
"In the same way, monks, the perception of impermanence ... [as before] ... uproots all conceit of 'I am.
Just as, monks, whatever petty kings there may be, they are all subordinate to a wheel-turning monarch, and that wheel-turning monarch is declared to be their chief;
even so, monks, the perception of impermanence ... [as before] ... uproots all conceit of 'I am.'"

“Just as, bhikkhus, whatever radiance there is from the stars, all that does not amount to a sixteenth part of the radiance of the moon; the radiance of the moon is declared to be the foremost among them;
even so, bhikkhus, the perception of impermanence … [as before] … uproots all conceit ‘I am.

Just as, bhikkhus, in the autumn season, when the sky is clear and free of clouds, the sun, rising in the vault of heaven, dispelling all darkness that has come into the atmosphere, shines, blazes, and radiates.”
In the same way, monks, the perception of impermanence, when developed and cultivated, exhausts all lust for sensual pleasures,
exhausts all lust for form, exhausts all lust for existence, exhausts all ignorance,
and uproots all the conceit "I am."

And how, monks, is the perception of impermanence developed and cultivated so that it exhausts all lust for sensual pleasures … [and so on] … so that it uproots all the conceit "I am"? "Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away; such is feeling …" [and so on] … [until: "such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away. Thus, monks, the perception of impermanence is developed and cultivated so that it exhausts all lust for sensual pleasures … [and so on] … so that it uproots all the conceit "I am."
‘Such is perception...
such are volitional formations...
such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’”
“Monks, when the perception of impermanence is thus developed and cultivated in this way, it exhausts all lust for sensual pleasures,
exhausts all lust for form, exhausts all lust for existence, exhausts all ignorance,
and uproots all the conceit ‘I am’.”
The tenth.

The Antasutta.
At Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, there are these four extremes."
Which four?
The end of identity, the end of the origin of identity, the end of the cessation of identity, and the end of the practice leading to the cessation of identity.
And what, monks, is the end of identity?
"One should say: 'The five aggregates of clinging.
Which five? Namely:

the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to mental formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness."
This, monks, is called the dimension of identity.
And what, monks, is the dimension of the origin of identity?
It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; that is to say:
Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
This, monks, is called the end of the origin of identity.
And what, monks, is the end of the cessation of identity?
The remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, its relinquishment, its abandonment, its release, and its non-attachment— this, monks,
is called the end of the cessation of identity.
And what, monks, is the end of the way leading to the cessation of identity?
It is precisely this Noble Eightfold Path;
that is to say: right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.
This, monks, is called the factor of the practice leading to the cessation of identity-attachment.
“Monks, these are the four extremes.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.105 (SN 22.105, PTS SN iii 159) 11. Antavagga Sakkāyasutta “Bhikkhus, I will teach you identity (*sakkāya*) and the origin of identity. Listen to that, pay close attention, and I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “And what, bhikkhus, is identity? It is the five aggregates subject to clinging. That is, the aggregate of form subject to clinging, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging, the aggregate of volitional formations subject to clinging, and the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging. This, bhikkhus, is called identity. “And what, bhikkhus, is the origin of identity? It is craving, which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, bhikkhus, is called the origin of identity. “And what, bhikkhus, is the cessation of identity? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the relinquishing of it, the abandoning of it, the liberation from it, and the non-attachment to it. This, bhikkhus, is called the cessation of identity. “And what, bhikkhus, is the way leading to the cessation of identity? It is simply this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called the way leading to the cessation of identity. “Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple thus understands identity, the origin of identity, the cessation of identity, and the way leading to the cessation of identity, he understands: ‘I have understood identity, the origin of identity, the cessation of identity, and the way leading to the cessation of identity. He understands: ‘Birth for me has been eradicated, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”

“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these five aggregates subject to clinging...
[they do not live having realized them for themselves with direct knowledge]. But those who understand them... live having realized them for themselves with direct knowledge.
The sixth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.109 (SN 22.109, PTS SN iii 160) 11. Antavagga Sotāpannasutta The Stream-enterer “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world.
What four? The stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arahant. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging.
Which five?
That is to say: the form aggregate subject to clinging …pe… the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.

When, monks, a noble disciple understands as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these five aggregates subject to clinging, this, monks, is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination.”
Seventh.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.110 (SN 22.110, PTS SN iii 161) 11.

“Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging.”
Which five? They are as follows:

“Monks, this bhikkhu is called an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly exhausted, and who is liberated through final knowledge.

11. The Chapter on Extremes:

[The same applies to] feeling …”
Whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving there is in regard to perception… in regard to volitional formations… in regard to consciousness, abandon that.

In this way, that form will be abandoned, cut off at the root... [the same applies to] feeling... [perception... volitional formations... consciousness].”
Regarding perception...
regarding volitional formations: whatever desire there is for them...

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.113 (SN 22.113, PTS SN iii 162) 12. Dhammakathikavagga Avijjāsutta (The Discourse on Ignorance) “Bhikkhus, what do you think? Is ignorance permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, venerable sir. “But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness? “Suffering, venerable sir. “But is it fitting to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. “Therefore, bhikkhus, any kind of form whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form should be seen with right wisdom exactly as it is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Any kind of feeling whatsoever... Any kind of perception whatsoever... Any kind of volitional formations whatsoever... Any kind of consciousness whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness should be seen with right wisdom exactly as it is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion toward form, revulsion toward feeling, revulsion toward perception, revulsion toward volitional formations, and revulsion toward consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One...
[as before] ...and sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“‘Ignorance, ignorance,’ it is said, venerable sir.
What now, venerable sir, is ignorance;
and in what way has one become possessed by ignorance?”

“Here, bhikkhu, the uninstructed worldling does not understand form, does not understand the origin of form, does not understand the cessation of form, and does not understand the way leading to the cessation of form;
he does not understand feeling … perception …”
One does not understand volitional formations …pe… one does not understand the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness. This,
bhikkhu, is called ignorance;
"And to this extent one is possessed of ignorance.
First.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya* 22.114 (SN 22.114, PTS SN iii 163).
12. The Chapter on Preachers of the Dhamma.
Discourse on Knowledge.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
As he was sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it is said, ‘true knowledge, true knowledge.
What now, venerable sir, is true knowledge?”
“And in what way, bhikkhu, is one possessed of true knowledge?
“Here, bhikkhu, the well-taught noble disciple understands form, the origin of form, the cessation of form, and the way leading to the cessation of form.
He understands feeling …”
He understands perception ... he understands volitional formations ... pe ...
he understands the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness.
“Monk, this is called true knowledge;
it is to this extent that one has attained true knowledge.
This is the second [sutta].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.115 (SN 22.115, PTS SN iii 163) 12. Dhammakathikavagga Dhammakathikasutta The Discourse on the Preacher of the Dhamma “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who preaches the Dhamma; the person who listens to the Dhamma; the person who practices in accordance with the Dhamma; and the person who is established in the fruit of the practice of the Dhamma. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it is said: ‘a Dhamma-preacher, a Dhamma-preacher.’”
“To what extent, venerable sir, is one a speaker of the Dhamma?
“If, bhikkhu, one teaches the Dhamma for the sake of revulsion toward form, for its fading away, and for its cessation, it is sufficient to call him a ‘bhikkhu who is a speaker of the Dhamma.
If, bhikkhu, one practices for the sake of revulsion toward form, for its fading away, and for its cessation, it is sufficient to call him a ‘bhikkhu who practices in accordance with the Dhamma.’”
“Bhikkhu, if through revulsion toward form, through its fading away and cessation, one is liberated by non-clinging, it is sufficient to say: ‘This bhikkhu has attained Nibbāna in this very life.
If, bhikkhu, [through revulsion toward] feeling … if, bhikkhu, [through revulsion toward] perception …”

If, bhikkhu, one teaches the Dhamma for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of volitional formations— and likewise for consciousness— if one teaches the Dhamma for these things, it is sufficient to call such a person a “bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma.

If, bhikkhu, one practices for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of consciousness, it is sufficient to call such a person a “bhikkhu who practices in accordance with the Dhamma.”

“Bhikkhu, if through revulsion toward consciousness, through its fading away and cessation, one is liberated by non-clinging, it is fitting to say of him: ‘This bhikkhu has attained Nibbāna in this very life.
This is the third [sutta]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.116 (SN 22.116, PTS SN iii 164).
12. Dhammakathikavagga.
Second Discourse on the Dhamma Preacher.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:

“To what extent, bhikkhu, is one practicing in accordance with the Dhamma? To what extent has one attained Nibbāna in this very life?

“If, bhikkhu, one teaches the Dhamma for the sake of revulsion toward form, for its fading away, and for its cessation, it is sufficient to call such a person ‘a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma.

If, bhikkhu, one practices for the sake of revulsion toward form, for its fading away, and for its cessation, it is sufficient to call such a person ‘a bhikkhu who is practicing in accordance with the Dhamma.’”
“Bhikkhu, if through revulsion toward form, through its fading away and cessation, one is liberated by non-clinging, it is sufficient to say: ‘This bhikkhu has attained Nibbāna in this very life.
If, bhikkhu, [through revulsion toward] feeling … perception …”

If, bhikkhu, one teaches the Dhamma for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of volitional formations— and likewise for consciousness— if one teaches the Dhamma for these things, it is fitting to call such a person a "bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma.

If, bhikkhu, one practices for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of consciousness, it is fitting to call such a person a "bhikkhu who practices in accordance with the Dhamma."

“Bhikkhu, if through revulsion toward consciousness, through its fading away and cessation, one is liberated by non-clinging, it is fitting to call such a person ‘a bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna in this very life.
The fourth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.117 (SN 22.117, PTS SN iii 164)
12. Dhammakathikavagga.
Bandhanasutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Here, monks, an uninstructed worldling, who has no regard for the noble ones and is untrained in their Dhamma,
regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. This, monks,
is called an uninstructed worldling who is bound by the bond of form, bound by internal and external bonds.”
Not seeing the near shore, not seeing the far shore, being bound, he ages; being bound, he dies; being bound, he goes from this world to the next world.
He regards feeling as self... [or] self as in feeling.
This, monks, is called an uninstructed worldling who is bound by the bond of feeling, bound by internal and external bonds.
Not seeing the near shore, not seeing the far shore, one who is bound suffers; one who is bound dies; one who is bound goes from this world to the next world.
[The same applies to] perception...
volitional formations...
One regards consciousness as self...
This, monks, is called an uninstructed worldling who is bound by the bond of consciousness, bound by internal and external bonds;
not seeing the near shore, not seeing the further shore, he is bound—he ages, he dies, and being bound, he goes from this world to the other world.
But, monks, the learned noble disciple, who has seen the noble ones...
and is well-trained in the Dhamma of the true person, does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as being in self, nor self as being in form.

This, monks, is called a learned noble disciple who is not bound by the bond of form, not bound by internal or external bonds; he sees this shore and sees the further shore. "He is liberated from suffering," I say.
One does not regard feeling as self … nor perception as self … nor volitional formations as self … [and so on].

“He does not regard consciousness as self … [as before] … This, monks, is called the learned noble disciple who is not bound by the bond of consciousness, not bound by internal or external bonds; he sees this shore and sees the further shore. ‘He is completely freed from suffering,’ I say.
The fifth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.118 (SN 22.118, PTS SN iii 165) 12. Dhammakathikavagga Paripucchitasutta “Monks, when a monk is questioned about the Dhamma, he should answer thus: ‘Form is impermanent; feeling is impermanent; perception is impermanent; volitional formations are impermanent; consciousness is impermanent. “If he is asked: ‘But, friend, what is form? What is the origin of form? What is the cessation of form? he should answer thus: ‘The four great elements and the form derived from them—this is called form. With the arising of craving and clinging as condition, there is the origin of form. With the cessation of craving and clinging, through the cessation of that, there is the cessation of form. “If he is asked: ‘But, friend, what is feeling? What is the origin of feeling? What is the cessation of feeling? he should answer thus: ‘Whatever is felt, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, this is called feeling. With the arising of contact as condition, there is the origin of feeling. With the cessation of contact, through the cessation of that, there is the cessation of feeling. “If he is asked: ‘But, friend, what is perception? What is the origin of perception? What is the cessation of perception? he should answer thus: ‘Whatever perceives, whether perceiving forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, this is called perception. With the arising of contact as condition, there is the origin of perception. With the cessation of contact, through the cessation of that, there is the cessation of perception. “If he is asked: ‘But, friend, what are volitional formations? What is the origin of volitional formations? What is the cessation of volitional formations? he should answer thus: ‘The six classes of volitional formations: the volitional formation of body, the volitional formation of speech, the volitional formation of mind, the volitional formation of merit, the volitional formation of demerit, and the volitional formation of the imperturbable. With ignorance as condition, there is the origin of volitional formations. With the cessation of ignorance, through the cessation of that, there is the cessation of volitional formations. “If he is asked: ‘But, friend, what is consciousness? What is the origin of consciousness? What is the cessation of consciousness? he should answer thus: ‘The six classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. With name-and-form as condition, there is the origin of consciousness. With the cessation of name-and-form, through the cessation of that, there is the cessation of consciousness.’”
At Sāvatthī.
"What do you think, bhikkhus,
do you regard form as 'this is mine, this I am, this is my self'?"
“No, venerable sir.
“Good, bhikkhus.
Form, bhikkhus, should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’”
Feeling … perception … volitional formations …
“Do you regard consciousness thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”—
“Certainly not, Bhante.”— “Good, bhikkhus.”
“Bhikkhus, consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
... Seeing thus ...
he understands: ‘... there is no more for this state of being.’”
Sixth. Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.119 (SN 22.119, PTS SN iii 166) 12. Dhammakathika-vagga (The Chapter on the Preacher of the Dhamma)
The Second Discourse on Being Questioned.
At Sāvatthī.
"What do you think, bhikkhus?"
“Regard form thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Good, bhikkhus.”
“Bhikkhus, form is to be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
Feeling … perception …”
“Do you regard volitional formations … consciousness thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’?”—
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Excellent, bhikkhus!
Consciousness, bhikkhus, should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. … [and so on] …”
“He understands: ‘There is nothing further beyond this state of being.
Thus ends the seventh [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.120 (SN 22.120, PTS SN iii 166).
12. The Chapter on Preachers of the Dhamma.
Discourse on the Fettering.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
“Monks, I will teach you the things that fetter and the fetter itself.
Listen to that.
And what, monks, are the things that fetter, and what is the fetter?
“Bhikkhus, form is a phenomenon that fetters;
whatever desire and lust there is for it, that is the fetter there.
Feeling … [and so on] …”
Perception … volitional formations … consciousness are phenomena that fetter.
Whatever desire and lust there is for them, that is the fetter therein.
These, monks, are called the things that fetter; this is the fetter.
Thus ends the eighth [sutta].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.121 (SN 22.121, PTS SN iii 167) 12. Dhammakathikavagga Upādāniyasutta (The Discourse on the Subject of Clinging) “Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates subject to clinging.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
"Monks, I will teach you the things that are subject to clinging and clinging itself.
Listen to that."
And what, monks, are the things that are subject to clinging, and what is clinging?
Form, monks, is a thing subject to clinging;
whatever desire and lust there is for it, that is the clinging therein.
Feeling … perception … volitional formations …
Consciousness is a phenomenon subject to clinging;
whatever desire and lust there is for it, that is the clinging therein.
These, monks, are called phenomena subject to clinging, and this is clinging."
The Ninth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.122 (SN 22.122, PTS SN iii 167) 12.
The Chapter on Preachers of the Dhamma (Dhammakathikavagga)
The Discourse on the Virtuous On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Sāriputta. ... [As before] ... he said this:
“Friend Sāriputta, what phenomena should a virtuous bhikkhu attend to wisely?

“Friend Koṭṭhika, a virtuous bhikkhu should attend wisely to the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, and as non-self. Which five? [The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of volitional formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.]”

That is to say: the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.

Friend Koṭṭhika, a virtuous bhikkhu should attend thoroughly to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, and as non-self.

"It is indeed possible, friend, that a virtuous bhikkhu, by attending thoroughly to these five aggregates of clinging as impermanent … [as suffering] … as non-self, might realize the fruit of stream-entry.
"But, friend Sāriputta, what things should a bhikkhu who is a stream-enterer attend to thoroughly?
"Friend Koṭṭhika, even a bhikkhu who is a stream-enterer should attend to these five aggregates of clinging as impermanent … [as suffering] … as non-self, attending to them thoroughly."

"It is indeed possible, friend, that a monk who is a stream-enterer, by attending wisely to these five aggregates of clinging as impermanent … [as suffering] … as non-self, might realize the fruit of once-returning.
"But, friend Sāriputta, what things should a monk who is a once-returner attend to wisely?
"Friend Koṭṭhika, a monk who is a once-returner should also attend wisely to these five aggregates of clinging as impermanent … [as suffering] … as non-self."

"It is indeed possible, friend, that a once-returner bhikkhu, by attending thoroughly to these five aggregates of clinging as impermanent … [as suffering] … as non-self, might realize the fruit of non-returning.
"But, friend Sāriputta, what things should a bhikkhu who is a non-returner attend to thoroughly?
"Friend Koṭṭhika, a bhikkhu who is a non-returner should also attend thoroughly to these five aggregates of clinging as impermanent … [as suffering] … as non-self."
"But it is possible, friend, that a non-returner bhikkhu, by attending thoroughly to these five aggregates of clinging as impermanent … [as suffering] … as non-self, might realize arhatship.
"But, friend Sāriputta, for one who is an arhat, what things should be attended to thoroughly?

"Friend Koṭṭhika, even for one who is an arhat, these five aggregates of clinging should be attended to thoroughly as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, and as non-self."
“Friend, for an arahant there is nothing further to be done, nor is there any addition to what has been done;
nevertheless, these states, when developed and cultivated, lead to a pleasant dwelling in this very life and to mindfulness and clear comprehension.
The tenth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.123 (SN 22.123, PTS SN iii 169) 12. Dhammakathika-vagga Sutavantasutta “Bhikkhus, those who are learned, those who have heard much, those who have retained what they have heard, those who have stored up what they have heard, those who have investigated the meaning of the teachings they have heard, those who have mastered them through reflection, and those who have penetrated the teachings with wisdom—such persons, bhikkhus, are rare in the world. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, Bhante, are those persons ‘learned, having heard much, having retained what they have heard, having stored up what they have heard, having investigated the meaning of the teachings they have heard, having mastered them through reflection, and having penetrated the teachings with wisdom’? “Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu has heard: ‘Form is impermanent; feeling is impermanent; perception is impermanent; volitional formations are impermanent; consciousness is impermanent. Thus he is learned, having heard much, having retained what he has heard, having stored up what he has heard. Furthermore, bhikkhu, that bhikkhu has investigated the meaning of these teachings, reflected upon them, and examined them with his mind. Thus he has investigated the meaning of the teachings he has heard, mastered them through reflection, and penetrated the teachings with wisdom. Furthermore, bhikkhu, that bhikkhu has understood as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he has understood as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he has understood as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he has understood as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Thus he has investigated the meaning of the teachings he has heard, mastered them through reflection, and penetrated the teachings with wisdom. Those persons, bhikkhu, who are thus learned, having heard much, having retained what they have heard, having stored up what they have heard, having investigated the meaning of the teachings they have heard, having mastered them through reflection, and having penetrated the teachings with wisdom—such persons, bhikkhu, are rare in the world.”
On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, he sat down to one side and said this:
"Friend Sāriputta, what phenomena should a learned bhikkhu attend to wisely?"
“Friend Koṭṭhita, a bhikkhu who is learned should attend wisely to the five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent … as non-self.
Which five?
That is to say: the form aggregate subject to clinging … the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.”
“Friend Koṭṭhita, a learned bhikkhu should attend appropriately to these five aggregates of clinging as impermanent … [as suffering] … as non-self.
It is possible, friend, that a learned bhikkhu, attending appropriately to these five aggregates of clinging as impermanent … as non-self, might realize the fruit of stream-entry.
“But, friend Sāriputta, what things should a bhikkhu who is a stream-enterer attend to appropriately?”
“Friend Koṭṭhita, a bhikkhu who is a stream-enterer should also attend wisely to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent … [as suffering] … as non-self.
It is possible, friend, that while a bhikkhu who is a stream-enterer attends wisely to these five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent … as non-self,
he will realize the fruit of once-returning … the fruit of non-returning …”
“...one might realize the fruit of arahantship.
“But, friend Sāriputta, for the sake of arahantship, what phenomena should be attended to wisely?

“For the sake of arahantship too, friend Koṭṭhika, these five aggregates of clinging should be attended to wisely as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, and as non-self.”
"Friend, for an arahant there is nothing further to be done, nor is there any adding to what has been done.
Nevertheless, these qualities, when developed and cultivated, lead to a pleasant dwelling in this very life and to mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Thus ends the eleventh [discourse].

Whatever feeling there may be … whatever perception there may be … whatever mental formations there may be …

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.130 (SN 22.130, PTS SN iii 173) 13. Avijjāvagga The Second Discourse on Gratification “Bhikkhus, form has gratification, it has danger, it has escape. Feeling has gratification, it has danger, it has escape. Perception has gratification, it has danger, it has escape. Volitional formations have gratification, they have danger, they have escape. Consciousness has gratification, it has danger, it has escape. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the gratification in form? What is the danger in form? What is the escape from form? What is the gratification in feeling? What is the danger in feeling? What is the escape from feeling? What is the gratification in perception? What is the danger in perception? What is the escape from perception? What is the gratification in volitional formations? What is the danger in volitional formations? What is the escape from volitional formations? What is the gratification in consciousness? What is the danger in consciousness? What is the escape from consciousness? “Bhikkhu, the pleasure and joy that arise in dependence on form: this is the gratification in form. That form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger in form. The removal and relinquishment of desire and lust for form: this is the escape from form. The pleasure and joy that arise in dependence on feeling: this is the gratification in feeling. That feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger in feeling. The removal and relinquishment of desire and lust for feeling: this is the escape from feeling. The pleasure and joy that arise in dependence on perception: this is the gratification in perception. That perception is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger in perception. The removal and relinquishment of desire and lust for perception: this is the escape from perception. The pleasure and joy that arise in dependence on volitional formations: this is the gratification in volitional formations. Those volitional formations are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger in volitional formations. The removal and relinquishment of desire and lust for volitional formations: this is the escape from volitional formations. The pleasure and joy that arise in dependence on consciousness: this is the gratification in consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger in consciousness. The removal and relinquishment of desire and lust for consciousness: this is the escape from consciousness. When this was said, that bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit? “Bhikkhu, when one sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘All phenomena are not self,’ then, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit. When this was said, that bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit? “Bhikkhu, when one sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self,’ then, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit. When this was said, that bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit? “Bhikkhu, when one sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is empty of self and of what belongs to self,’ then, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit. When this was said, that bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit? “Bhikkhu, when one sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is cessation, this is nibbāna,’ then, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit. Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.132 (SN 22.132, PTS SN iii 174) 13. Avijjāvagga Dutiyasamudayasutta: The Second Discourse on Origination “Bhikkhus, what is the origin of form? What is the origin of feeling? What is the origin of perception? What is the origin of volitional formations? What is the origin of consciousness? “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and take recourse in the Blessed One. It would be good if the Blessed One would clear up the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from him, the bhikkhus will remember it. “Then listen, bhikkhus, and attend closely. I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, the origin of form is the origin of feeling; the origin of feeling is the origin of perception; the origin of perception is the origin of volitional formations; the origin of volitional formations is the origin of consciousness. “But, venerable sir, what is the origin of form? What is the origin of feeling? What is the origin of perception? What is the origin of volitional formations? What is the origin of consciousness? “Bhikkhus, the craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there—that is the origin of form; that is the origin of feeling; that is the origin of perception; that is the origin of volitional formations; that is the origin of consciousness. “This, bhikkhus, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. [The Blessed One further said: “Now, bhikkhus, this noble truth of the origin of suffering is to be abandoned. And this noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned by me through direct knowledge. The knowledge regarding this noble truth of the origin of suffering has arisen in me, the vision regarding it has arisen, the wisdom regarding it has arisen, the understanding regarding it has arisen, the light regarding it has arisen. “And, bhikkhus, as long as this knowledge and vision of mine regarding these four noble truths—such as they really are—was not thoroughly purified in this way, I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. But when this knowledge and vision of mine regarding these four noble truths—such as they really are—was thoroughly purified in this way, then I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. “The knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘My liberation is unshakable; this is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. (This concludes the second discourse on origination in the Chapter on Ignorance.)

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.142 (SN 22.142, PTS SN iii 178) 14. Kukkuḷavagga Third Discourse on Suffering "Bhikkhus, form is suffering; feeling is suffering; perception is suffering; volitional formations are suffering; consciousness is suffering. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion towards form, revulsion towards feeling, revulsion towards perception, revulsion towards volitional formations, revulsion towards consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion [his mind] is liberated. When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. This, bhikkhus, is called the noble truth of suffering. "Bhikkhus, the origin of form is the origin of suffering; the origin of feeling... the origin of perception... the origin of volitional formations... the origin of consciousness is the origin of suffering. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion towards the origin of form, revulsion towards the origin of feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion [his mind] is liberated. When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. This, bhikkhus, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. "Bhikkhus, the cessation of form is the cessation of suffering; the cessation of feeling... the cessation of perception... the cessation of volitional formations... the cessation of consciousness is the cessation of suffering. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion towards the cessation of form, revulsion towards the cessation of feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion [his mind] is liberated. When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. This, bhikkhus, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. "Bhikkhus, the way leading to the cessation of form is the way leading to the cessation of suffering; the way leading to the cessation of feeling... the way leading to the cessation of perception... the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations... the way leading to the cessation of consciousness is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion towards the way leading to the cessation of form, revulsion towards the way leading to the cessation of feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion [his mind] is liberated. When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. This, bhikkhus, is called the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. "Bhikkhus, as long as this noble truth of suffering has not been fully understood by me—unheard before—so long, bhikkhus, have I not claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. But when this noble truth of suffering was fully understood by me—unheard before—then, bhikkhus, I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. "As long as this noble truth of the origin of suffering had not been abandoned by me—unheard before—so long, bhikkhus, have I not claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.

But when this noble truth of the origin of suffering was abandoned by me—unheard before—then, bhikkhus, I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. "As long as this noble truth of the cessation of suffering had not been realized by me—unheard before—so long, bhikkhus, have I not claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. But when this noble truth of the cessation of suffering was realized by me—unheard before—then, bhikkhus, I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. "As long as this noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering had not been developed by me—unheard before—so long, bhikkhus, have I not claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. But when this noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering was developed by me—unheard before—then, bhikkhus, I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. "The vision arose, bhikkhus, the knowledge arose, the wisdom arose, the true knowledge arose, the light arose in me: ‘My heart’s deliverance is unassailable; this is the last birth; there is now no further becoming.’"

Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.145 (SN 22.145, PTS SN iii 178) 14. Kukkuḷavagga Third Discourse on Non-Self "Bhikkhus, form is non-self. If form were self, this body would not be subject to affliction. It would be possible to have it of form: ‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus. But because form is non-self, this body is subject to affliction, and it is not possible to have it of form: ‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus. "Feeling is non-self... Perception is non-self... Volitional formations are non-self... Consciousness is non-self. If consciousness were self, this body would not be subject to affliction. It would be possible to have it of consciousness: ‘Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus. But because consciousness is non-self, this body is subject to affliction, and it is not possible to have it of consciousness: ‘Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus. "What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent? "Impermanent, venerable sir. "But is what is impermanent suffering or happiness? "Suffering, venerable sir. "But is what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change fit to be regarded thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? "No, venerable sir. "Is feeling permanent or impermanent?... Is perception permanent or impermanent?... Are volitional formations permanent or impermanent?... Is consciousness permanent or impermanent? "Impermanent, venerable sir. "But is what is impermanent suffering or happiness? "Suffering, venerable sir. "But is what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change fit to be regarded thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? "No, venerable sir. "Therefore, bhikkhus, any kind of form whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form should be seen with right wisdom as it actually is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. "Any kind of feeling whatsoever... Any kind of perception whatsoever... Any kind of volitional formations whatsoever... Any kind of consciousness whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness should be seen with right wisdom as it actually is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. "Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion toward form, revulsion toward feeling, revulsion toward perception, revulsion toward volitional formations, and revulsion toward consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion [his mind] is liberated. When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’"
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Monks, whatever is not-self, therein you should abandon desire and lust.

“Bhikkhus, form is not-self; in regard to it, you should abandon desire and lust.
Feeling is not-self… perception is not-self…”
“Volitional formations are non-self … consciousness is non-self; in regard to that, you must abandon desire and lust.
Whatever is non-self, bhikkhus, in regard to that, you must abandon desire and lust.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.153 (SN 22.153, SN 22.152, PTS SN iii 183) 15. Diṭṭhivagga Nocamesiyāsutta “Bhikkhus, there are these six standpoints for views. What six? ‘The world is eternal’—this is the first standpoint for views. ‘The world is not eternal’—this is the second standpoint for views. ‘The world is finite’—this is the third standpoint for views. ‘The world is infinite’—this is the fourth standpoint for views. ‘The soul and the body are the same’—this is the fifth standpoint for views. ‘The soul is one thing and the body another’—this is the sixth standpoint for views. These, bhikkhus, are the six standpoints for views. One who does not cling to these six standpoints for views, does not adhere to them, does not settle upon them, does not hold them as ‘my self,’ and does not say, ‘This alone is the truth, everything else is false’—that person, I say, has transcended all standpoints for views.”

Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.157 (SN 22.157, SN 22.156, PTS SN iii 186) 15. Diṭṭhivagga Abhinivesasutta The Discourse on Insistence At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins, whether past or future, have adhered to a view or will adhere to one, all of them have adhered to it or will adhere to it in these four cases or in these four grounds. What four? ‘The world is eternal’—this is the first case. ‘The world is not eternal’—this is the second case. ‘The world is finite’—this is the third case. ‘The world is infinite’—this is the fourth case. Whatever ascetics or brahmins, whether past or future, have adhered to a view or will adhere to one, all of them have adhered to it or will adhere to it in these four cases or in these four grounds. “Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single case of adherence to a view that is more blameworthy than this: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, this adherence to a view is the root of suffering, the root of vexation, the root of despair, and the root of fever; and for a long time it leads to what is unbeneficial, to suffering, to vexation, and to pain. “Therefore, bhikkhus, you should abandon such adherence to views. And how, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves so as to abandon such adherence to views? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu does not assume form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form in self, nor self in form. He does not assume feeling as self... perception as self... volitional formations as self... consciousness as self, nor self as possessing consciousness, nor consciousness in self, nor self in consciousness. “When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu does not assume form as self... nor self in consciousness, he does not cling to anything in the world; when he does not cling, he is not agitated; when he is not agitated, he personally attains Nibbāna. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. “This, bhikkhus, is how you should train yourselves so as to abandon such adherence to views.”
